articles.title: Your Employees Work Everywhere. Your Infrastructure Has to Follow Them - Tech Guide
articles.text:
For most of the history of corporate IT, infrastructure was built around a place. Employees travelled to an office, connected to a corporate network and accessed applications running in a company data centre.
The boundaries were relatively obvious. IT knew where users were, where applications lived and which networks connected them.
That model has largely disappeared, but many organisations are still operating technology environments shaped by its assumptions.
An employee might now start the day answering emails from home, join a video meeting while travelling, access a cloud-based CRM from a customer site and return to the office in the afternoon. During that same day, they may move between Microsoft 365, an ERP platform, an AI assistant, collaboration software and several SaaS applications. Customers and partners are similarly distributed.
The workplace has become geographically fluid, while the technology supporting it has become more interconnected.
This creates an infrastructure challenge that is easy to underestimate. The objective is no longer simply to connect offices. It is to give people reliable and secure access to the applications, data and services they need, regardless of where any of those things happen to be.
The Office Is No Longer the Centre of the Network
Traditional corporate networks were designed around predictable traffic. Employees connected inside the office and most important applications lived within environments controlled by the organisation. Even remote access was generally treated as an exception to normal working patterns.
Cloud computing, SaaS and hybrid work reversed that relationship.
For many employees, travelling through the corporate office network to reach an application hosted somewhere else can make less sense than connecting directly to the service. At the same time, organisations still need to maintain security, visibility and consistent performance across those interactions.
AI is adding another layer. Employees increasingly use cloud-based AI tools alongside traditional enterprise applications, while software vendors embed AI functionality directly into their platforms. The modern working session may therefore involve connections between a user, identity provider, cloud application, corporate dataset, AI service and several external APIs.
The network has not disappeared. It has become distributed.
That distinction matters because infrastructure strategies designed primarily around locations can struggle when work is increasingly organised around identities, applications and data.
Employees Experience Infrastructure Differently From IT Teams
Infrastructure teams naturally monitor technical indicators such as uptime, latency, bandwidth utilisation and availability. Employees experience infrastructure through something much simpler: whether they can get their work done.
Those two perspectives do not always align.
A network can technically be available while an employee waits repeatedly for a cloud application to respond. Wi-Fi can remain online while video calls become unstable. A remote worker can successfully authenticate yet encounter enough latency to make a business application frustrating to use.
None of these situations necessarily creates a major incident. That is precisely why they can persist.
Employees are remarkably good at adapting to small technology problems. They reconnect to meetings, switch networks, restart applications and create manual workarounds. After a while, they stop raising tickets because they assume the inconvenience is simply part of the system.
This creates a blind spot for organisations. The absence of support tickets does not necessarily indicate the absence of technology friction.
A useful principle for modern infrastructure teams is that reliability should be measured not only by whether systems are available, but by whether people can use them without repeatedly thinking about the infrastructure underneath them.
More Flexibility Creates More Dependencies
There is an operational contradiction at the centre of the modern workplace. Businesses have made technology more flexible for employees while simultaneously making the environment supporting that flexibility more complex.
A salesperson can work from almost anywhere, but their productivity may depend on home broadband, identity services, cloud connectivity, CRM availability, collaboration platforms and security controls all functioning together.
When everything works, that complexity is invisible.
When something fails, ownership becomes much less obvious.
Is the problem the employee’s connection? The corporate network? The cloud provider? The application vendor? Authentication? A security policy? An integration?
Modern technology incidents increasingly cross organisational and vendor boundaries. This means one of the biggest infrastructure challenges is no longer simply fixing individual components. It is understanding the relationships between them.
The complexity is in the connections.
AI Will Put Even More Pressure on Connectivity
The next phase of workplace technology will make this issue more pronounced.
Generative AI is moving from standalone chat interfaces into productivity suites, customer service platforms, development tools, analytics environments and enterprise applications. Increasingly, an employee will not consciously “use AI”. It will simply be part of the applications they already use.
This matters for infrastructure because AI often depends on access to data and services distributed across multiple environments. An employee may request an AI-generated analysis that requires information from a cloud application, corporate database and external service before returning a useful result.
As these interactions become routine, connectivity becomes part of AI performance.
A sophisticated application is of limited value if employees cannot reliably reach the systems and data it depends upon.
This is where managed infrastructure becomes relevant to a broader operational conversation. Monitoring networks, maintaining secure connectivity and understanding performance across hybrid environments are no longer background IT tasks when so much of the employee experience depends on them.
The Cost of Poor Connectivity Is Usually Distributed
A major outage is easy to calculate. Systems stop, employees cannot work and customers may be affected.
Persistent minor friction is harder.
Imagine 500 employees each losing only several minutes per day to slow connections, unstable calls, authentication delays or applications that intermittently fail to respond. There may never be an incident serious enough to reach senior management, yet the accumulated productivity loss can be substantial.
More importantly, technology friction changes behaviour.
Employees avoid unreliable tools. Teams develop alternative workflows. People download information locally because accessing the central system feels too slow. Departments adopt new software to solve problems they believe existing technology cannot handle.
Infrastructure problems can therefore create application sprawl and process inconsistency elsewhere in the organisation.
This is why apparently small connectivity problems deserve more attention than their individual severity suggests. Operational friction compounds.
Infrastructure Has to Follow the Business
The most important change may ultimately be conceptual.
Businesses once built infrastructure around buildings. Increasingly, they need to build connectivity around people, applications and data.
That means understanding how employees actually work rather than assuming where they work. It means considering customer and partner access alongside internal connectivity. It also means recognising that cloud adoption, AI and SaaS are making the corporate technology environment more distributed rather than less dependent on infrastructure.
The organisations that handle this transition well will not necessarily be those with the newest networking technology. They will be the ones that make complexity least visible to the people trying to do their jobs.
As work continues moving across offices, homes, customer locations, cloud platforms and increasingly AI-enabled applications, managed infrastructure becomes less about maintaining a traditional corporate network and more about sustaining secure, reliable connections across a business that no longer has one obvious technological centre.
Employees should not need to understand that complexity.
They should simply be able to work wherever the business requires them to be.

articles.title: Spotify prueba un límite de caché en Android para ahorrar almacenamiento y no eliminar la app
articles.text:
Spotify estaría trabajando en una función de límite de caché para su aplicación de Android que permitiría a los usuarios controlar cuánto espacio de almacenamiento ocupan los archivos temporales.
La herramienta permitiría establecer un máximo para la caché, es decir, los datos que la aplicación guarda de forma temporal para reproducir música y podcast con mayor fluidez y consumir menos datos móviles, según Android Authority.
PUBLICIDAD
Actualmente, Spotify almacena en caché canciones reproducidas en línea, podcast y carátulas de álbumes.
Aunque la plataforma separa ese espacio de las descargas que cada usuario guarda para escuchar sin conexión, la caché puede crecer hasta ocupar varios gigabytes y llenar la memoria del teléfono.
Los usuarios pueden eliminar esos archivos desde Ajustes de Spotify > Ahorro de datos y sin conexión > Borrar caché. Sin embargo, es un proceso manual que puede resultar incómodo para quienes necesitan liberar espacio con frecuencia.
Cómo funcionaría el límite de caché
Según el medio, la versión 9.1.88.815 de Spotify para Android incluye código que sugiere el desarrollo de un apartado llamado “Límite de caché”. Desde allí, los usuarios podrían elegir la cantidad máxima de almacenamiento que la aplicación puede destinar a esos archivos temporales.
PUBLICIDAD
Las cadenas de texto encontradas indican que Spotify explicará las consecuencias de cada elección. Si el límite es demasiado bajo, la aplicación advertirá: “Una caché pequeña puede afectar la reproducción y aumentar el consumo de datos”.
En cambio, un límite más alto permitiría guardar más información temporal. Spotify indicará que “Una caché mayor permite una reproducción más fluida y un menor consumo de datos”.
La aplicación también incluiría un límite recomendado por Spotify. Cuando la función esté disponible, la plataforma pediría a los usuarios que definan ese máximo al borrar la caché.
El límite de caché no afectaría la música ni los podcast descargados para escuchar sin conexión, de acuerdo con las cadenas de texto detectadas en el código.
PUBLICIDAD
La plataforma lanzó en 2019 Spotify Lite, una versión más ligera de su aplicación móvil para Android. La app ocupaba entre 10 MB y 15 MB de espacio de almacenamiento y estaba optimizada para funcionar en teléfonos antiguos o con poca memoria RAM.
Además, permitía establecer un límite para el consumo de datos móviles y enviar alertas automáticas. También incluía una opción para borrar la caché con un solo toque. No obstante, esta versión ya no está disponible, ya que fue discontinuada.
Qué nuevas funciones ha agregado Spotify
Spotify ha incorporado nuevas funciones centradas en la personalización de las recomendaciones, la interacción mediante inteligencia artificial, el ejercicio y el contexto de las playlists.
PUBLICIDAD
Entre las novedades se encuentra “Talk to Spotify”, una experiencia conversacional que permite pedir música mediante mensajes de texto o voz, guardar canciones, seguir artistas y consultar información sobre lo que está sonando.
La herramienta está en beta para usuarios Premium mayores de 18 años en Estados Unidos, Irlanda y Suecia, inicialmente en inglés.
La plataforma también actualizó herramientas para corredores, controles de recomendaciones, listas colaborativas y perfiles familiares. Algunas funciones se encuentran disponibles de forma global, mientras que otras se despliegan de manera limitada según el sistema operativo, el país y el tipo de cuenta.
Spotify sumó además un modo Running dentro de Fitness Hub. La herramienta adapta la música al ritmo y las etapas del entrenamiento, con opciones para definir la duración, los beats por minuto, el estilo musical y el tipo de sesión.
PUBLICIDAD
El modo incluye 25 preajustes para entrenamientos de intervalos, carreras continuas o sesiones de tipo pirámide. Por ahora, está destinado a usuarios Premium de iOS en determinados países y sus indicaciones de audio están disponibles en inglés.
Con Playlist Notes, los usuarios pueden añadir una nota a una playlist propia o colaborativa para explicar su propósito, la selección de canciones o el contexto en el que fue creada.
Los editores de Spotify también pueden incorporar estas notas a algunas listas editoriales. La función está disponible en Android e iOS en más de cien mercados.
Spotify también habilitó un interruptor para evitar que la música infantil o familiar influya en recomendaciones como Discover Weekly, Daily Mix y el resumen anual Wrapped. La opción está disponible a nivel global para cuentas gratuitas y Premium en celulares.

articles.title: GTA 6 : Rockstar lance le coffret collector ultime à 400 euros (sans le jeu à l'intérieur)
articles.text:
Le produit avait d’abord fuité ce jeudi matin. Des fans avaient repéré dans les données du Rockstar Store une liste de 55 produits dérivés, avec cette « Vice City Collection » perdue entre des t-shirts et un tas de goodies, comme l’a rapporté Insider Gaming.
La fiche indiquait un colis lourd, limité à un exemplaire par personne, de quoi faire espérer une vraie édition du jeu. Rockstar l’a officialisé dans la journée et le moins que l’on puisse dire c’est que le contenu est assez décevant.
Que contient le coffret à 400 € ?
Sur le papier, c’est l’édition collector que les fans réclament depuis l’ouverture des précommandes, fin juin. Seulement voilà, la boîte baptisée « Grand Theft Auto VI : The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection » ne contient ni disque ni code de téléchargement. Pour jouer, il faudra payer le jeu en plus, à 79,99 € en édition standard. Le coffret coûte donc à lui seul cinq fois le prix du jeu qu’il accompagne.
Tout tourne autour de Macca the Gator, un alligator mascotte d’une émission de télé fictive de Leonida, l’État inspiré de la Floride où se déroule GTA 6. D’après la fiche du Rockstar Store, la boîte mesure 48 x 33 x 30 cm et n’a pas droit à la livraison gratuite.
On y trouve :
- une figurine de Macca the Gator d’environ 15 cm, avec un compartiment caché ;
- des lunettes de soleil Oakley Frogskins ;
- une casquette New Era ;
- un sac bandoulière Leonida Keys ;
- un miroir magnétique ;
- une cuillère à cocktail ;
- un porte-clés en forme de lame de rasoir ;
- un verre à shot ;
- des pin’s dans une boîte en métal ;
- des autocollants ;
- et un poster recto verso.
Pour le jeu lui-même, rien ne change. Rockstar ne vend toujours que deux éditions, la standard à 79,99 € et l’Ultimate à 99,99 €, cette dernière uniquement en numérique. Une version en boîte, qui on le rappelle, ne contient qu’un code de téléchargement, un choix que Strauss Zelnick, CEO de Take-Two, maison mère de Rockstar, a défendu en août.
Le collector de GTA V coûtait 130 €, jeu compris
En 2013, on pouvait acheter l’Édition Collector de GTA V pour 129,99 €. Elle comprenait déjà une casquette New Era, un sac de sécurité avec sa clé, un boîtier métallique, une carte de Los Santos et plusieurs bonus en jeu. Et surtout, l’exemplaire de GTA V était dans la boîte. Une précision qui semblait assez superflue à l’époque.
Pourtant, le procédé n’est pas nouveau chez Rockstar. En 2018, le studio vendait déjà une « Collector’s Box » pour Red Dead Redemption 2 : une boîte métallique à cadenas, une pièce et quelques babioles, sans le jeu, pour environ 100 €. Huit ans plus tard, le prix a été multiplié par quatre.
Ce nouveau coffret s’ajoute à la liste de produits dérivés : les manettes DualSense aux couleurs de GTA 6 à 84,99 € pièce ou encore l’album officiel en CD et en vinyle dans une période marketing déjà bien entamée par le studio.

articles.title: Apple vai corrigir bug que trava e reinicia o iPhone 18 Pro • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Apple vai corrigir bug que trava e reinicia o iPhone 18 Pro
Atualização deve ser liberada na próxima semana. Falha faz aparelhos reiniciarem após Face ID não reconhecer o rosto.
A Apple prepara uma atualização de software para corrigir o bug que faz alguns iPhone 18 Pro e iPhone 18 Pro Max travarem e reiniciarem após falha de autenticação pelo Face ID. A correção deve ser liberada no início da próxima semana.
A informação foi divulgada pelo site 9to5Mac nesta quinta-feira (24/09). Os primeiros relatos do problema surgiram no começo desta semana e, inicialmente, levantaram suspeitas de uma possível falha de hardware nos aparelhos.
O problema aparece após um erro de autenticação pelo Face ID dentro de aplicativos protegidos. Nos testes conduzidos pelo 9to5Mac, o iPhone deixou de responder aos comandos por toque e reiniciou alguns segundos depois. O portal conseguiu reproduzir a falha ao tentar acessar o aplicativo Passwords com o rosto parcialmente coberto pela mão.
Também foi encontrado um registro de “panic” na seção de análise do sistema após a reinicialização. Esse tipo de registro é criado quando o sistema enfrenta uma falha grave que força uma reinicialização.
Ainda assim, o problema não parece afetar todos os usuários do iPhone 18 Pro, mas relatos de casos semelhantes apareceram nas redes sociais.
Antes da confirmação da Apple, alguns clientes chegaram a substituir seus iPhones por novas unidades por acreditarem que as reinicializações poderiam estar relacionadas a um defeito físico. No entanto, a troca não deve ser necessária, já que a empresa confirmou uma correção por software.
A Apple não informou exatamente o que provoca o bug, mas os iPhone 18 Pro e 18 Pro Max estrearam uma versão redesenhada do sistema Face ID. A câmera infravermelha passou a ficar posicionada sob a parte inferior da tela, perto da região ocupada pelo relógio na barra de status. A mudança permitiu reduzir em 25% o tamanho da Ilha Dinâmica.

articles.title: We are telling AI chatbots our biggest secrets, but Proton warns our privacy is at huge risk
articles.text:
We are telling AI chatbots our biggest secrets, but Proton warns our privacy is at huge risk
A new Proton survey shows two-thirds of Brits are using AI as a judgment-free confidant, despite having major trust issues when it comes to their data privacy
- 66% of UK AI users have discussed highly sensitive topics with a chatbot
- Yet, 64% of respondents are worried that chats will be used to profile them
- Proton's privacy-first chatbot, Lumo, aims to fix this trust gap
Late at night, when you need to vent about a relationship, ask for career advice, or check a worrying health symptom, who do you turn to? For a rapidly growing number of people, it isn't a friend, family member, or doctor; it's a chatbot.
A new piece of research published today by Proton, the Swiss tech firm behind some of the best VPN services on the market, reveals that a staggering 66% of British AI users have discussed at least one sensitive topic with an artificial intelligence assistant.
However, there is a massive contradiction at the heart of this new digital relationship: we are pouring our hearts out to these chatbots, but we do not actually trust them. According to the survey, 42% of UK users have little or no trust in AI companies to protect their private information, and 11% don't trust them at all.
Despite these glaring privacy reservations, 55% of Brits admit that AI has fundamentally changed their everyday decision-making.
Proton VPN – best for privacy 
Based in Switzerland, this privacy-first VPN offers good speeds, advanced anti-censorship features, and a server network that spans 145 countries around the world — including across Africa and Asia, where other providers tend to struggle. While its free VPN plan is handy, it comes with limitations. The good news is that upgrading to a premium subscription will cost you only the equivalent of $2.99 per month.
The ultimate judgment-free zone
So, why are we sharing our most intimate thoughts with machines we don't trust? The answer is simple: freedom from judgment.
While friends and family remain the preferred choice for most sensitive discussions, AI offers a 24/7 digital confidant that won't react with surprise or embarrassment.
Proton's data shows personal finance is the most commonly discussed sensitive topic (33%), followed closely by work or career problems (32%), mental health struggles (27%), and relationship issues (20%).
"AI is learning far more about us than a search engine ever could," said Eamonn Maguire, Director of AI Engineering at Proton. "We’re not just asking questions. We’re sharing deeply personal context about our health, finances and relationships. And when technology knows that much about us, privacy can't be an afterthought."
The primary worry isn't just about the AI remembering a single chat, or even the risk of human reviewers reading your logs. Users are increasingly terrified of the bigger picture.
In the UK, 64% of respondents are concerned that their vulnerable conversations are being weaponized to build detailed advertising or marketing profiles. Meanwhile, 52% are worried their secrets are being fed back into the machine to train future AI models.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
How Lumo promises a private alternative
Despite these valid fears, Brits are highly receptive to a more secure way forward. A massive 82% of users said they would be more likely to use an AI chatbot specifically designed around privacy, and 44% would be far more willing to share sensitive information if they were given a cast-iron guarantee that their chats wouldn't be used for AI training.
This is exactly where Proton hopes to fill the gap with Lumo. Built with the same end-to-end encryption ethos as the company's famous email client, Lumo is an open-source, privacy-first ChatGPT alternative.
To help users understand the scale of their digital footprint, Proton recently launched AI Paper Trail, a tool from Lumo that visually demonstrates exactly how much personal information an average AI conversation leaks about a user's inner life.
"People have already decided that AI is useful enough to hear their money worries, doubts and everyday concerns. They are handing AI companies their inner lives and biggest secrets on the assumption that they will protect them when it's actually the opposite. AI's business model depends on learning from them" Maguire added.

articles.title: TI's October Price Hike: How to Secure ADI/TI Stock - EE Times
articles.text:
TI has officially announced another round of price increases, effective October 1st. For procurement teams and engineers around the world, this means longer lead times, tighter allocation from the original manufacturer, and spot-market spreads widening fast — while most supply chains simply can’t react in time.
The question is no longer whether prices will move. It’s whether your supply chain is ready when they do.
Every price adjustment from a manufacturer sends a ripple through the entire market. Contract customers wait for allocation. Spot buyers scramble for whatever is left. And somewhere in between, production schedules quietly slip. The companies that come out ahead in moments like this are rarely the ones with the biggest budgets — they are the ones who already have the right parts on the shelf, and a partner who picks up the phone.
That is exactly the position SKYEAST has built for itself.
Stock on Hand, One Step Ahead of Demand
Founded in 2015 and headquartered in Shenzhen, SKYEAST is a professional company engaged in electronic component sourcing and distribution. We work with renowned semiconductor brands worldwide, dedicating ourselves to providing comprehensive, high-quality, and efficient products and services to our customers.
In a market defined by volatility, inventory is leverage. When the manufacturer raises prices, buyers who stocked up early hold the advantage — and the gap between contract pricing and spot availability often decides whether a production line keeps running.
SKYEAST currently holds over $30 million in ready stock, covering industrial, automotive, AI, and other key applications. TI sits at the core of our product line, supported by ADI and MAXIM as key brands, covering analog, signal processing, and power management components across the full range of mainstream demand — serving R&D and mass production across industrial control, automotive electronics, smart devices, consumer electronics, and more.
We operate dual warehouses in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, with business reaching markets across the US, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Japan, Singapore, Australia, Canada, and beyond. Our product portfolio spans everything from 3C to industrial, automotive, and medical electronics, from basic to core components — meeting the diverse procurement needs of our customers.
But depth of stock is only half the story. What matters just as much is how that stock is managed. Our rolling pre-stock programs are built around each customer’s production plan, positioning inventory ahead of demand rather than chasing after it. For buyers who have watched one shipment slip too many times, that difference is everything.
The point isn’t simply having parts. It’s having the right parts, in the right place, at the right time.
Response Speed Is the Real Differentiator
In a fast-moving market, how quickly a supplier responds can matter more than the price itself. A quote that arrives two days late is a quote that arrives after the decision has already been made.
SKYEAST commits to quotes within two hours, with 7×24 online inquiry support across all time zones. For overseas buyers, that means no waiting overnight for a reply, no missed windows, and no guessing games while a competitor moves first.
And for orders placed before October 31st, we are holding quotes valid for a full week — giving buyers the room to plan, compare, and commit without being chased by a price that shifts by the hour.
Around our customers’ needs, we have built five core services: Global Strategic Solutions, Quick Inventory Response Support, Quality Inspection Services, Replacement Selection Support, and Financial Support Services. From component selection to delivery, from technical coordination to financial arrangements — one-stop coverage that makes procurement simple.
Trust Built on Consistency, Not Promises
In a rising market, the two things buyers care about most are the two things we take most seriously.
The first is price stability. When the manufacturer raises prices, many suppliers pass that increase straight through — sometimes mid-order, sometimes onto customers who had already agreed to terms. SKYEAST does not. We do not raise prices on contract customers simply because the manufacturer did. An order placed is an order honored.
The second is quality. Every shipment passes through a full-process inspection by our independent quality department, operating under an ISO9001-certified system. Products are checked for appearance, performance, and parameter accuracy, and every batch is traceable and verifiable. It is this discipline that has kept us at a zero major quality incident record — and kept our customers coming back.
That record was not built overnight. Over the years, SKYEAST has served more than 5,000 customers, with over 3,000 long-term partners who return order after order. In an industry where suppliers come and go with every market cycle, that kind of consistency says more than any advertisement could.
A Partner for the Long Run
Behind our service capability sits a stable and carefully built supply chain. We work closely with original manufacturers and have established long-term strategic relationships with experienced solution providers and spot suppliers across the domestic market. That foundation allows us to keep supply stable, pricing transparent, and lead times controllable — responding quickly to market shifts and customer demand alike.
Our vision is to be the preferred integrated service provider of electronic components for our global customers. Our mission is to provide global customers with the highest quality electronic components distribution services, improve the efficiency of global electronic intelligence, and promote technological progress and social development. Embrace change, honest and upright, optimistic and never give up, professional and persistent — these are not slogans on a wall, but what we do every day.
Beyond supply, we offer the kind of support that turns a vendor into a partner: component selection guidance, solution optimization, and technical coordination, all designed to lower R&D costs and shorten time to market. For customers navigating a price increase while trying to hit a launch date, that combination is what truly works.
The Window Is Open Now
The October price adjustment is coming. Buyers who prepare now will be the ones who stay ahead — and buyers who wait will be the ones paying spot premiums later.
If you are sourcing TI or ADI components and want to lock in stable supply before the market moves, now is the time to reach out. We are online around the clock, and we will get you a quote within two hours.

articles.title: Alternative zum Task-Manager: Dieses kostenlose Windows-Tool kann mehr als Microsofts Lösung
articles.text:
Alternative zum Task-Manager: Dieses kostenlose Windows-Tool kann mehr als Microsofts Lösung
Wer Windows nutzt, kennt wahrscheinlich auch die Tastenkombination „Strg + Alt + Entf“. Über den Shortcut rufst du den Task-Manager des Betriebssystems auf. Dort werden alle laufenden Programme angezeigt und du kannst dir einen Überblick verschaffen, wie stark CPU, GPU, Festplatten und dein Netzwerk aktuell von den Programmen in Windows ausgelastet werden.
Diese Informationen dürften für die meisten Windows-User:innen mehr als ausreichen. Das ist primär dann der Fall, wenn sie den Task-Manager nur nutzen, um stehen gebliebene Programme zu beenden. Doch wer mehr über seinen Windows-PC und mögliche Fehlerquellen lernen will, sollte auf eine quelloffene Task-Manager-Alternative zurückgreifen.
System Informer: Task-Manager mit Superkräften
Das Tool trägt den Namen „System Informer“ und kann kostenlos auf der zugehörigen Webseite oder im Microsoft Store heruntergeladen werden. Nach der Installation wird schnell ersichtlich, warum es eine starke Alternative zum Task-Manager von Windows ist. System Informer geht bei allen laufenden Anwendungen deutlich tiefer ins Detail und zeigt neben den Hauptprozessen auch Unterprozesse, die möglicherweise Probleme verursachen können.
Das ist in Kombination mit der Tastenkombination „Strg + F“ nützlich. Dadurch aktivierst du die Suchfunktion und kannst einzelne Programme aus der Liste herauspicken. Gibt es etwa ein Programm, das sich nicht schließen lässt, weil es von anderen Apps benutzt wird, kannst du nach dem Programm selbst suchen. System Informer zeigt dir dann alle Tasks und Apps an, die auf diese Anwendung zugreifen. Beendest du sie, sollten auch die Fehlermeldungen ein Ende haben.
Über die Tastenkombination „Strg + I“ können die Systeminformationen aufgerufen werden. Wie beim Task-Manager werden hier die Auslastungen von CPU, Arbeitsspeicher und Co. gezeigt. Allerdings kannst du in System Informer den Graphen mit der Maus abfahren und dabei nicht nur sehen, wann wie viele Ressourcen verbraucht wurden, sondern auch, welches Programm daran den Hauptanteil getragen hat. So lassen sich schneller ressourcenhungrige Apps ausfindig machen.
„Tastenkombination „Strg + Alt + Entf“. Über den Shortcut rufst du den Task-Manager des Betriebssystems auf.“ Das ist Quatsch. Den TM ruft man mit STRG-Shift-Esc auf. Der Affengriff Str-Alt-Entf ruft dagegen ein Minimenü mit mehreren Optionen auf, darunter auch der Taskmanager. Ist halt umständlicher.

articles.title: How Meta says it's addressing privacy concerns amid new smart glasses lineup
articles.text:
It’s no secret that Meta has privacy issues.
After all, there’s been a lot of apprehension surrounding the company’s ever-growing lineup of smart glasses. In particular, these products have sometimes been called “pervert glasses” due to being used to harass people and, according to a recent lawsuit, even allegedly capture and share intimate images without consent.
Naturally, this was a big topic of discussion during a media roundtable at Meta’s Menlo Park, California, headquarters. Speaking with Ming Hua, VP of wearable devices, MobileSyrup and several other international outlets had some questions about Meta’s continued approach to addressing privacy concerns with its products.
“Privacy is always front and centre when we design [wearables],” said Hua. “Actually, from the first generation, we’ve had a privacy LED, where it’s signalling to people when you are capturing. So that continues to be very core.”
However, we’ve seen instances where people have covered up the LED to remove that layer of transparency, and a quick Google search will show countless products that are specifically designed to do just that. To address this, Hua points out, Meta recently closed a loophole that allowed cameras to cover the light after recording had begun without issue.
“We’ll continue to make sure that the algorithm is very robust, and also really bring awareness about how things work,” she added, referring to a recent marketing campaign that promotes the glasses’ privacy features.
She also cited a new feature that was announced at Connect 2026: private processing. This technology, which is already used to encrypt WhatsApp chats, will allow glasses to keep data used by AI features secure and inaccessible even from Meta. During the Connect 2026 keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg confirmed that private processing will be rolled out “soon” to features like Live Translations before expanding to “more and more” features.
When asked about how the discussion surrounding “pervert glasses” influences Meta’s approach to privacy, Hua stressed that moderation in addition to all of the aforementioned initiatives, content moderation is a big focus for Meta.
“We’re also taking actions to take down the content that’s not good,” she said. “[We] take down the accounts if they continuously violate the platform policy, and also [are] blocking the search terms. We also are taking down content that teach people how to tamper with glasses.”
Time will tell what else Meta may do to improve privacy. In the meantime, it should be noted that the company just unveiled a new pair of audio-only glasses that remove the camera entirely.

articles.title: Nouveau déluge de failles Chrome : Google corrige plus de 100 vulnérabilités, dont 11 brèches critiques
articles.text:
Google vient de lancer le déploiement de Chrome 154 sur Windows, macOS et Linux. L’éditeur colmate d’un seul coup 108 vulnérabilités. C’est nettement plus qu’à l’accoutumée. On reste néanmoins loin des 400 failles corrigées en juillet dernier.
11 failles critiques de Chrome
Parmi les 108 failles, on trouve 11 vulnérabilités critiques. Le niveau « critique » est le plus haut degré de gravité chez Google. Ce niveau désigne les failles qui permettent à un pirate de prendre le contrôle de l’ordinateur, simplement en poussant l’internaute à visiter une page web piégée. Plusieurs des brèches critiques concernent ANGLE, le composant graphique de Chrome qui traduit les commandes d’affichage pour les adapter aux différentes cartes graphiques. On recense plusieurs problèmes de mémoire. Un bug du même acabit touche WebGL, la technologie qui affiche des graphismes 3D dans le navigateur.
D’autres failles critiques visent le composant GPU, chargé de dialoguer avec la carte graphique. Google a colmaté deux vulnérabilités de type « écriture hors limites », capables d’aboutir à la corruption de la mémoire de l’ordinateur. Google a aussi corrigé plusieurs bugs estampillés « use-after-free ». Ces failles découlent de l’utilisation d’une zone mémoire qui n’est plus libre par le programme. Ce type de faille est très prisé des pirates. Dans certaines conditions, elles permettent de manipuler la mémoire du navigateur pour y exécuter du code malveillant sans la moindre autorisation.
Des failles graves dans V8
Au-delà des failles critiques, Chrome 154 comble 25 vulnérabilités de gravité « élevée ». On y trouve une douzaine de bugs relatifs à la mémoire et plusieurs bugs dans V8, le moteur qui exécute le code JavaScript des sites web. Deux des failles de V8 ont été signalées par l’équipe de sécurité d’OpenAI, qui s’est servie de l’IA pour analyser le code de Chrome.
À lire aussi : Google colmate plus de 40 nouvelles failles Chrome, installez la mise à jour sans tarder
Sur les 108 failles corrigées, 32 ont été découvertes par des chercheurs extérieurs à Google. La firme a donc versé 18 000 dollars de primes aux chercheurs. Les autres brèches ont été débusquées en interne, grâce à des outils automatisés.
Bonne nouvelle, Google assure n’avoir constaté aucune preuve que des pirates ont exploité les failles pour lancer des cyberattaques. Par précaution, la firme américaine garde tout de même secret certains détails techniques, tant que la majorité des internautes n’a pas installé la mise à jour. Quoi qu’il en soit, on vous invite à mettre à jour votre navigateur sans tarder. Ouvrez le menu de Chrome, rendez-vous dans « Aide », puis dans « À propos de Google Chrome ». La mise à jour se télécharge alors toute seule et s’applique après un redémarrage du navigateur.

articles.title: Groundcover picks up Kubernetes optimization startup Wand in its first acquisition - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Groundcover picks up Kubernetes optimization startup Wand in its first acquisition
Observability company groundcover Inc. today disclosed its first acquisition, picking up Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd. for an undisclosed sum.
Wand’s founders and employees are moving across to groundcover as part of the deal. The purchase is part of a push by groundcover toward what it calls autonomous infrastructure, with software taking action on production systems directly.
The groundcover platform collects telemetry from applications and infrastructure. Under a bring-your-own-cloud model, the resulting production history stays inside each customer’s own cloud account.
Engineers and artificial intelligence agents use the data to investigate problems and work out what changed. Wand’s technology adds the ability to make and carry out decisions about live Kubernetes clusters, based on how workloads actually behave.
Wand targets the processor and memory requests Kubernetes asks engineers to set in advance, usually before a workload has run under real load. Overestimate and the wasted capacity is multiplied across every replica and node. A request set too low risks throttling and outages when traffic shifts. Even a correct setting drifts out of date as services change.
Kubernetes autoscalers already take on parts of that job. According to groundcover, the vertical, horizontal and cluster-level versions typically run independently of one another. A tighter resource request pushes measured utilization up, for example, and the horizontal autoscaler may respond by adding replicas that are not needed. Workload packing on the nodes then shifts, and so does the cluster autoscaler’s behavior.
Wand’s software sits inside the cluster and makes all three kinds of scaling decisions at once. Engineers are not left with a queue of right-sizing recommendations to work through later, because central processing unit and memory allocations change on live infrastructure as demand moves. Wand said it tunes a cluster for performance and availability first, with cost savings following once unneeded headroom is stripped out.
Shon Lev-Ran, Wand’s co-founder and chief executive, said right-sizing “assumes we know the future.” Infrastructure changes continuously, he said, and joining groundcover gives Wand a much deeper view of what is happening across production.
Groundcover’s case for the deal rests on that deeper view. A workload can look overprovisioned when judged on the past hour and still be sized correctly for the traffic that arrives every Monday morning, the company said. Production data is kept at high fidelity on its platform, so teams do not have to decide ahead of time what to sample or throw away.
Groundcover co-founder and Chief Executive Shahar Azulay said production data is increasingly the context AI agents rely on to build, fix and run software.
“For infrastructure to become autonomous, systems also need to act safely on what they know,” Azulay said. “Wand has spent years building exactly that capability for Kubernetes.”
The company plans to use Wand’s technology in two places. The first is groundcover’s own platform, which runs inside customer cloud accounts. Whatever it consumes shows up on those customers’ cloud bills, and a leaner footprint should make it cheaper for them to keep more telemetry at full fidelity. The second is putting Wand’s Kubernetes resource optimization directly in the hands of groundcover customers. No timeline was given.
Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July. Other investors in the company include Morgan Stanley Expansion Capital, Zeev Ventures, Angular Ventures, Heavybit and Jibe.

articles.title: 5 Lessons from the Grammar of Silence by R Seshasayee
articles.text:
5 Lessons from the Grammar of Silence by R Seshasayee
Discover 5 powerful lessons from The Grammar of Silence on resilience, courage, identity, and challenging social barriers.
History is often told through the stories of kings, leaders, and revolutions. Yet some of the most remarkable acts of courage happen quietly, far from the spotlight. In The Grammar of Silence: Five Centuries.
Three Women. Towards Liberation, R. Seshasayee follows the lives of three women, Dharma, Vinodhini, and Mary Amelia, as they navigate the constraints of patriarchy, caste, and social expectations across different periods of Tamil history. Through their journeys, the novel explores resilience, agency, and the enduring pursuit of freedom.
5 Thought-provoking lessons from the book
1. Silence does not always mean surrender
One of the novel's most compelling ideas is that silence can sometimes be a form of strength rather than weakness. The women in the story often face situations where open rebellion is impossible, yet they find subtle ways to challenge the systems that seek to control them. Their quiet determination becomes a tool for survival and resistance.
The book encourages readers to rethink the assumption that power only exists in loud acts of defiance. Sometimes resilience is found in persistence, patience, and refusing to give up one's sense of self.
2. Courage takes many forms
The protagonists come from different backgrounds and eras, but each demonstrates courage in her own way. Whether it is questioning restrictive traditions, seeking independence, or pursuing opportunities that society denies them, their actions show that bravery is not limited to dramatic gestures.
The novel reminds readers that courage often appears in everyday decisions: the choice to keep learning, keep hoping, and keep moving forward despite obstacles.
3. Social barriers are powerful but not permanent
Throughout the story, caste, gender, and social status shape the lives of the characters. Yet the novel also shows that these barriers, while deeply entrenched, can be challenged and overcome. The journeys of Dharma, Vinodhini, and Mary Amelia reveal the possibility of change even within restrictive systems.
This lesson remains relevant today. Progress may be slow, but history is filled with individuals who expanded opportunities for those who came after them.
4. Identity should not be defined by society alone
The women in the novel are frequently judged according to the roles society assigns them. However, each character struggles to define herself on her own terms rather than accepting the limitations others impose. Their stories highlight the importance of self-belief and personal agency.
The book suggests that true empowerment begins when people stop allowing external labels to determine their worth and potential.
5. Shared struggles can create lasting solidarity
Although the protagonists live in different centuries, their experiences are connected by common themes of perseverance and resistance. The novel emphasises the importance of solidarity among women and how one generation's struggles can inspire the next.
Readers are reminded that personal victories rarely exist in isolation. Every act of courage can create possibilities for others, building a legacy that extends far beyond a single lifetime.
Why these lessons matter
The Grammar of Silence is more than a historical novel. It is a reflection on how ordinary people confront extraordinary challenges and how change often begins with small acts of determination. Through the lives of its three protagonists, the book explores themes of resilience, identity, and liberation that continue to resonate in the modern world.
Its greatest lesson may be that even when voices are ignored or silenced, the desire for dignity, freedom, and self-expression endures across generations.

articles.title: Flock is finally requiring police to have a real reason before searching its camera database
articles.text:
What just happened? Flock Safety is changing how police search its license plate camera database as the company faces growing questions in Washington over privacy, accuracy, and misuse. The company told Senator Josh Hawley that it has added more controls to its search system, which scans about 20 billion license plates a month.
Until recently, users were required to explain why they were conducting a search by typing into an open text field. Flock said those entries were not always specific enough. The company has replaced the field with a drop-down menu of standardized categories based on the FBI's crime-reporting system.
By the end of the year, law enforcement users will also need to enter a case number before running a search. Flock said that requirement can be waived in emergencies.
The changes were outlined in a letter from Flock's chief legal officer to Hawley, the Missouri Republican who opened an investigation into the company last month. Hawley led a Senate hearing on Wednesday examining Flock and three other companies that provide similar surveillance technology.
The hearing featured a Florida woman who spent 13 days in jail after her car was detected by a Flock camera near the scene of a fatal crash. Authorities were looking for a similar vehicle.
Flock's automated license plate recognition system has spread quickly. The company says it has about 120,000 cameras nationwide. Police departments and public-safety officials argue that the technology can help find missing children, track stolen vehicles, and investigate hit-and-run crashes.
The system has also drawn criticism from privacy advocates, civil-liberties groups, and people on both sides of the political divide. Critics are concerned that agencies can use the cameras to follow a person's movements over time. They also point to allegations that some officers have used the system for personal reasons, including stalking.
Flock said it does not maintain "a single consolidated count of confirmed customer misuse." The company said its customers determine whether a search was justified and whether discipline is appropriate when an employee abuses access.
The company has also started adding its own monitoring tools. In April, it introduced a system designed to flag unusual search activity. Flock said the system has identified several cases of misuse, including some that led to arrests. It is also working on a feature that would lock users out when their behavior appears abnormal.
Hawley said the issue could prompt congressional action. "We have an entire constitutional system to protect individual liberty," he told The Wall Street Journal. Without limits from companies or the government, he added, "we're going to have a huge problem with the invasion of basic rights and liberties."
The company is also reducing the amount of data it stores by default. New customers will have a seven-day retention period, down from 30 days. Existing customers will have to opt in if they want the shorter period.
Agencies can still seek permission to retain data longer, but Flock said those requests must be approved "either by an elected governing body...or by an elected official." The company said about 3% of its law-enforcement customers keep data for more than 30 days. Its maximum retention period is one year.

articles.title: The three-pronged future of custom PC building — from repurposing forgotten parts to ultra-premium works of gaming art
articles.text:
The three-pronged future of custom PC building — from repurposing forgotten parts to ultra-premium works of gaming art
How and why PC building and PC gaming have a future worth looking forward to
With RAMageddon, the storage apocalypse, GPU stagnation, and GPU price increases all happening more or less simultaneously, this is the worst time to build a PC that I can remember — and I built my first PC in the previous century (powered by an AMD K6-2). If you have a rig that meets your needs at the moment (even if just barely), current prices probably make you more interested in keeping it running than in considering major upgrades or, even more daunting, starting over from scratch with a new build.
But fret as we might about the future of our much-beloved component-swapping hobby, a few articles and experiences in recent weeks have given me glimpses of the PC-building future, and I don’t think it’s all bad — at least so long as you have time to research and tinker, you can live without the highest-end components, or you have enough of a build budget that price doesn’t matter much.
Old parts get a new life, with some patient tweaking
First off, we recently tested AMD’s BC-250, a 2021-era APU that started off as defective or cut-down PS5 silicon, repurposed as a cryptomining card. But more recently, a community-developed BIOS and drivers have turned this custom hardware into a Linux-based competitor to Valve’s much-hyped Steam Machine, while costing roughly half the price of a similarly configured system, once you source the power supply and other necessary parts. It even comes with 16GB of shared GDDR6, sidestepping the current RAM pricing issue altogether. 
Now, this is more of a project than a PC. You have to source the card (from places like AliExpress, eBay, or Etsy), then research and figure out how to flash the board so that it will even boot, followed by getting Linux and the requisite drivers installed, before you can even think about playing games. But depending on your sample, you might also be able to unlock extra CPU cores and compute units for even better performance.
It’s far from a simple setup. But this kind of community-led hardware repurposing and enhancement reminds me of two distinct hardware eras: The very early days of PC kits (which I wasn’t really around for), and the early 2000s, when you could unlock AMD Athlon and Duron multipliers with a pencil (or later, conductive silver lacquer). Unlocking higher clocks and extra performance without paying for a much pricier chip is exactly the kind of achievable dream that the PC enthusiast hobby was founded on, and it’s good to see it making a comeback – even if it’s with this one very specific piece of hardware. 
But as AI hardware development continues — and especially if (or when) specific areas of the hardware bubble pop or deflate – I expect to see more situations where communities of tinkerers figure out how to get discarded hardware to run games and other compute tasks, giving budget buyers hope for acceptable performance at reasonable prices. Ironically, AI tools like Claude Code will almost certainly make breakthroughs in hardware repurposing much easier.
To boldly go (to price brackets) where no PC has gone before
On the other end of the PC price spectrum, I recently assembled a PC using parts from Asus’ ROG Edition 20 line. The anniversary hardware, which debuted earlier this year at Computex, ignores affordability concerns entirely. Asus instead opted to celebrate two decades of its Republic of Gamers sub-brand by taking several of its already expensive parts and peripherals, adding a few (mostly aesthetic) features and some gold accents, and charging even more for them. 
How much more? The finished PC, with about $2,000 worth of peripherals, a $3,300 motherboard and cooler combo, and a $6,000 RTX 5090, costs roughly $15,000 – and that’s with a modest 2TB SSD and 32GB of RAM. If you opt for a more fitting 128GB kit with tight timings and 8TB of solid-state storage, you could easily spend $20,000 on a build like this.
As tough as it is for many of us to swallow, there’s likely a large enough customer base of gamers and PC enthusiasts who can and will pay whatever it takes to own high-end, high-performance PCs to keep options like this afloat. Because while the cost of individual parts has certainly increased, the luxury PC market has existed for decades. I know because in the years before I joined Tom’s Hardware, I reviewed several PCs with custom cooling loops and multiple graphics cards (up to quad-SLI) from the likes of Digital Storm and Maingear. That market isn’t going away; it’s just getting more expensive.
The murky future of mainstream desktop gaming PCs
So what about the mainstream PC gaming market? Things are tougher there, and I suspect that space will continue to shrink due to, well, everything I linked to up top. Those looking for gaming options in the sub-$2,000 range that “just work” without much tinkering are more likely to make do with consoles (which are, of course, also getting more expensive), gaming laptops or handhelds, or console-like PCs like Valve’s Steam Machine.
Intel and AMD are reviving or extending the lifespan of chips and platforms that support last-gen DDR4, but older memory isn’t getting any cheaper either. And our own testing has shown that DDR4 is increasingly holding back gaming performance.
There was a brief hope that Chinese memory makers like CXMT might help bring down DDR5 prices. But U.S. approval for that seems unlikely, especially as the FCC is busy banning humanoid robots and robot vacuum cleaners built overseas. And, of course, companies like CXMT aren’t looking to be PC saviors. They want to sell their RAM to AI hyperscalers for the same high prices as SK hynix, Micron, and Samsung. And even if DDR5 somehow suddenly became more affordable, GPU prices are also continuing to climb, and storage (SSDs and hard drives) faces similar pricing issues.
Can software save the day?
Like it or not, we’ll certainly see further advancements in AI upscaling and other VRAM tweaks and tricks that make modern gaming possible on older and current-gen cards with 8GB or even 4GB of VRAM before the price of RAM, storage, and GPUs drop significantly. 
Will it be enough to keep PC gaming enticing and affordable enough to prop up the mainstream PC gaming market? That’s tough to say with any certainty at this point, but if being a PC enthusiast since the 1990s (and a PC gamer since the late 1980s) has taught me one thing, it’s that this hobby is resilient. Some will pay what they need to pay for high-end hardware. Some will find suitable solutions by tinkering with repurposed silicon. And others will forge a middle ground that works for them.
I transitioned from a PC enthusiast to a full-time professional covering the PC and related hardware space in 2008. Even back then, people were telling me that the desktop was dead or dying. Instead, it has evolved and survived for nearly 20 years, through the smartphone revolution, past soldered-on laptop components, through two cycles of Steam Machines, and the death of physical game media. Meanwhile, game stores like Steam rake in record profits, indicating that the demand for PC gaming remains high. All this tells me that PC building and PC gaming will need to continue to evolve, but it’s not quite on the endangered hardware list yet.
After a rough start with the Mattel Aquarius as a child, Matt built his first PC in the late 1990s and ventured into mild PC modding in the early 2000s. He’s spent the last 15 years covering emerging technology for Smithsonian, Popular Science, and Consumer Reports, while testing components and PCs for Computer Shopper, PCMag and Digital Trends.

articles.title: Explorateur, touche Copilot, Bluetooth… la dernière mise à jour de Windows 11 fait le plein de nouveautés et de correctifs
articles.text:
Windows 11 reçoit une nouvelle mise à jour facultative bien chargée. Microsoft y déploie plusieurs fonctions testées ces dernières semaines et corrige une série de bugs apparus en septembre.
L’Explorateur évolue, la touche Copilot se reconvertit
Annoncée dès le mois d’août dernier, la première nouveauté concerne l’Explorateur de fichiers, pour lequel Microsoft a finalement accepté d’assouplir les restrictions imposées à l’aperçu des fichiers téléchargés sur Internet. Les PDF et autres formats non HTML peuvent de nouveau s’afficher directement dans le volet prévu à cet effet, tandis que les fichiers HTML affichent toujours un avertissement, désormais accompagné d’un bouton « Afficher quand même » pour passer outre.
En parallèle, la page d’accueil mémorise l’état de ses sections. Si vous repliez « Récent », par exemple, elle apparaîtra encore repliée au prochain lancement de l’Explorateur, alors que Windows la déployait systématiquement jusqu’ici. Microsoft améliore également les miniatures des fichiers stockés dans le cloud et réorganise le panneau Détails pour présenter davantage d’informations sans ouvrir le document.
Autre changement intégré à KB5124010, la possibilité de réaffecter la touche Copilot à Ctrl droit ou au menu contextuel, deux commandes qu’elle avait parfois remplacées sur les nouveaux claviers.
La mise à jour entérine aussi la disparition du transfert direct entre deux PC dans Windows Backup. L’outil, qui permettait de récupérer fichiers et paramètres depuis une ancienne machine via le réseau local pendant la configuration de la nouvelle, cède sa place aux fonctions de sauvegarde et de restauration liées à OneDrive.
Comme d’habitude, Microsoft déploie toutes ces évolutions progressivement, si bien qu’elles peuvent ne pas apparaître immédiatement après l’installation de KB5124010.
Bluetooth, sauvegardes et webcam passent à l’atelier réparation
Derrière cette poignée de nouveautés, KB5124010 consacre une large part de son contenu à corriger les ratés accumulés ces dernières semaines. Microsoft renforce ainsi la stabilité des connexions Bluetooth et la détection des périphériques, alors que Windows pouvait encore signaler un accessoire comme connecté après sa déconnexion ou indiquer que le Bluetooth était activé alors qu’il avait été coupé.
L’audio hérite au passage d’une série de retouches plus ciblées, destinées à améliorer la prise en charge des microphones Bluetooth Classic et des périphériques LE Audio. Le niveau sonore affiché par Windows doit également mieux suivre les réglages effectués depuis les commandes d’un casque, tandis que Microsoft corrige plusieurs problèmes susceptibles de perturber les appels et la lecture audio.
Le Patch Tuesday de septembre n’avait pas non plus épargné Historique des fichiers, qui pouvait interrompre les sauvegardes et restaurations vers un disque externe ou un emplacement réseau, puis réclamer de reconnecter un support pourtant accessible. KB5124010 rétablit leur fonctionnement et en profite aussi pour corriger l’affichage de la date de dernière sauvegarde ainsi que celui des versions précédentes des fichiers.
Les webcams intégrées bénéficient elles aussi d’un correctif après avoir, sur certaines machines, cessé de répondre dans l’application Caméra comme dans les logiciels qui les utilisent. Sysmon en reçoit trois, dont un pour les fausses alertes Event ID 25 générées à tort pour le processus système smss.exe, ainsi que deux anomalies pouvant perturber la détection des tentatives d’altération ou provoquer un arrêt système.
Le mois de septembre laisse malgré tout deux dossiers ouverts. Le correctif hors cycle du 14 septembre a bien réglé le cas des périphériques USB Audio Class 1.0 utilisés en 8 canaux ou en 3D, mais pas les autres symptômes apparus après le Patch Tuesday : code 10 dans le Gestionnaire de périphériques, absence de son, commandes de volume figées ou paramètres audio inaccessibles. Microsoft cherche encore comment les corriger. Les machines protégées par Credential Guard peuvent également perdre leur relation d’approbation avec un domaine Active Directory local ; un contournement est disponible en attendant une prochaine mise à jour.

articles.title: Cuisson à 350 °C et pierre volcanique italienne : deux atouts du four encastrable Whirlpool Pizza Atelier
articles.text:
Cuisson à 350 °C et pierre volcanique italienne : deux atouts du four encastrable Whirlpool Pizza Atelier
Whirlpool commercialise le four encastrable PizzaAtelier, une référence capable d'atteindre une température de 350 °C. Livré avec une pierre en lave de l'Etna et une pelle en bois, cet appareil de 73 litres promet de cuire une pizza dans les règles de l'art, en trois minutes.
Whirlpool WOI78FPT1SBAP PizzaAtelier
C'est LA tendance du moment dans le monde des fours encastrables : la fonction pizza qui fait monter la température dans le moufle au-dessus des 300°C pour réussir sa pizza comme à Palerme. On l'a déjà croisé chez Hisense sur le HO66MB PIZZACHEF et chez Electrolux avec le série 700 MealAssist Y8POX28Z. C'est au tour de Whirlpool de s'essayer à cette catégorie qui, on n'en doute pas, va prendre de plus en plus d'ampleur avec l'annonce du four encastrable WOI78FPT1SBAP, baptisé PizzaAtelier. Conçu et testé près de Milan par des ingénieurs culinaires et des chefs italiens, ce modèle associe de hautes températures à des accessoires spécifiques afin de reproduire les méthodes de cuisson traditionnelles à domicile.
Une cuisson à 350 °C soutenue par une pierre de lave de l'Etna
La spécificité principale de cet appareil réside dans sa capacité à monter jusqu'à une température de 350 °C mesurée au centre de la cavité supérieure. Rappelons que chez Hisense et chez Electrolux, l'astuce pour atteindre cette haute température était de rapetisser l'enceinte de cuisson grâce à une plaque pour concentrer la chaleur. Cette haute température, donc, combinée à une plaque de cuisson taillée dans de la pierre de lave de l'Etna fabriquée en Italie, doit permettre de cuire une pizza fraîche en seulement trois minutes, après un préchauffage de 20 minutes. La structure naturellement poreuse de la roche volcanique absorbe l'excès d'humidité pour garantir une croûte dorée en dessous et moelleuse à cœur, tout en favorisant le phénomène de léopardage de la pâte. Cette pierre amovible peut également servir pour la cuisson du pain ou d'autres préparations culinaires. Le four est livré d'origine avec sa pelle à pizza en bois.
Une cavité XXL de 73 litres et des équipements multifonctions**
Au-delà de sa spécialisation culinaire italienne, le PizzaAtelier propose une cavité de 73 litres affichant une efficacité énergétique de classe A+. La technologie de chaleur tournante pulsée s'associe au dispositif Cook 4 pour autoriser la cuisson simultanée sur quatre niveaux distincts, sans risque de mélange de goûts ou d'odeurs. L'appareil embarque l'écosystème 6ème Sens incluant 40 recettes automatiques, qui vient compléter un total de 15 fonctions de cuisson distinctes. Un mode AirFry est également intégré avec son accessoire dédié, permettant d'obtenir des préparations croustillantes en réduisant l'ajout de matière grasse.
Sur le plan de la maintenance et du confort d'utilisation, le four fait appel à un double système de nettoyage réunissant la pyrolyse et l'hydrolyse SmartClean. Sa façade en verre noir intègre un affichage sensitif LCD, une porte froide à fermeture douce ainsi qu'un jeu de rails télescopiques sur un niveau. Livré avec une grille, une lèchefrite et une lèchefrite profonde, le meuble affiche des dimensions standards de 59,7 × 59,5 × 56,4 cm. La sortie du four Whirlpool PizzaAtelier est annoncée pour la mi-octobre 2026, à un prix public indicatif de 799 €.

articles.title: Ni cristal ni policarbonato: este invernadero escolar está hecho enteramente con miles de botellas de plástico recicladas
articles.text:
Un puñado de escuelas y estudiantes universitarios en Australia dieron con una idea bastante ingeniosa, pues en lugar de tirar las botellas de plástico, se preguntaron por qué no construir algo útil con ellas. Con esta premisa en mente, construyeron una serie de invernaderos caseros bastante baratos de hacer, pues se levantaron casi por completo con botellas recicladas. Estas estructuras han servido además como aulas, huertos y otros proyectos comunitarios.
La idea. Se cogen miles de botellas de plástico vacías, se lavan y se utilizan para rellenar las paredes de una estructura básica de madera. La luz pasa a través del plástico igual que lo haría a través del cristal o del policarbonato, atrapando el calor en el interior y creando las condiciones cálidas y húmedas que las plantas necesitan para crecer, dándole así una segunda vida a las botellas.
Canberra. En 2014, 33 estudiantes del Máster en Terapia Ocupacional de la Universidad de Canberra asumieron un trabajo que consistía en diseñar y construir un invernadero de botellas desde cero, para luego donarlo. Utilizando más de 1.500 botellas y financiándolo a través de 1.000 dólares recaudados mediante colectas, los estudiantes montaron la estructura en el campus antes de transportarla a Nowra, Nueva Gales del Sur, para regalársela a Slice of Life Australia, una organización sin ánimo de lucro que apoya a jóvenes con discapacidad.
Otro de los ejemplos más conocidos fue construido en 2015 por alumnos de la escuela primaria Richardson Primary School en Canberra, quienes pasaron 18 meses reuniendo más de 2.000 botellas para construir su “Palacio de Plástico”, que era como denominaron al invernadero. Una subvención de 2.000 dólares del fondo medioambiental del Teachers Mutual Bank cubrió la estructura de madera, las herramientas y los plantones, e incluso las partes sobrantes de las botellas se reutilizaron como macetas.
Tal como explicó en su momento la profesora de sexto curso Kate Davis, el plan original de 2.000 botellas creció rápidamente para que pudiera caber una clase entera dentro, según compartía el medio ABC. Jason Borton, director de la escuela, contaba que el proyecto ofreció a los estudiantes “muchas oportunidades de aprendizaje práctico y con un propósito real”, combinando lecciones medioambientales con matemáticas, medición y diseño.
Tasmania. Un proyecto similar tomó forma en 2016 también en la escuela primaria Youngtown Primary School en Launceston, Tasmania, donde los estudiantes reunieron unas 6.000 botellas para su propio invernadero. Allí, el trabajo de construcción real fue llevado a cabo por participantes de un programa de trabajo a cambio de prestación por desempleo. El director del proyecto, Craig Williams, declaró en su momento a la ABC que la iniciativa ofrecía a los participantes experiencia práctica en construcción, al tiempo que dotó a la escuela de una herramienta docente práctica.
El profesor Brad Colson señalaba por aquel entonces que el invernadero permitía que los plantones empezaran a crecer mucho más rápido que si se cultivaban directamente en la tierra, y utilizó el espacio para hablar con los alumnos sobre reciclaje, consumo y alimentación.
Todos estos proyectos individuales que se remontan a principios y mediados de la década de 2010, han continuado con iniciativas similares, pues la idea de usar materiales baratos y darle una segunda vida al plástico en un esfuerzo comunitario como este ha seguido inspirando proyectos parecidos en escuelas, universidades y huertos comunitarios de todo el mundo. Y es que resulta que un montón de botellas de plástico y un poco de imaginación pueden llegar bastante lejos.
Imágenes | Fred Hooper, Hannah Walmsley y Jamila Toderas (Canberra Times y ABC)
