articles.title: Couverture 5G : SFR s'empare de la première place, mais les opérateurs sont au coude-à-coude
articles.text:
Ce classement a été dévoilé ce jeudi 24 septembre en exclusivité par DegroupTest, avant sa mise en ligne complète par nPerf ce vendredi 25 septembre. Il montre surtout que les quatre opérateurs sont désormais au coude-à-coude : 1,27 point sépare SFR d’Orange, contre 11,51 points dans l’édition 2024. Vous hésitez entre deux forfaits 5G ? La couverture 5G nationale ne vous aidera pas beaucoup à choisir.
nPerf est une société française qui édite une application de test de débit. Son baromètre repose sur des mesures relevées sur le terrain par ses utilisateurs de smartphones Android. Les cartes de couverture publiées par les opérateurs sont, elles, simulées par ordinateur.
Le score final fait la moyenne de deux indicateurs : la part du territoire où les abonnés ont capté la 5G, et la part de la population couverte en mobilité. SFR arrive premier avec 72,78 %, devant Bouygues Telecom (72,34 %), Free (71,55 %) et Orange (71,51 %).
Le détail est plus nuancé. SFR a la meilleure couverture géographique (58,62 %), mais le plus faible score sur la population (86,94 %). Free présente le profil inverse : dernier sur le territoire (54,49 %), premier sur la population (88,61 %).
iPhone 18 Pro à 99€ + forfait 250Go à 29,99€/mois pendant 12 mois. Profitez de 50€ de remise immédiate avec le code NEW50 et jusqu’à 150€ de bonus reprise pour votre ancien mobile. Livraison offerte.
Orange reste quatrième, mais il revient de loin : son score a grimpé de 23,13 points depuis 2024, la plus forte hausse des quatre. Attention toutefois, cela ne veut pas dire qu’Orange couvre 23 % de territoire en plus. L’indicateur ne porte en effet que sur les zones fréquentées par ses propres abonnés.
Surtout, ce baromètre dit seulement si la 5G est présente. nPerf prend en compte toutes les bandes de fréquences, y compris le 700 MHz, qui porte loin mais offre des débits plus faibles que le 3,5 GHz, la bande des hauts débits. Être couvert en 5G ne garantit donc pas une connexion rapide. Si l’on y regarde de plus près, Orange est l’opérateur qui couvre plus la 5G en 3,5 GHz avec 14 302 sites répertoriés sur mon réseaumobilearcep.
Débits et qualité d’appel : Bouygues en tête
Pour les performances, il faut regarder un autre classement de nPerf, publié en janvier 2026 et qui porte sur toute l’année 2025. Bouygues Telecom y a pris la première place. Le même prestataire publie aussi chaque année un classement des fournisseurs d’internet fixe.
L’Arcep, le gendarme des télécoms, mesure elle-même la qualité des réseaux chaque été. Sa dernière campagne, publiée ce même 24 septembre 2026 met en avant d’autres données.
Orange y domine au niveau national. 91 % de ses appels sont en qualité parfaite, c’est-à-dire maintenus deux minutes sans perturbation audible. Bouygues Telecom suit avec 88 %, SFR avec 87 % et Free avec 84 %.
Hors des villes, l’écart grandit. En zones rurales, Orange réussit 83 % d’appels parfaits, contre 76 à 79 % pour les trois autres. Dans les TGV, il maintient 74 % des appels, contre 61 % pour Free, 58 % pour Bouygues Telecom et 56 % pour SFR.
En revanche, Bouygues Telecom fait jeu égal avec Orange en zones denses : 96 % d’appels parfaits contre 95 %, un écart que l’Arcep classe dans la marge d’erreur. Sur l’internet mobile en ville, il passe devant tout le monde au seuil de 3 Mbit/s, le minimum pour naviguer sur le web. Il fait aussi jeu égal avec Orange aux seuils de 8 et 30 Mbit/s, ceux du streaming vidéo et des usages professionnels.
Vérifiez la couverture là où vous vivez
Région par région, les écarts redeviennent nets. DegroupTest a calculé plus de 22 points d’écart entre le meilleur et le moins bon opérateur en Normandie, et plus de 21 points en Bretagne. Dans 9 des 13 régions étudiées par nPerf, l’écart dépasse 10 points.
Pas de panique, l’Arcep propose un outil gratuit pour vérifier chez vous. Lancé en septembre 2017, Mon réseau mobile compare la couverture des quatre opérateurs là où vous vivez et sur vos trajets, en métropole comme en outre-mer. La carte affiche aussi les points de mesure réels de l’Arcep, colorés selon le débit relevé, de moins de 3 Mbit/s à plus de 30 Mbit/s.
Nous vous recommandons de regarder les zones où vous passez le plus de temps : domicile, travail et trajets. Si vous prenez souvent le train ou vivez à la campagne, Orange garde l’avantage dans les mesures de l’Arcep. En ville, Bouygues Telecom fait jeu égal avec lui. La campagne 2026 de l’Arcep n’est pas encore publiée : l’édition 2025 était sortie le 20 novembre.

articles.title: Could AI threaten humanity? 8 Africans weigh the risks
articles.text:
Will AI kill us all?
It sounds like the plot of a science fiction movie, but in 2026, the question is being taken seriously by some of the people building the technology. As AI systems become more capable of reasoning and carrying out tasks with less human input, concerns are growing about what happens when humans can no longer fully control them.
Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, recently resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies are racing towards self-improving systems and “gambling with our lives.” OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki also warned that no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.
But this debate is not only about what happens in Silicon Valley. Africans are already using AI in their businesses and everyday lives, while local innovators are building with it and investors are putting money into the industry.
So we asked eight people across five groups —everyday users, educators, innovators, policy experts, and investors—one question: do you think AI could eventually become a threat to humanity, potentially even to the point of killing us all?
“Which AI is going to kill us exactly?” Sarah Pra, Ghana
Sarah Pra, a restaurant owner in Kumasi, Ghana, has heard the warnings and seen people talking about AI taking over and eventually killing humans. But the idea did not seem particularly convincing to her.
“Which AI is going to kill us exactly? Is it ChatGPT or Meta AI?” she asked, rhetorically.
She had seen the conversation on the short-form video-sharing platform, TikTok, but she was not buying it.
“How is the AI going to kill us, honestly?” she said. “They are all shouting that AI is going to kill us, but I have not seen where they showed me exactly how it is going to do it.”
For now, Pra’s experience with AI looks nothing like a science fiction apocalypse.
When she wants to learn how to cook something she has never made before, she used to turn to Google. Now she asks Meta AI or ChatGPT. She uses ChatGPT to help make flyers for her restaurant and turns to the tools for personal questions too.
“You don’t want to see my WhatsApp Meta AI or my ChatGPT history,” she said.
There is a contradiction at the heart of Pra’s relationship with AI: she does not trust it completely, but she has already made it part of her daily life.
“ChatGPT can lie,” she said. “I always take what I want from whatever it tells me and leave the rest.”
She has caught it giving her wrong information before, including advice about a food she wanted to cook. And while she has not worked out exactly what she would never share with an AI system, she knows there are limits.
“It is not human in any way,” she said. “So, not everything.”
For Pra, the threat is what people might choose to do with it.
She has seen AI used to create fake nude images of women and to spread false information about people. She worries about people using the technology to harm, but she sees that as a problem with its users rather than proof that AI itself is becoming dangerous.
“If anyone is using it to build anything bad, the owners of the AI should know what to do,” she said.
And if AI becomes substantially more capable? Pra would welcome more capable AI if it helped people do things more easily and quickly.
“If it can get better to help us do things easily and quickly, I will not mind,” she said.
“Artificial Intelligence was created to help the Natural Intelligence”, Elijah, Nigeria
Elijah Akuma, a master’s student at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, a public university in Enugu state, eastern Nigeria, is not convinced that AI will kill humanity either.
To him, the technology is still fundamentally a human creation and therefore limited by the people who build and use it.
“AI was made by man; every good product has its deficiencies too,” he said. “But to the point of AI killing us all is unrealistic.”
Akuma is a writer, researcher and teacher, and AI has become part of how he works. He uses it to test ideas, criticise his drafts and suggest ways to improve his work.
Before AI, he said, he would spend more time at the ideation stage, trying to work out which direction to take. Now he can put an idea into an AI tool, ask it to challenge him, and decide for himself what is useful.
“I always have my ideas and plans figured out, but AI helps me polish it, criticise it, and make suggestions on what could be done to enhance it,” he said.
He does not see that as handing over his thinking to a machine.
“AI doesn’t think for me,” he said. “It makes suggestions, and I consider them and pick which is relevant to what I’m working on.”
For him, the relationship is closer to collaboration. “We are more like a team,” he said.
But Akuma worries that not everyone is using AI that way.
Students, he said, are increasingly turning to AI for almost everything, and some are no longer engaging deeply with problems themselves.
A 2026 study by researchers Patience Ebekeyi Bakre and Fa’iza Tukur-Bello, published by Springer in Discover Education, surveyed 535 students across eight Nigerian tertiary institutions and found that they used AI tools including ChatGPT, Grammarly and Gemini for academic work such as coding, writing essays, finding materials and summarising information.
“The most worrisome of them all is that students now depend so much on it that it is difficult for them to think any longer,” he said. “They literally depend on it for everything without engaging their ingenuity.”
That, rather than a machine independently deciding to destroy humanity, is the future that concerns him most.
“Artificial Intelligence was created to help the Natural Intelligence,” he said. “I worry that the overdependence on AI will make their thinking degenerate into a pitiable state.”
He is also wary of trusting AI with decisions that require human judgment or experience. He would not use it to diagnose or prescribe treatment, seek marital advice, or write his research papers.
For his research, there is a reason he prefers to speak directly to people.
“I’d rather get my responses directly from people affected by what I am writing about,” he said.
For Elijah, authenticity is something AI cannot provide. He knows the technology can be useful. He also expects it to become more capable. But he believes the more powerful it becomes, the more important it will be to decide where its boundaries should lie.
“The horror comes in when it is designed to uproot the principles and values that guide human existence,” he said.
“The important question is: Do you understand the answer?”, Akpan, Nigeria
If Akuma worries that students are becoming too dependent on AI, Aniedi Akpan sees the same concern from inside the education system.
Akpan is the Head of Careers and Team Lead, Relationship Management at 16 Plus Schools, a private co-educational school in Lagos that offers secondary and sixth-form education. He thinks AI could eventually become a threat to humanity, although he is cautious about presenting that as inevitable.
He is more concerned about what humans do with increasingly powerful systems: deploying them without sufficient safeguards or using them to amplify existing problems such as warfare, misinformation, cybercrime, surveillance and inequality.
In education, however, AI is already changing the way students learn.
“A student can now ask a question, receive an explanation at an appropriate level, explore alternative approaches to a problem, practise a skill and receive immediate feedback,” Akpan said.
For students who may not always have access to one-to-one support, he said, this can be powerful. But the availability of instant answers is also changing what students need to learn.
“The important question is becoming less ‘Can you find the answer?’ and more ‘Do you understand the answer, and can you determine whether it is correct?’” he said.
Akpan worries about what happens when students allow AI to do the difficult parts of learning for them.
“If a student routinely asks AI to write the essay, solve the equation, or formulate the argument without first attempting it, the student may complete the task while missing the learning,” he said.
He does not think AI will inevitably make people less intelligent. A calculator did not make mathematics disappear, and the internet did not eliminate the need to think, he said. The difference is how the technology is used.
His biggest concern is dependency. He worries about a generation becoming so accustomed to having AI think, write, remember, and decide for them that they gradually lose confidence in their own ability to struggle through difficult problems.
“I am less worried about students using AI than I am about students using it without understanding what it is doing,” he said.
AI can be confidently wrong, reproduce biases, and produce convincing information without genuine understanding. Akpan wants students to grow up neither fearing AI nor treating it as an unquestionable authority.
“They should be comfortable using it, but equally comfortable challenging it,” he said.
“Humans should hold the reins”
ThankGod Obiechina is not particularly worried that AI will wipe out humanity. The business growth strategist at Wehostname.com, a Nigerian web hosting company, thinks there are more immediate threats to human survival, including the possibility of another world war.
“I believe AI can threaten humanity, but not to the point of killing us all,” he said.
The idea of AI causing human extinction, he believes, has been amplified by science fiction and popular imagination.
“If we start talking about human extinction, there are other issues we should be concerned with, and one of them is World War III,” he said.
But like Akuma, Obiechina has a different concern about where AI could take humanity. He worries that people may become so dependent on AI that they gradually lose the ability to think independently and interact with one another.
“The next generation would completely resolve to rely absolutely on Artificial intelligence, thereby stripping themselves of the ability of reason, logic and interaction,” he said.
That fear is already influencing the way Obiechina uses AI. He relies on it to make his work more efficient, accurate and timely, but he does not completely hand over decisions to it.
“I trust the AI tools I use, but I don’t completely rely on them,” he said.
There are certain decisions he would not leave to a machine at all, particularly those involving human relationships, spirituality, and instinct.
“There’s a human touch to everything I do with AI,” he said, “because I believe AI can never replace humans.”
He is not opposed to AI becoming more powerful. In fact, he expects it to evolve as humans do. He just wants humans to remain in charge of that evolution.
“We are evolving; I would be happy if AI evolves too,” he said. “However, I would be more glad if humans hold the reins of that evolution.”
“We don’t need an extinction scenario to take AI risk seriously,” Adetona, founder, Decide
AI becoming very good at doing the work humans currently depend on for a living may be a more immediate danger than AI deciding to kill humanity, said Abiodun Adetona, an AI developer and founder of Decide AI, which helps users analyse spreadsheets and business data using natural-language prompts. He thinks talk of AI wiping out humanity can sometimes distract from risks that are already much easier to imagine.
“I think the idea that AI will kill all of us gets into fear-mongering,” he said. “But there are legitimate risks.”
One of those risks is what happens when increasingly capable AI gives ordinary people access to capabilities that once required years of expertise.
Bad actors, he said, could use AI to penetrate fragile systems. But the consequences could also be economic.
“I also worry about labour displacement,” he said. “If millions of people are displaced from their jobs without alternatives, the political and economic consequences could be serious.”
For Adetona, that is enough reason to take the technology’s risks seriously.
“We don’t need an extinction scenario to take AI risk seriously,” he said.
That concern is particularly relevant as AI systems become capable of performing more tasks that once required human workers. Adetona is himself building AI systems, so he does not see the answer as stopping development. Instead, he believes capability needs to be matched with control.
“As our agents become more capable, we have to be deliberate about what they can access, what actions they can take and what requires approval,” he said.
The principle is simple: an AI system being technically capable of doing something does not automatically mean it should be allowed to do it.
“The more consequential the action, the stronger the controls around it should be,” he said.
Adetona also does not think the industry should slow down simply because the technology carries risks.
“We shouldn’t stop building because there are risks,” he said. “But moving fast doesn’t mean being careless.”
“Responsible stewardship will determine our future,” Roman, founder, Daraja AI
Kelvin Roman is building AI at a time when the technology’s capabilities are advancing faster than many people expected. As founder of Daraja AI, which builds AI tools and infrastructure for African languages and contexts, Roman is helping build the technology he is assessing for risk. Roman does not dismiss the possibility that AI could cause serious harm.
“AI, like many transformative technologies before it, carries risks if not developed and used responsibly,” he said.
But he does not believe the technology itself determines what happens next.
“The real risk comes from how humans design, deploy, and govern these systems,” he said.
That responsibility shapes how Daraja AI develops its systems, with safety checks, testing protocols, and transparent oversight built into the process. Daraja AI also places limits on what Babel, its AI system, can be used for. Roman said the company does not allow it to generate harmful content, violate privacy, or support illegal activities.
“Public safety always comes first,” he said.
Roman also thinks some of the public conversation about AI risk focuses too heavily on science-fiction scenarios, while more immediate problems include AI systems reinforcing biases, spreading misinformation, or making critical errors at scale. These risks do not require an AI system to become independently hostile to humanity; they can happen while the technology is still being designed, deployed, and controlled by people.
He sees rapid progress as an opportunity, particularly for countries like those in Africa, where AI could help improve healthcare access, education, and business efficiency.
“I wouldn’t say we are moving fast or slow,” he said. “We are moving at the speed of AI.”
For Roman, the answer to the risks created by that speed is not to abandon the technology, but to make sure safeguards evolve alongside it.
“Our focus should be on building robust safeguards and ethical guidelines around AI,” he said. “Ultimately, responsible stewardship — not the technology itself — will determine our future.”
“AI is a force multiplier,” Bankong, investment associate, Oui Capital
For Pius Bankong, an investment associate at Oui Capital, an Africa-focused venture capital firm that invests in early-stage technology companies, AI is worth investing in because of the economic possibilities it could unlock.
“AI is a force multiplier,” he said. “It has the potential to add to global GDP through productivity, enable economic activity that was previously limited or locked, and unlock new economic possibilities that could have positive social effects.”
Those possibilities extend beyond software. Bankong also sees opportunities in hardware and robotics, but says investors have to account for the risks that come with developing and deploying the technology. AI’s potential to create and destroy is not unique to the technology, he said. He compares it with nuclear energy, another technology whose impact depends on how it is used.
“There is a considerable argument that AI could threaten humanity,” he said. “But whether it does or not depends on corporate governance, policies, organisations being intentional about the technology and the power that it wields.”
For Bankong, that becomes particularly important as companies compete to develop AI and investors look for returns.
“In capitalism, the first objective is to maximise profits and returns,” he said. But there are checks and balances through policy, legislation, safeguards, corporate governance and long-term thinking.
“What’s the use of maximizing profits only then for certain hazards to erase them?” he said.
He believes investors have a role in that process, although they are not solely responsible for how AI companies operate. Management has primary responsibility, while investors can provide oversight and guidance through their involvement with companies.
The responsibility, he said, is shared across management, investors, policymakers, and others in the ecosystem. And if he believed there was a significant chance that advanced AI could cause catastrophic harm, that would change his investment decision.
“Of course,” he said. “Why would you invest in something that is catastrophic? Short-term stellar returns are pointless if eventually a catastrophe wipes them out.”
“It’s a chicken-and-egg thing,” Adeniyi, AI policy expert and researcher
Kayode Adeniyi, an AI policy expert and researcher, sees both real risks and exaggerated fears in the conversation about AI and human extinction. He believes some of the fear surrounding AI may be amplified because fear itself can be useful, but that does not mean the underlying risks are imaginary.
“It’s a chicken-and-egg thing,” said Adeniyi, who is pursuing a PhD at Imperial College London on using machine learning to develop sensors for monitoring global water risk.
“There’s a part of AI news that you hear about AI is incredibly very dangerous. We need to take it very serious. We need to be cautious about the development. That is marketing.”
But there is another side, he said, where the threats are real. One concern is what happens when AI systems become capable of combining and applying knowledge at a scale no individual human can match. “It’s just like combining the brains of millions of people together,” he said. “So what a single individual cannot achieve, when you have multiple brains together, they should be able to do times a hundred, or times one thousand.”
That possibility, he said, creates risks on different timescales, some of which are already visible. Misinformation and disinformation can be generated and distributed rapidly, while people can use AI to create convincing fake images and videos that could influence how others understand events or make decisions. Other risks are more difficult to see.
Adeniyi works in AI safety, including the problem researchers call AI alignment—the challenge of making sure increasingly capable AI systems behave in ways consistent with human values and intentions.
He offered a hypothetical example. If a sufficiently capable AI were asked to find the best way to solve climate change, it could identify humans as a major source of environmental damage. A system that did not properly understand or share human values could, in theory, arrive at a solution that humans would consider unacceptable.
“The best solution for an AI that is not aligned to human values, or doesn’t have the real emotions that we have, is to kill all of us,” he said.
That scenario is not inevitable, Adeniyi stressed. An AI system does not simply wake up with its own intentions and decide to destroy humanity.
But he believes the possibility becomes more serious as systems become more capable — particularly if humans fail to understand how to make them reliably follow human intentions.
“We need to take the alignment research right,” he said, referring to efforts to understand and control the behaviour of advanced AI systems.
Adeniyi believes African governments also need to do more to prepare for the risks of increasingly capable AI. “Most governments on the continent are not really doing enough,” he said. While countries focus on adopting AI, developing infrastructure and encouraging people to build with the technology, he said, AI safety and evaluation have received less attention. African countries will also continue to use AI systems developed elsewhere, making it important to evaluate them before they are deployed in sensitive sectors.
For African governments, Adeniyi believes preparation should therefore go beyond regulation. The continent needs people who understand how to build AI safely, evaluate its behaviour and test systems for vulnerabilities.
“Talent development is very key,” he said.
Africa may not have the resources to compete immediately with the largest technology companies in building enormous AI models. But Adeniyi believes it can develop expertise in AI safety, research, engineering, and evaluation — areas that will become increasingly important as the technology advances.
“The best thing we can do for ourselves,” he said, “is to develop the right talent.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Managing 3D-IC Design And IP
articles.text:
Design data management, traceability, and revision control are critical for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration.
By Keith Felton and Todd Burkholder
The trend towards multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration is here to stay. It promises faster innovation, more powerful and specialized devices, and greater design flexibility. However, realizing its potential hinges on our ability to manage the complexity that comes with it.
However, with this newfound modularity comes a significant challenge: managing the vast and intricate web of data that defines these systems. This is where robust data management and meticulous data traceability become not just beneficial, but essential. Without data management, even the most brilliant multi-chiplet design can quickly become a tangled mess, leading to costly errors, delays, and a loss of confidence in the final product.
In the first three articles of this series (published in the June, July and August editions of Semiconductor Engineering), we covered the first seven steps toward streamlining your 3D-IC design process. This article focuses on design data and design IP management, traceability, and revision control. This is a critical step for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration, as there is so much design data and IP involved that using an incorrect version or missing an ECO can mean product failure.
Data management can be broken down to four components that will help you streamline your 3D-IC design flow:
In the world of multi-chiplet design, we often bring together various pieces of IP from different sources—from internal teams, external vendors, or even open-source initiatives. Each piece of design IP comes with its own set of design files, specifications, and usage guidelines.
When you have multiple chiplets from different sources, potentially designed with different tools and at different times, the sheer volume and diversity of this data can be overwhelming. Without a well-defined data management strategy to manage these diverse sources, the risk of introducing defects is significantly higher.
Innovator3D IC Data Management software supports robust data and design IP management to provide single moment-of-truth management of design IP data. It treats the design itself as a work-in-progress, applying a revision-controlled and access-rights managed process at every stage of design, all the way to tape out.
Fig. 1: Innovator3D IC Data Management’s centralized cockpit.
Multi-chiplet designs inherently involve a complex hierarchy. Chiplets are integrated into a larger multi-chiplet heterogeneous assembly using interposers and substrates. Managing this hierarchy effectively, especially with the inevitable design iterations, requires a powerful revision control system. When you manage your design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking, you avoid errors. Revision control is like a time machine for your designs. It allows you to track every change, revert to previous versions, and allow different teams to work on separate features or bug fixes concurrently without interfering with each other. Once a team’s work is complete and verified, their changes can be merged back into the main design.
Without this meticulous historical tracking, understanding how a design evolved, diagnosing issues, or even just knowing which version is currently “in play” becomes a monumental task. Errors can appear through miscommunication or accidental overwriting, leading to significant delays and increased costs. A well-managed design hierarchy with robust revision control is fundamental to preventing these types of errors.
In a distributed design environment, where different teams might be working on different chiplets across various locations, having a single, centralized hub for all design data is invaluable. This hub acts as the single source of truth, providing direct access to all relevant information for authorized personnel.
When engineers can quickly access information they need, cycle times are dramatically reduced. This direct access speeds up design, verification, and debugging processes, leading to faster time-to-market.
Beyond just storing data, an effective data management system provides real-time visibility into a project’s status. This capability is crucial for efficient project management, especially in the complex landscape of multi-chiplet integration.
Instant access to status tracking and analytical data empowers project managers and engineering leads to make informed decisions, proactively address issues, and ensure that the project stays on track. It transforms data from a passive record into an active tool for driving project success.
By embracing robust data management practices, including diligent management of the design and its IP sources, meticulous revision control, centralized information hubs, and comprehensive status tracking for traceability, you establish a solid foundation for success. These “unseen architects” ensure that your multi-chiplet designs are not only functional and perform well, but also are reliable, maintainable, and auditable — allowing you to build the complex, interconnected systems of tomorrow with confidence and clarity.

Todd Burkholder is a senior editor at Siemens DISW. For over 25 years, he has worked as editor, author, and ghost writer with internal and external customers to create print and digital content across a broad range of EDA technologies. Burkholder began his career in marketing for high-technology and other industries in 1992 after earning a Bachelor of Science at Portland State University and a Master of Science degree from the University of Arizona.

articles.title: Après les avoir installées de force sur votre PC, Microsoft abandonne ces 3 applications
articles.text:
En octobre 2025, Microsoft annonçait en grande pompe l’arrivée de trois nouvelles applications compagnons pour les utilisateurs de Microsoft 365. « Conçues pour rationaliser les flux de travail quotidien », ces trois applications devaient également aider « les utilisateurs à rester concentrés, à réduire les changements de contexte et à effectuer des tâches plus rapidement ».
Moins d’un an plus tard, les résultats escomptés par Microsoft ne sont visiblement pas au rendez-vous. La firme de Redmond vient en effet d’officialiser leur abandon.
Des fonctions déjà présentes dans d’autres applis
À l’époque, Microsoft avait jugé bonne l’idée d’installer ces trois applications (Contact, Calendrier et Fichiers) par défaut chez les utilisateurs Microsoft 365. Ces applications compagnons squattaient donc la barre des tâches de Windows 11 pour vous permettre d’accéder en un clic à des informations essentielles pour vos tâches quotidiennes.
Leur utilité ne semble malheureusement pas avoir convaincu beaucoup de monde. C’est sans doute ce qui a poussé Microsoft à les abandonner. L’entreprise vient d’annoncer qu’elles cesseront totalement de fonctionner à compter du 16 décembre 2026. Elle a d’ailleurs déjà interrompu les mises à jour et les correctifs de sécurité à destination de ces applications, et à même bloqué leur installation automatique via les mises à jour Microsoft 365.
La fin précipitée de ces applications n’a rien de très étonnant. Car les fonctionnalités qu’elles proposaient faisaient doublon avec d’autres fonctions déjà présentes dans les différents outils de Microsoft. Le Calendrier et les Contacts sont déjà intégrés à Outlook et Microsoft Teams, et les Fichiers sont accessibles via la recherche Windows, l’Explorateur de fichiers, Sharepoint, OneDrive et même directement dans les applis Office. Sans oublier l’assistant intelligent Copilot qui peut être interrogé pour retrouver rapidement des fichiers, des personnes ou des rendez-vous.
Des applis installées de force, mais à supprimer manuellement
Si Microsoft n’a pas eu de mal à imposer l’installation de ses applications compagnons sur le PC des utilisateurs Microsoft 365, l’entreprise semble avoir un peu plus de mal pour ce qui est de leur désinstallation. Comble de l’ironie, ces trois applications, bien que rendues inutilisables, resteront installées sur votre machine. Microsoft n’a prévu aucune mise à jour permettant de les faire disparaître. C’est à vous que reviendra la charge de leur désinstallation.
Une opération, somme toute simple, que vous devrez réaliser manuellement, mais dont vous auriez pu vous passer. Vous devrez en effet vous rendre dans les Paramètres > Applications > Applications installées afin de rechercher les applications Microsoft 365 Compagnons pour enfin les Désinstaller.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.
Source : Microsoft

articles.title: Rayman Legends Retold's PC specs range from a GTX 1660 to an RTX 4080 – with upscaling throughout
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Do any developers release their games' PC system requirements without upscaling enabled these days? Based on the new Rayman Legends Retold reveal, it's become very rare. Once again, the game can run on a potato-like PC, and once again, the caveat is that upscaling is required at every level.
The good news for fans of the long-running platforming franchise is that the latest entry will play at 1080p@60FPS on an Intel Core i3-8100 or Ryzen 3 3100 paired with a GTX 1060, RX 5500 XT, or Intel Arc A580 and 8GB of RAM. However, graphics need to be set to the lowest preset and you still need upscaling (quality).
That quality upscaling setting is present in all four levels. Interestingly, the required hardware for the Recommended (1080p@60FPS with high graphics preset) and 2K (1440p@60FPS high preset) levels is pretty much identical. Only the AMD GPU (RX 5700 to an RX 6750 XT) and Intel GPU (Arc A750 to Arc B580) change.
Finally, the 4K ultra preset level is still quite demanding, considering this is a platformer (an admittedly pretty one) and upscaling is enabled. It asks for an RTX 4080 or Radeon RX 7900 XTX. The CPU requirements are more forgiving: a Core i5-9400 or Ryzen 5 3600.
The modest storage requirement is nice to see: 33GB of SSD space. That's around half of what's needed for The Blood of Dawnwalker, and almost 100GB less than Gears of War: E-Day.
Back in 2023, Remnant II set what was then considered a worrying precedent: it was the first PC game "designed with upscaling in mind."
While developers have avoided that kind of language since then, more games are adopting this thinking. Monster Hunter Wilds, Assassin's Creed Shadows, Rise of the Ronin, F1 25, DOOM: The Dark Ages, FBC: Firebreak, Mafia: The Old Country, Silent Hill f, Resident Evil Requiem, and Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced are just some that explicitly included upscaling in their published PC hardware requirements. Upcoming releases Gears of War: E-Day and Phantom Blade Zero have also included upscaling. Some titles, like The Blood of Dawnwalker, go out of their way to emphasize that upscaling is not part of the requirements.
Rayman Legends Retold is scheduled to release on PC and consoles on December 3, 2026. It had been set to launch on October 1, but Ubisoft delayed it to allow extra time for polish. It also allows the game to land after big releases like Gears of War, Call of Duty, and, of course, GTA 6.

articles.title: Canvas UI Ships 35 HTML-in-Canvas Components That Run WebGL and WebGPU Effects Over Live DOM
articles.text:
Canvas UI, an open source component library from React Bits creator David Haz, has launched as the first library built on the experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, running GPU effects over real, interactive page content.
The library ships 35 components, including pointer-driven fluid, fire, glass lenses, ASCII filters, VHS grain and particle reveals. Every effect has a WebGL build using GLSL and a WebGPU build using WGSL through vgpu, with wrappers for React, Solid, Preact, Vue, Svelte and dependency-free vanilla TypeScript.
Rather than painting a dead bitmap, most components use Chrome's html-in-canvas API to lay out live DOM inside a canvas, capture it with drawElementImage, upload it as a texture and distort it in a shader. Text stays selectable, links stay clickable, and the content stays in the accessibility tree. Components are distributed as source through a shadcn-compatible registry rather than as a package:
npx shadcn@latest add @canvas-ui/liquid-react
The full experience needs Chrome with the canvas-draw-element flag, or an origin trial token, which runs from Chrome 148 through 150 and is bound to a single domain. Elsewhere, html-in-canvas effects fall back to a plain GPU overlay or render the wrapped content unchanged, and the 3D object components work everywhere.
Because code is copied into the repository, upgrades mean re-running the install command and reconciling local edits. Switching renderers is mostly replacing the installed file with the -webgpu registry item, which adds vgpu and @webgpu/types. The project also documents that Chrome 150's changes to texElementImage2D and copyElementImageToTexture require no migration, since capture happens through the 2D API and uploads use standard texImage2D or copyExternalImageToTexture.
shadcn called it one of the most impressive registries they have seen, and the Chrome for Developers account said it was good to see html-in-canvas empowering new frameworks. Writing a detailed teardown, Flavio Copes praised the unglamorous engineering: the Liquid component stops its loop with IntersectionObserver when off-screen, honours prefers-reduced-motion, and releases textures, programs and listeners on unmount. His advice was to use one strong effect rather than six, and to avoid dashboards, checkout flows and documentation sites.
On Hacker News, one commenter responded to a demo's banner with scepticism about a Google-only capability:
Use Chrome... and aren't we supposed to reject these technologies that allow Google to Embrace, Extend, Extinguish?
Kudos to the artist in spite of this unfortunately esoteric (wish it weren't) concern
Another user replied:
The standardization process requires implementations before standardization. And the most recent comments on the WHATWG issue are from Jake Archibald (Mozilla) and Anne van Kesteren (Apple). This isn't a unilateral Google project.
Accessibility discussion in the WICG explainer is still open, including how drawable subtrees without updated geometry are exposed.
Paper Shaders offers zero-dependency canvas shaders installed from npm, but they sit behind or around content as texture. React Bits, from the same author, animates DOM directly. Canvas UI is the only option using the page itself as shader input, which is also why it depends on a feature that Safari and Firefox do not implement.
Licensing is MIT plus the Commons Clause, so commercial use is allowed but reselling the components is not. The repository has passed 4,600 stars, and the registry is MCP-ready, letting assistants browse and install components through the shadcn MCP server.

articles.title: What managing 150,000 AI agents could look like for database teams
articles.text:
What managing 150,000 AI agents could look like for database teams
The database administrator of the future will spend considerably less time administering databases.
That sounds contradictory, but AI agents are taking over that work. For decades, DBAs have handled the decidedly hands-on work of keeping databases available, performant, secure, and affordable. They provision capacity, troubleshoot slow queries, manage migrations, and step in when something inevitably goes sideways.
AI is already taking on some of that work. At the same time, it is creating a much bigger data infrastructure fleet to manage.
The result is likely to be a very different kind of DBA: one who spends less time tending individual databases and more time supervising the autonomous systems doing it for them.
Congratulations, you’re managing robots now
This shift starts with a familiar problem: more infrastructure needs managing than the people available to manage it.
Database automation is hardly new, but agents can potentially go further than the scripts and rules DBAs already rely on. Rather than automating one predetermined task, an agent can inspect what is happening, decide what needs attention, use tools to act on it, and check whether its intervention worked.
That changes the DBA’s relationship with the database. A performance problem that once required someone to dig through metrics, identify the troublesome query, and decide how to respond could increasingly be investigated by an agent before a human gets involved.
It doesn’t remove the DBA from the equation. Someone still has to decide what an agent can do, where human approval is required, and what happens when it gets something wrong. But the work moves up a layer. Instead of personally performing every operational task, DBAs start managing the systems carrying them out.
Instead of personally performing every operational task, DBAs start managing the systems carrying them out.
And before anyone gets too comfortable with that idea, the number of those systems could become enormous.
150,000 agents walk into a database…
Gartner predicts that the average global Fortune 500 company will have more than 150,000 AI agents in use by 2028, up from fewer than 15 in 2025. Only 13% of organizations currently believe they have the right governance in place to manage them.
Not every agent will need its own database, but plenty will. They will create state, retrieve data, remember previous interactions, and exchange information with other agents. Many will also behave very differently from the applications DBAs are used to supporting: spinning up quickly, sitting idle for long stretches, and suddenly becoming busy when there is work to do.
Nobody is hiring 150,000 DBAs to manage them.
That is the scale problem Yugabyte is targeting with YugabyteDB AMP, or Agentic Multitenant PostgreSQL. Rather than treating each new agent workload as another database for an administrator to provision and babysit, AMP manages databases as a fleet.
The platform packs hundreds of small Postgres workloads onto shared distributed infrastructure while keeping their databases isolated. Lifecycle operations, including provisioning, branching, scaling, migration, and teardown, can be exposed to agents through MCP. Yugabyte has also built specialized agents for setup, migration, performance tuning, and integrations.
In that model, a DBA is no longer provisioning database number 14,372. The interesting job is setting the rules for how database number 14,372 is provisioned, operated, and fine-tuned without them.
Do more with less (no, really)
Scale is only half of the problem. Someone also has to pay for all this stuff.
Agent workloads make traditional capacity planning particularly awkward because many are bursty and frequently idle. Giving every experimental agent permanently provisioned infrastructure could leave companies paying for many databases that spend much of their lives doing very little.
This is where consolidation becomes as much an economic question as an operational one.
AMP’s approach is serverless multitenancy and scale-to-zero. Multiple small workloads share the underlying distributed infrastructure, while customers pay by CPU minute and idle agents consume no compute. Resource governance can impose CPU limits on individual workloads, preventing a single overeager agent from consuming the capacity intended for its neighbors.
The human equivalent matters too. If routine setup, migrations, tuning and other database operations can increasingly be delegated, a smaller database team can potentially look after a much larger estate.
That doesn’t mean companies get to fire the DBAs and hand the keys to the robots. It means scarce database expertise can be spent on architecture, governance, and genuinely difficult problems instead of repeatedly doing the work that software can handle.
Your 2028 database problem starts now
The harder question is what to build underneath all of this when nobody really knows what the enterprise AI estate will look like in two years.
An agent that begins as an experiment today could disappear next month. Another could suddenly become a production application used across the business. Building one infrastructure stack for cheap experiments and another for serious workloads risks creating a migration problem every time an experiment succeeds.
Yugabyte bets that both ends of that journey should sit on the same foundation.
YugabyteDB AMP lets workloads start on serverless Postgres and transition to fully distributed YugabyteDB as their scale and criticality increase, without rewriting the application or migrating data to a different database platform.
Then there is the problem above the individual database: agents need to remember what happened, and not just in a silo.
That’s where Meko fits into the Yugabyte stack. Meko is an agent-native context engine designed for multi-agent AI systems. It provides persistent memory, shared knowledge, decision traces, and autidability across multiple agents, rather than leaving each agent working from its own isolated context. An agent can pick up information learned by another agent instead of retrieving it again or restarting the reasoning process.
Taken together, it delivers a single data stack for an agent’s entire lifecycle: Meko for the context shared among agents, YugabyteDB AMP for agentically managing fleets of Postgres databases, and distributed Postgres-compatible YugabyteDB for workloads that outgrow their serverless beginnings.
Of course, there’s no guarantee that 2028 will look exactly like today’s forecasts. That’s rather the point. The safest architectural bet may be one that doesn’t require you to know in advance which of today’s tiny AI experiments will become tomorrow’s critical applications.
The DBA is still critical in that world, but the job will look different. The DBA of the future may manage fewer databases directly, while taking responsibility for vastly more of them. Instead, managing the autonomous systems that do the administering.

articles.title: Cologne-based Metycle secures €131.7 million credit facility to scale secondary copper and aluminium supply | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Metycle, a Cologne-based supplier of secondary copper and aluminium, has secured a €131.7 million ($150 million) credit facility.
The credit facility was provided by Rivonia Road Capital, a California-headquartered private capital manager specialising in asset-backed lending. The credit facility comes after the company raised €14 million in Series A funding in February 2025. In December 2023, it announced the closure of its €4.7 million Seed funding round.
Daniel Zinn, co-founder and Managing Partner of Rivonia Road Capital, said, “We are proud to support Metycle’s next phase of growth. The company has built a differentiated platform that brings greater transparency, reliability and efficiency to the global recycled metals market, while helping meet growing demand for sustainable raw materials.
“We have been particularly impressed by the management team’s deep industry expertise, disciplined execution and clear vision for scaling the business.
Alongside Rivonia Road Capital, Metycle’s investors and financing partners include 2150, which led its Series A round, Project A, Partech, Market One Capital, Dutch Founders Fund, Crédit Agricole Leasing & Factoring, and SCCF.
Founded in 2022 by Rafael Suchan and Sebastian Brenner, Metycle is a vertically integrated secondary metals company that buys, upgrades and supplies copper, aluminium and other non-ferrous metals to industrial customers globally. The company says it has traded more than €103 million ($120 million) worth of secondary metals over the past 12 months, a growth of 150% versus the prior year, with a team present in 15 countries.
Its business is built on three pillars: a global trading operation that manages sourcing, contracts and risk; SmartSorting Hubs that use AI-enabled sorting, mechanical separation and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy to convert mixed scrap into feedstock matched to buyer specifications; and TrustTrack, a digital layer that links records on material origin, quality, processing and logistics to each batch and trade. Metycle’s first SmartSorting Hub is located in Maasmechelen, Belgium.
Metycle argues that demand for secondary metals is not the constraint holding back the market, but predictability is. It points to the central role of copper and aluminium in electrification, power grids, data centre infrastructure and manufacturing, arguing that reliable secondary supply can enable material security while primary mine supply takes years to develop.
Despite its significance, the secondary metals market remains fragmented, with inconsistent specifications and documentation that make transactions hard to standardise, verify, and finance at scale, a gap it is trying to address with a combination of trading, physical processing, and digital verification.
“Our opportunity is to make secondary supply behave more like an industrial raw material: specified, traceable, and reliably delivered. This facility gives us the capacity to finance substantially more material through that system and serve customers at a much greater scale,” said Suchan, co-founder and CEO, Metycle.
The company says the facility will enable it to finance larger physical metal transactions, move greater volumes of recycled feedstock, and expand its supply to industrial buyers and smelters worldwide. The credit facility also gives it a repeatable framework to speed up execution for suppliers while delivering larger and more consistent flows of specified secondary feedstock to its industrial customers.

articles.title: Trump, presidente da Câmara dos EUA e CEOs de tecnologia terão reunião sobre inteligência artificial na terça (29)
articles.text:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, o presidente da Câmara dos Representantes, Mike Johnson, e CEOs de empresas de tecnologia terão uma reunião sobre inteligência artificial (IA) no dia 29 de setembro. A informação foi divulgada na noite desta quinta-feira (24) por uma fonte familiarizada com o encontro planejado ao Axios.
A reunião ocorre em meio ao avanço acelerado da IA e às discussões sobre como governos devem lidar com os riscos associados a sistemas cada vez mais poderosos. As principais empresas de IA do mundo já alertaram sobre os riscos que a tecnologia representa para a humanidade e defendem que os governos trabalhem em conjunto para administrar seu desenvolvimento.
Ao mesmo tempo, governos de diferentes países têm enfrentado dificuldades para acompanhar a velocidade dos avanços na área.
Reunião já vinha sendo articulada
- O encontro do dia 29 não surgiu de forma repentina. Em 15 de setembro, Johnson afirmou que havia conversado com Trump sobre a realização de uma reunião com os principais executivos do setor de IA na Casa Branca;
- Na ocasião, o presidente da Câmara disse que as empresas poderiam se autorregular e rejeitou a possibilidade de uma moratória sobre o desenvolvimento da tecnologia;
- “Não podemos ter uma moratória sobre o desenvolvimento da IA, certo? Porque então perderemos nossa vantagem sobre a China, e isso terá sérias implicações para a segurança nacional de todas as famílias americanas”, afirmou Johnson;
- Ao mesmo tempo, o republicano defendeu mecanismos para aumentar a segurança dos sistemas. Segundo ele, auditores independentes e transparência por parte das empresas que desenvolvem IA poderiam fazer parte das salvaguardas adotadas para a tecnologia.
EUA e China adotam abordagens diferentes
Os Estados Unidos e a China, as duas principais potências no desenvolvimento de IA, adotaram abordagens diferentes em relação à supervisão da tecnologia.
Trump defende que os Estados Unidos não precisam criar novas regulamentações específicas para a IA. A China, por outro lado, estabeleceu regras para algoritmos de IA e dados utilizados no treinamento dos sistemas.
Entre as exigências chinesas está a determinação de que conteúdos gerados por IA sejam claramente identificados como tal.
O encontro entre Trump, Johnson e executivos de tecnologia ocorre justamente nesse cenário de divergências sobre o nível de controle que deve ser aplicado à tecnologia.
Trump rejeita controle global da IA
Durante a Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas (ONU), na terça-feira (22), Trump afirmou que rejeita iniciativas internacionais para estabelecer um mecanismo global de controle da IA. O presidente estadunidense disse que “rejeita qualquer tentativa de construir um esquema globalista para controlar a inteligência artificial”.
Trump classificou a tecnologia como extraordinária, mas afirmou que os Estados Unidos terão cautela em relação ao seu desenvolvimento.
Leia mais:
- Google, OpenAI e Anthropic se unem para criar órgão de segurança para inteligência artificial
- Efeito “bomba atômica” da IA: mundo volta a tratar uma tecnologia como ameaça à paz mundial após mais de 80 anos
- Trump e Xi parecem ter caminhos diferentes para o futuro das IAs
Segurança sem perder vantagem sobre a China
A discussão sobre possíveis regras para a IA nos Estados Unidos também está diretamente ligada à competição tecnológica com a China.
Ao defender que não haja pausa no desenvolvimento da IA, Johnson argumentou que reduzir o ritmo poderia comprometer a vantagem estadunidense diante dos chineses. Ao mesmo tempo, ele afirmou que seria necessário encontrar uma abordagem equilibrada para criar mecanismos de segurança.
A posição coloca no centro do debate uma questão que deverá acompanhar a reunião: como estabelecer salvaguardas para sistemas cada vez mais avançados sem comprometer o desenvolvimento da tecnologia nos Estados Unidos.
Quem participará da reunião?
A Reuters informou que Trump, Johnson e CEOs de empresas de tecnologia participarão do encontro de 29 de setembro, mas ainda não foram divulgados os nomes dos executivos que estarão presentes nem detalhes sobre a agenda. Mais informações sobre os participantes e os temas que serão discutidos ainda não estavam disponíveis.
A reunião acontecerá poucos dias depois de um jantar na Casa Branca com o presidente chinês Xi Jinping, que também deverá reunir alguns dos principais executivos da indústria de tecnologia. Entre os convidados previstos para o evento estão nomes, como Sam Altman, da OpenAI, Sundar Pichai, da Alphabet, Tim Cook, da Apple, Elon Musk, da Tesla, e Jensen Huang, da Nvidia.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Meta puts its AI assistant on a keychain
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg said Meta’s new personal AI agent Muse has become the “centerpiece” of his AI vision, as he unveiled a new handheld AI “charm” device that will feature the interactive assistant.
The Meta chief used the company’s annual Connect event at its Silicon Valley headquarters to announce Muse Charm, a small pendant-like device that fits on a keychain and is activated by a fingerprint sensor.
The device, which features a screen showing the Muse avatar, will also have real-time voice interactivity and is set to be released in December.
“If you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you,” the chief executive said.
Muse, development of which was first revealed by the FT in May, has helped change the momentum of Zuckerberg’s huge bet on AI, quickly becoming the most downloaded app on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US since its launch two weeks ago.
The easy-to-use app offers consumers a team of autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries, booking travel and organising finances.
Zuckerberg on Wednesday also announced new capabilities for Muse, including the ability to have live conversations with the interactive AI assistant, and insisted that it has “state-of-the-art privacy and security.”
The Meta founder has come under increasing pressure from Wall Street as he pours billions of dollars into AI infrastructure and talent, with Meta’s share price falling by more than a quarter between last September and the beginning of August.
But Meta’s stock has bounced back since the September 8 launch, adding $300 billion to its market capitalisation. The stock was slightly higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday.
The release of a breakout product to Meta’s 3 billion users caps a turbulent two years in which Zuckerberg has repeatedly struggled to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic in developing frontier AI models and features.
Zuckerberg on Wednesday said he believed Muse would “make users money.” As a result, the company would offer a free Muse tier “with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions.”

articles.title: Massive Chinese hack uses AI agents to steal over 600,000 credit cards and hit hundreds of sites with malware
articles.text:
Massive Chinese hack uses AI agents to steal over 600,000 credit cards and hit hundreds of sites with malware
It only cost them around $25 per target
- Gambit researchers uncovered ongoing AI‑driven skimming campaign stealing 600,000+ payment records since July 2026
- Attackers used three autonomous harnesses (Strix, Cairn, Hermes) to compromise dozens of retail sites cheaply
- Victims include major US firms; campaign shows AI enables faster, persistent, low‑cost cyberattacks at scale
In July 2026, a hacker tasked autonomous AI agents to attack retail organizations around the world, deploy credit card skimmers, and steal payment data.
Since then, the bots launched hundreds of attack projects, compromised dozens of organizations, and stole at least 600,000 payment records - and to make matters worse, the campaign is still live, attacking and breaking into websites as we speak.
All of this was reported by security researchers Gambit, who said they managed to recover the operator’s staging server and through it - reconstruct the ongoing campaign. They also saw the skimmers live on victim websites, and sifted through logs and AI claims found on the attacker’s server. In just five days, between September 10 and 15, the agents made 105 attack waves and compromised 27 organizations “to varying degrees.”
Among the victims are a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a “major” US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer. One of the AI tools would use a website ranking service to produce a list of potential targets, focusing primarily on those running custom-built software.
A fistful of dollars
But the victims are not the “interesting” part of this story - the attackers are. Gambit believes they are financially motivated Chinese threat actors. They are using three AI “harnesses” (frameworks, essentially), which can run almost the entire attack chain autonomously, striking around 10 companies a day, for a handful of dollars per company.
In four weeks, the attackers spent around $7,000, meaning that their entire cost for the operation so far was no more than $18,000. Breaking it down, it means that the attacker spent around $25 per target.
“Spread over the companies attacked, this is a marginal cost of a few US dollars to a few tens of US dollars for each targeted company,” Gambit’s researchers said. “The operator’s own cost review gives a similar figure, a mean of $25.46 over 101 completed scans, from $3.13 for the cheapest target to $79.31 for the most expensive.”

“Where access was achieved, it usually took less than a day, and in many cases just a few hours. We also detected instructions in the attacker’s playbook that could disrupt the operations of a company as a result of data deletion or cleanup procedures run by the agent - and this has indeed happened in some of the breaches,” Gambit said.
The three harnesses
The three harnesses are called Strix, Cairn, and Hermes.
Gambit describes Hermes as an open source autonomous AI agent with a persistent memory, skills that the agent wrote and edited itself, a searchable archive of past sessions, scheduled jobs, and a web console. On the staging server the researchers analyzed, it loaded a Chinese system persona called “SOUL - Red Team Operator”, which contained 121 skills (78 attack skills).
“Hermes is the operator’s console for orchestrating the activity and for direct hacking activities,” Gambit explained. “It used Anthropic’s opus-4.6 (after newer models refused its requests), with 1,951 prompts typed by the human across 260 sessions - only a few prompts per target. The human prompts are short instructions in Chinese, usually launching an attack, tasking the agent with a general next step, or what to do next after achieving access.”
Strix is an open-source AI pentest tool, while Cairn is an autonomous pentest engine. It receives target domains and an objective, such as to get a shell or admin access, then runs for hours until it achieves the objective, times out, or is stopped. Cairn used DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, it was said.
Gambit’s researchers seem to be rather impressed with the campaign. They described it as very low cost, with a level of patience, persistence, and creativity that most human attackers would be “unlikely to sustain”, managing to achieve “far greater results, far faster.”
They have also called to arms, urging organizations to “adapt to a reality where attacks are significantly faster and more comprehensive.” To do that, they must adopt a resilience-first mentality and deploy a security stack that can match the AI on speed.
Many of the affected organizations were notified, and the skimmers were removed, they said.

articles.title: Google Photos 'Clueless'-inspired virtual closet is now available on Android and iOS | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google’s new AI-powered feature that turns photos of your outfits into a virtual closet — one seemingly inspired by Cher’s iconic virtual wardrobe app featured in the movie “Clueless” — is now available to everyone in the U.S., Brazil, and India, on both iOS and Android devices.
The company announced the feature earlier this year with plans to begin the rollout in the summer. Android users gained access first, starting in June, and now the virtual closet is available to all Android and iOS users in the supported markets.
The idea of a digital closet in “Clueless” was meant to highlight Cher’s privileged life, where she had so many outfits that she needed a digital system to help her choose what to wear and keep everything organized. Now, you don’t have to be a rich Beverly Hills teenager to take advantage of such technology.
Instead, Google uses AI technology to create a copy of your wardrobe, based on the items you wore in your photos. From the app, you can also filter items by category — like tops, bottoms, jewelry, and more — then mix and match them to create different outfits.
Google says the feature is designed to assist the user, and the data about how you dress or what you wear is not being shared with third parties, like retailers.
The broader rollout of the virtual closet feature arrives alongside a handful of other Google Photos updates, including a way to select, brighten, and share photos using a single prompt in Gemini Spark, an upgraded markup tool, and more Remix templates that use AI to transform your photos. (The Gemini Spark feature requires a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription in the U.S.)
With Markup, you’ll be able to use a redacting pen to blur sensitive information like license plates, access precise thickness sliders for custom sketches, and pick from different fonts when adding text to photos.
For Android users, there are also new photo filters, called “Moods,” that let you give your images different looks, like 35mm film, 2000s digicam, and more.

articles.title: Wenn KI deinen Job übernimmt: Diese Rechte kannst du bei einer Kündigung für dich nutzen
articles.text:
Wenn KI deinen Job übernimmt: Diese Rechte kannst du bei einer Kündigung für dich nutzen
Nathalie Oberthür ist Fachanwältin für Arbeitsrecht und Partnerin bei der Kanzlei RPO, die sowohl Arbeitgeber als auch Arbeitnehmer und Betriebsräte vertritt. Einer von Oberthürs Schwerpunkten ist die Vertretung von Klient:innen in Kündigungsschutzverfahren. articles.title: Microsoft is killing off the ‘Copilot Plus PC’ brand
articles.text:
Remember when Microsoft wanted everyone to know that “Copilot Plus PCs” were the ones to get, because those were the PCs that that’d have enough built-in AI muscle to get things done? Two and a half years later, Microsoft and Qualcomm seem to be admitting the brand is already dead.
Microsoft is killing off the ‘Copilot Plus PC’ brand
What will Microsoft’s next buzzword be?
What will Microsoft’s next buzzword be?
Windows Central’s Zac Bowden reports that even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. “These are not called Copilot Plus PCs,” Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrom told the publication.
Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s SVP of compute and gaming, seemed to agree that the brand’s time is done, telling Bowden that computers that offer the same experiences will “probably” not use that branding anymore.
It’s not surprising to me that Microsoft and its partners would back away. Back in 2024, smart minds pointed out that (almost) every PC would soon contain the basic levels of AI hardware that the brand was supposed to reflect. The flagship feature of Copilot Plus PCs, Microsoft’s Recall feature, wasn’t well received, and Microsoft took flak for constantly annoying Windows users with AI upsells, not to mention the dedicated Copilot keyboard key that you can now finally remap.
Besides, Microsoft’s flagship hardware is now about to have Nvidia chips instead, which will supposedly kick off a new era of personal AI in Windows. On October 7th, when Microsoft hosts a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” I’m guessing it will have a shiny new brand to replace “Copilot Plus PC.”

articles.title: Apple promete solucionar un molesto bug que provoca cuelgues en los iPhone 18 Pro
articles.text:
Usuarios de los iPhone 18 Pro y Pro Max se han topado con un molesto bug que provoca cuelgues y reinicios forzados, pero una solución está en camino. Según publica 9to5Mac, Apple ha confirmado que la próxima semana se lanzará una actualización que corregirá un inconveniente vinculado con Face ID.
En los últimos días aparecieron varios reportes que indicaban que los iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max se bloqueaban tras un intento fallido de desbloqueo a través del reconocimiento facial. Esto provocaba que los dispositivos se reiniciaran pocos segundos más tardes, sin saber realmente cuál era la raíz del problema.
En un principio se especuló con que podía ser un fallo de hardware vinculado con la nueva ubicación de la cámara infrarroja de Face ID. Sin embargo, todo apunta a que se trata de un bug en iOS 27, lo cual es un alivio para quienes creían que el problema radicaba en un potencial desperfecto de su iPhone 18 Pro o Pro Max y que tendrían que cambiarlo por otra unidad.
De acuerdo con el reporte, el fix estará disponible a principios de la próxima semana. De modo que una mera actualización del sistema operativo sería suficiente para que Face ID funcione con normalidad y no "congele" los iPhone 18 Pro tras un intento de autenticación fallido.
Un fallo de software, la causa de los cuelgues de los nuevos iPhone 18 Pro
Que la causa de los cuelgues de los iPhone 18 Pro y Pro Max fuese un problema de hardware, tenía su lógica. Después de todo, Apple ha decidido reubicar el sensor infrarrojo de Face ID en la esquina superior izquierda de la pantalla, debajo del panel. Esto ha permitido a la compañía implementar una Isla Dinámica bastante más pequeña que la vista en modelos anteriores.
Sin embargo, la confirmación por parte de Apple de que el inconveniente está en el software y no en un componente físico, lleva calma a los compradores del más reciente móvil de la manzana. Y la rapidez de la solución también hace pensar que no se trata de un inconveniente extremadamente complejo.
De momento, se desconoce si existe alguna recomendación en particular para tratar de mitigar el fallo de cuelgues en los iPhone 18 Pro. Según se reporta, los intentos fallidos con Face ID se producían el bloquear parte del rostro u oscurecerlo en demasía. Pero como el fallo no afecta a todas las unidades por igual, es difícil saber hasta qué punto se puede contrarrestar el bug. Por suerte, en cuestión de pocos días debería resolverse de forma definitiva.

articles.title: China’s ultimate gaming GPU hits a performance wall — LX 7G100 barely crawls past AMD’s nine-year-old RX 580; hyped as an RTX 4060 rival, China's LX 7G100 trails RTX 2060 by 35%
articles.text:
China’s ultimate gaming GPU hits a performance wall — LX 7G100 barely crawls past AMD’s nine-year-old RX 580; hyped as an RTX 4060 rival, China's LX 7G100 trails RTX 2060 by 35%
Despite strong launch sales, the Lisuan Tech LX 7G100 was clearly more of a domestic win for China than a contender against the best graphics cards on the market. Recent benchmark results published by German outlet PC Games Hardware (PCGH) show that the Chinese-made LX 7G100 still has a long way to go, offering only comparable performance to the nine-year-old Radeon RX 580 — but trailing by as much as 35% behind the seven-year-old GeForce RTX 2060.
Originally touted as a competitor to the GeForce RTX 4060, the LX 7G100 hit the market with high expectations. Initial benchmarks, however, quickly dispelled much of the early hype. Now, four months after its launch and following several driver updates, we once again see the LX 7G100 in the spotlight, but despite ongoing driver refinements, the graphics card's performance looks like it has flatlined.
The LX 7G100’s current performance closely matches AMD’s Radeon RX 580 and delivers a modest 5% boost over the Polaris-based card. It also outpaces Nvidia’s GeForce GTX 1060 6GB by a notable 23%. In its current state, the LX 7G100 does not have what it takes to challenge more modern models in the upper echelon of the mid-range graphics card market.
The LX 7G100 lags by more than 2.2X behind current models, such as the GeForce RTX 4060 or GeForce RX 5050. When benchmarked against the latest GeForce RTX 5060, the LX 7G100 delivers only about a third of the performance. An obvious technological gap remains between Lisuan Tech and industry giants such as Nvidia, AMD, and even Intel, and it still has a lot of catching up to do.
Lisuan Tech LX 7G100 Benchmarks
| Graphics Card | 14 Game Performance Index | Relative Performance Versus GeForce RTX 5060 | 
|---|---|---|
| GeForce RTX 5060 | 33.0 | 100% | 
| Arc B580 | 31.6 | 96% | 
| Radeon RX 9060 | 31.2 | 94% | 
| Radeon RX 7600 XT | 28.8 | 87% | 
| Arc A770 16GB | 27.1 | 82% | 
| Arc B570 | 26.8 | 81% | 
| Radeon RX 7600 | 25.8 | 78% | 
| GeForce RTX 4060 | 25.2 | 76% | 
| GeForce RTX 5050 | 24.9 | 75% | 
| GeForce RTX 3060 12GB | 23.3 | 71% | 
| Radeon RX 5700 XT | 22.1 | 67% | 
| GeForce GTX 1080 Ti | 21.7 | 66% | 
| Radeon RX 6600 | 20.0 | 61% | 
| GeForce RTX 2060 | 17.2 | 52% | 
| LX 7G100 | 11.1 | 34% | 
| Radeon RX 580 | 10.6 | 32% | 
| GeForce GTX 1060 6GB | 9.0 | 27% | 
In its defense, the LX 7G100 has already cleared one of the biggest hurdles that typically hinder Chinese chipmakers: driver support. Many graphics cards from emerging Chinese manufacturers have historically suffered from poor compatibility and software support. Lisuan Tech not only became the first Chinese chipmaker to obtain WHQL support for a graphics card, but the LX 7G100 launched with stable DirectX 12 gaming compatibility from the get-go. This alone has enabled the LX 7G100 to run a wide variety of modern games, including Cyberpunk 2077, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Assassin’s Creed Shadows, and Battlefield 6, to name a few.
Lisuan Tech is clearly committing to improving its drivers. In the past four months alone, the Chinese chipmaker has rolled out three WHQL-certified driver updates. Drivers take time to mature, and given that the LX 7G100 has not even been on the market for a year, it is unreasonable to expect Lisuan Tech to match decades of expertise like Nvidia and AMD.
From a hardware standpoint, the LX 7G100, which leverages TSMC’s N6 FinFET process node, is not a bad graphics card. The silicon houses 6,144 shading units and clocks up to 2,000 MHz to deliver a peak FP32 performance of 24.5 TFLOPs. The LX 7G100's 12GB of GDDR6 memory runs across a 192-bit memory interface to provide a maximum bandwidth of up to 432 GB/s. On paper, these metrics place the LX 7G100 close to the GeForce RTX 3060 12GB or Radeon RX 6700 XT. Currently, the GeForce RTX 3060 12GB is twice as fast as the LX 7G100.

A 2X performance gap is certainly not something that's easy to close. Who knows just how much is left in the tank for the LX 7G100. Maybe Lisuan Tech has already pushed the hardware to its limits, or maybe some driver magic will put the LX 7G100 a few steps closer to the GeForce RTX 3060 12GB. Only time will tell, and it will be interesting to revisit the LX 7G100 in a few months' time.
