articles.title: Energiebranche: CX schlägt den günstigsten Tarif
articles.text:
Was entscheidet, ob ein Energiekunde bleibt – wenn nicht der Preis?
Der Wettbewerb verlagert sich
Es war lange Zeit eine einfache Gleichung: Wer den günstigsten Tarif anbietet, gewinnt den Kunden. Wer ihn günstig hält, behält ihn. Diese Logik hat die Energiebranche über Jahre geprägt, doch sie greift immer weniger.
Tarife werden transparenter, Vergleichsportale mächtiger, Anbieterwechsel reibungsloser. Was einmal Kunden gehalten hat, verliert an Wirkung. Der Preis bleibt relevant. Aber er reicht nicht mehr aus, um eine Kundenbeziehung zu tragen.
Was bleibt, wenn der Tarif sich nicht mehr unterscheidet? Die Erfahrung, die ein Unternehmen hinterlässt. Die Art, wie es kommuniziert, wenn etwas nicht stimmt. Wie es sich anfühlt, ein Anliegen zu klären und eine Antwort zu bekommen, die wirklich weiterhilft. Customer Experience ist kein Servicethema. Sie ist die Frage, womit Energieunternehmen künftig noch unverwechselbar sind.
Jede Interaktion prägt die Marke
Was Kunden über ein Energieunternehmen denken, entsteht selten in großen Momenten, sondern in den alltäglichen Interaktionen, von denen es mehr gibt, als man zunächst vermuten würde. Ob eine Anfrage schnell und verständlich gelöst wird, ob Kommunikation proaktiv kommt oder ob Self-Service-Angebote wirklich funktionieren: Jeder dieser Kontaktpunkte ist eine stille Entscheidung. Vertrauen aufbauen oder abbauen, Bindung stärken oder schwächen.
In einem Markt, in dem der nächste Anbieter nur einen Klick entfernt ist, summieren sich diese Momente schneller, als es Preismodelle ausgleichen können. Wer seine Customer Journey deshalb nur als Abfolge von Prozessen betrachtet, die es zu optimieren gilt, denkt zu kurz. Es geht um Momente, die eine Marke prägen und darüber entscheiden, ob ein Kunde bleibt, wechselt oder weiterempfiehlt.
Warum Kundenbindung sich rechnet und Wechsel teuer ist
Wer Kundenbindung als weiches Ziel betrachtet, unterschätzt ihren wirtschaftlichen Wert. Ein Kunde, der bleibt, ist nicht nur gesicherter Umsatz. Er ist vermiedener Akquisitionsaufwand, ein stabilerer Planungshorizont und ein potenzieller Multiplikator.
Umgekehrt gilt: Wechsel ist teuer. Nicht nur wegen der Kosten für Neukundengewinnung, sondern weil abwandernde Kunden oft in Momenten gehen, in denen eine bessere Erfahrung sie hätte halten können. Schlechte Serviceerlebnisse, fehlende Transparenz bei Preisanpassungen, ungelöste Anliegen: Das sind keine Zufälle, sondern vermeidbare Verluste.
Die Verbindung aus Markenerlebnis und wirtschaftlichem Wert ist damit keine weiche These, sondern eine unternehmerische Entscheidung. Wer in die Qualität der Kundenbeziehung investiert, investiert in die Stabilität seines Geschäftsmodells, gerade in einem Markt, der sich strukturell weiter liberalisiert.
Technologie und KI als Gestaltungsmittel, nicht als Selbstzweck
Hier kommt Technologie ins Spiel, aber anders, als sie oft diskutiert wird. KI ist in der Energiebranche kein Differenzierungsmerkmal mehr: über 80 Prozent der KI-Anbieter für die Energiewirtschaft sind mittlerweile branchenspezialisiert, 2024 waren es erst 60 Prozent. Entscheidend ist, was Unternehmen daraus machen. Denn nicht die Technologie selbst schafft Unverwechselbarkeit, sondern die Frage, wo und wie sie eingesetzt wird.
Wer Technologie primär als Kostenhebel betrachtet, optimiert Teilbereiche und tut damit genau das, was aktuell 36 Prozent der Energieunternehmen tun, die im größten KI-Nutzen vor allem Effizienzgewinne sehen, während nur 22 Prozent auf das Kundenerlebnis zielen. Wer sie als Gestaltungsmittel für Kundenerlebnisse begreift, verändert die Beziehung zur Marke. Der Unterschied liegt nicht in der Technologie selbst, sondern in der Frage, mit der man anfängt. „Wie reduzieren wir Kontaktvolumen?“ führt zu einem anderen Ergebnis als: „Wie stellen wir sicher, dass Kunden in kritischen Momenten die Erfahrung machen, die sie bindet?“ Beide Fragen können zur selben Lösung führen, aber nur die zweite baut eine Marke.
Proaktive Kommunikation, intuitive Self-Service-Angebote, KI-gestützte Erkennung von Abwanderungsrisiken, bevor ein Kunde kündigt: Das sind keine reinen Effizienzmaßnahmen, sondern Markenerlebnisse. Und sie entstehen nur, wenn Technologie von Anfang an im Dienst der Kundenbindung gedacht wird, nicht umgekehrt.
Eine positive Customer Journey entscheidet über den weiteren Prozess der Kundenbindung. (Bild: Getty Images)
Warum das Zusammendenken entscheidet
Der häufigste Grund, warum CX-Initiativen in der Energiebranche hinter ihren Möglichkeiten bleiben, ist nicht fehlende Ambition, sondern fehlende Verbindung.
Wenn CX-Strategie, Technologieprojekte und operative Umsetzung in getrennten Verantwortlichkeiten laufen, entstehen Reibungsverluste, die sich im Kundenerlebnis zeigen, auch wenn jeder Bereich für sich funktioniert. Prozesse sind optimiert, aber nicht verbunden. Lösungen sind implementiert, aber nicht integriert. Kommunikation ist geplant, aber operativ nicht skalierbar.
Die Antwort auf die Frage, was ein Energieunternehmen künftig unverwechselbar macht, lässt sich nicht in einer Abteilung entwickeln. Sie entsteht, wenn Customer Experience, Technologie und Operations gemeinsam auf dasselbe Ziel ausgerichtet sind: eine Kundenbeziehung, die hält.
Erfahrung, die zählt
Concentrix begleitet Energieunternehmen im DACH-Raum und weltweit durch genau diesen Prozess. Was Concentrix dabei einbringt, ist ein Ansatz, der Kompetenzen vereint, die in der Praxis selten in einer Hand liegen: die strategische Perspektive eines Consultants, die technische Umsetzungsstärke eines Integrators und die operative Verlässlichkeit eines langfristigen Outsourcing-Partners. Verbunden mit tiefem Branchenwissen und echter Expertise in Customer Experience und Enterprise-Prozessen.
Dieser Ansatz ermöglicht es, nicht nur zu beraten oder zu implementieren, sondern Verantwortung über den gesamten Prozess zu übernehmen: von der ersten strategischen Frage bis in den laufenden Betrieb. Und genau das ist der Unterschied, der darüber entscheidet, ob aus einer CX-Initiative ein Kundenerlebnis wird, das wirklich hält.
Folge Concentrix auf LinkedIn für weitere Perspektiven zu CX, KI und Transformation in der Energiebranche.
Was künftig unverwechselbar macht
Tarife werden sich weiter angleichen, Wechsel werden einfacher werden. Was bleibt, ist die Frage, welche Erfahrung ein Energieunternehmen hinterlässt. Unternehmen, die das heute als strategische Frage begreifen, bauen einen Vorsprung auf, den kein Preismodell schnell einholt.
Mehr aus Customer Experience machen
Wie Customer Experience in der Energiebranche konkret wirkt und welche Leitfragen Entscheider dabei leiten sollten, zeigt der Concentrix-Blog: Warum der günstigste Tarif den Klick gewinnt, aber nicht die Beziehung

articles.title: Sadly, this $1,549 RTX 5070-equipped gaming PC is a very good deal
articles.text:
While PC component prices remain high, you can save a good bit of money on a system by purchasing a prebuilt desktop. Walmart has a well-equipped CyberPowerPC gaming PC on sale for $1,549, almost $600 off its original price of $2,139. It’s powered by an Intel Core i7-14700KF processor, and paired with 32GB of 6000MHz DDR5 memory and an Nvidia RTX 5070 Founders Edition with 12GB of VRAM. The case is a CyberPowerPC MA-O1, an in-house design with extensive cooling options and three dedicated knobs for adjusting internal RGB lighting colors.
Sadly, this $1,549 RTX 5070-equipped gaming PC is a very good deal
We also spotted a discounted OLED gaming monitor, Anker wireless chargers, and Nintendo’s sale is still going.
While it might not feel like it at first blush, this is a solid value for a gaming PC that’s ready to rock out of the box. The RTX 5070 in this machine is likely to run you upwards of $800 by itself at the moment (it launched in 2025 for $549), and 32GB of fast memory can be $400 or more. For just a small premium, you get those components packed into a nice case with a panoramic glass panel and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD inside. The whole kit is tested, with a one year warranty for parts and labor. It also includes a keyboard and mouse, so you can start gaming right away once it arrives.
Other deals to consider
- If you need a gaming monitor with spectacular colors and clarity to go with your new gaming PC, Newegg has the ASRock PGO27QSA-W discounted to $299.33, a significant discount from its original price of $476. This 27-inch screen supports 1440p resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate with FreeSync Premium for variable refresh rate, and an OLED panel for deep black levels.
- A two pack of Anker Zolo MagSafe wireless chargers is discounted to $25.99 at Amazon, where it would normally cost $39.99. Each charger is Qi2 certified, with support for up to 15W of charging power, and includes a five-foot cable for convenient positioning on your desk or nightstand. You’ll have to use your own wall charger, though.
- The Nintendo Customer Appreciation sale is live until September 26th at 8:59 PM PT, and is a great time to pick up an extra set of controllers, among other game and accessory deals. The Switch Pro Controller is only $56 (usually around $70) at both Amazon and Best Buy, and a duo of Joy-Con are only $62.99 at Best Buy, although only the pastel purple and green combo are currently in stock. The controllers are compatible with both the original Switch and Switch 2, although owners of the newer console will need a separate charger, and they won’t wake the system from sleep.

articles.title: Lovable's annualized revenue crosses $600M as vibe coding takes off | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Lovable has crossed annual run-rate revenue of $600 million, the company’s co-founder Fabian Hedin said at the HumanX summit in Amsterdam on Thursday. The vibe-coding platform in June said that number was around $500 million.
Hedin said the startup has focused on growing its enterprise business, and claimed that people at two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies are now using its product. Its customers include Microsoft, Nvidia, and Deutsche Telekom.
He also said apps created by users on the platform are together attracting nearly a billion views per month.
“You can use these tools [like Codex or Claude code] to output code. The difference is that Lovable does not output code. The output is a product, and increasingly so, a business. We do a lot of things around hosting, deployment, and scaling apps. We have close to a billion visits per month to the apps that we’ve created, which is an order of magnitude more than Lovable itself,” he said.
The company has raised over $700 million in two rounds just eight months apart. Last December, it raised $300 million from Menlo Ventures and CapitalG at a $6.6 billion valuation. Then, this August, the startup raised $400 million from Menlo Ventures and the Scaleup Europe Fund at a $13.3 billion valuation.
Lovable clarified that Hadin meant to say that people at two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies are using the platform.

articles.title: Aderant builds intelligent ticket triage with Amazon Nova | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Aderant builds intelligent ticket triage with Amazon Nova
This guest post is co-written by Angela Mapes and Adam Walker of Aderant.
In this post, we share how Aderant, a global provider of business management software for the legal industry, built an intelligent ticket triage system using Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock. Aderant’s solution automates much of the context gathering, classification, routing, and knowledge enrichment required for support-ticket triage.
The Intelligent Ticket Analyzer supports Aderant’s 38-person SierraOps team, which operates Expert Sierra across 268 client environments globally. It reviews newly submitted, unassigned tickets during scheduled hourly processing cycles on business days. It gathers operational context from Jira, Confluence, Amazon Athena, and Microsoft SharePoint to recommend a team assignment and resolution starting point, and it automates approved routing and communication actions.
During the first 2.5 weeks of production, from June 30 through July 17, 2026, the analyzer reviewed 109 tickets and achieved approximately 96% routing accuracy. Based on the team’s measured pre-automation triage baseline, Aderant estimates that the system recovers 8–14 engineering hours per week at a total operating cost of less than $30 per month.
The deployment extends Aderant’s earlier AI journey from unified search and on-demand investigation with Amazon Quick to scheduled, autonomous operational workflows powered by Amazon Nova.
The challenge: Reduce operational toil without losing control
Aderant’s SierraOps team processes an average of 34–40 support tickets per week. Before automation, each ticket required 15–25 minutes of manual investigation before resolution work could begin. Engineers had to interpret the request, locate client-environment details, determine ownership, search documentation and ticket history, and then assign or redirect the work.
The cost was broader than triage time alone. Misrouted tickets could remain in the wrong queue until an engineer identified them, while less-experienced team members needed more time or senior-engineer guidance to find the right context and make routing decisions.
Aderant needed automated, repeatable investigative workflows so engineers could focus on complex troubleshooting, platform improvement, and proactive operations while preserving human review for lower-confidence decisions.
The solution: Autonomous ticket analysis with human safeguards using Amazon Nova
Aderant built the Intelligent Ticket Analyzer as a serverless workflow orchestrated by a single AWS Lambda function and triggered hourly on weekdays by Amazon EventBridge. For each unassigned ticket in the CloudOps queue, the solution follows five stages:
- Identify: Retrieve unassigned tickets from Jira.
- Enrich: Gather client metadata from Amazon Athena, relevant knowledge from Confluence and SharePoint, and comparable resolved tickets from Jira.
- Classify: Send the ticket and assembled context to Amazon Nova Lite through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API for structured classification and recommended next steps.
- Act: Post analysis and acknowledgments, reassign misrouted tickets, notify the appropriate Microsoft Teams channel, and apply predefined actions for support-resolvable scenarios.
- Observe and improve: Publish operational metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and route lower-confidence classifications to human review.
Routing and reassignment decisions can operate autonomously when confidence meets the configured threshold. Lower-confidence tickets are flagged for human review. The team monitors confidence, misroutes, and processing latency, reviews routing corrections weekly, and uses the findings to refine prompts and routing logic.
Why Amazon Nova
Aderant chose Amazon Nova Lite after evaluating multiple foundation models through Amazon Bedrock using real ticket data. Three factors drove the decision.
Operational specificity: In comparisons using the same ticket content, environment data, runbooks, and resolution history, the team found that Amazon Nova Lite extracted more specific resolution steps and correlated past issues more effectively than the other evaluated models.
Native AWS integration: Amazon Nova Lite integrates with the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, the AWS SDK, and the existing AWS environment, reducing the need for an additional external model provider or vendor contract.
Economics at ticket scale: The model’s cost profile made it practical to analyze routine tickets, not only high-priority cases. In the initial production period, total system cost remained under $30 per month and Bedrock inference cost remained under $1 per month.
Architecture
The following diagram shows the architecture of the Intelligent Ticket Analyzer. The data flow moves sequentially from left to right through seven stages, all deployed through a single AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) and AWS CloudFormation template.
Amazon EventBridge triggers AWS Lambda. The function retrieves credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, queries environment metadata through Amazon Athena, and calls Jira, Confluence, and Microsoft Graph APIs for ticket and knowledge context. Amazon Bedrock returns structured classification output from Amazon Nova Lite. Amazon DynamoDB supports cross-ticket pattern tracking, while Jira, Microsoft Teams, and Confluence receive the resulting actions and updates. Amazon CloudWatch provides operational monitoring.
Data boundary: The analyzer uses internal operational ticket data, operational metadata, and internal knowledge sources. It does not access, process, or store client matter data or client application business data.
Early operational impact
The first 2.5 weeks of production provided an early view of both accuracy and efficiency. Routing accuracy was measured by comparing the analyzer’s assignment with the team that ultimately resolved each ticket. Time savings were based on a four-week pre-deployment baseline of 15–25 minutes of manual triage per ticket.
| Metric | Early production result | 
| Production measurement period | June 30–July 17, 2026 | 
| Tickets analyzed | 109 | 
| Routing accuracy | Approximately 96% (4 misroutes) | 
| Average ticket volume | 34–40 per week | 
| Measured manual triage baseline | 15–25 minutes per ticket | 
| Estimated engineering time recovered | 8–14 hours per week | 
| Estimated monthly time recovered | 32–56 hours | 
| Total system cost | Under $30 per month | 
| Amazon Bedrock inference cost | Under $1 per month | 
The recovered capacity is redirected toward complex troubleshooting, infrastructure improvements, and proactive work requiring human judgment. These findings represent an early production period and should be read as initial operational results rather than a long-term performance benchmark.
Three production examples
Correcting a misrouted request 
         A ticket describing a 404 error on an Azure DevOps site arrived in the CloudOps AWS queue. The analyzer classified it as a CloudOps Azure issue, updated the team field, and notified the requester of the reroute.
Accelerating resolution readiness 
         For an after-hours remote-access configuration request, the analyzer combined client-environment data with a relevant Confluence article and posted the procedure as an internal comment. The engineer completed the task in under 30 minutes the next morning without additional research.
Extending expertise to newer engineers 
         For a deployment request requiring PowerShell scripts and service verification, the analyzer provided commands, expected outputs, troubleshooting guidance, and related references. The engineer resolved the request the same day without escalating to a senior engineer.
Turning recurring issues into reusable knowledge
The analyzer also detects recurring issue patterns across clients running the same software version. When the configured threshold is reached, the workflow records the pattern, updates a dedicated Confluence tracking page, monitors resolved tickets for confirmed fixes, and links future matching tickets to the documented resolution.
This creates a continuous knowledge loop: identify a recurring pattern, document it, capture the confirmed resolution, and make that resolution available to future tickets. The capability reduces repeated discovery work and helps operational knowledge become reusable across the team.
Accelerating onboarding and knowledge access
Before the analyzer, unfamiliar ticket types often required manual Confluence searches or guidance from senior engineers. The automated workflow now places client-environment context, matched knowledge articles, and recommended steps directly in the ticket before an engineer begins work.
This does not replace engineering judgment. It gives newer engineers a stronger starting point, helps them handle unfamiliar scenarios earlier in onboarding, and allows experienced engineers to spend more time on complex work.
Five weeks from concept to production
Aderant used progressive validation rather than moving directly to autonomous actions:
- Rules-based start: A Jira automation rule established the initial routing concept but could not incorporate AWS context, ticket history, or model reasoning.
- AI-assisted validation: The existing Amazon Quick CloudOps Helper agent demonstrated that operational data could support useful routing and resolution recommendations.
- Production build: The team implemented the workflow with AWS Lambda and Amazon Nova Lite. Kiro supported integration scaffolding, architecture validation, and test generation.
- Monitoring-only testing: The analyzer ran against live tickets for approximately two weeks while its classifications were compared with manual decisions and the prompts and routing logic were refined.
- Production launch: The solution went live June 30, 2026, five weeks after the initial concept.
Looking ahead
Deeper client-history analysis: Connect related tickets over time to provide a broader view of ongoing client work.
Improved knowledge matching: Evaluate Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for semantic matching when ticket and documentation terminology differ.
Layered AI support: Continue using the analyzer for scheduled triage while retaining the CloudOps Helper bot for deeper, on-demand investigation and follow-up questions.
Conclusion
Aderant’s Intelligent Ticket Analyzer shows how operations teams can move from AI-assisted search to governed automation. In its first 2.5 weeks of production, the system reviewed 109 tickets, achieved approximately 96% routing accuracy, and was estimated to recover 8–14 engineering hours each week while operating for less than $30 per month.
The central design choice was not to ask AI to replace engineers or independently solve every issue. Instead, Aderant applied Amazon Nova Lite to the repeatable investigative work that delayed resolution: assembling context, identifying relevant knowledge, detecting patterns, and routing work with a useful starting point. Human review remains part of the control model for lower-confidence decisions.
By combining autonomous triage, operational safeguards, and a reusable knowledge loop, Aderant created a scalable foundation for reducing operational toil and directing engineering capacity toward higher-value work.
Learn more about Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Nova.

articles.title: How founders are rethinking capital in the AI era | BetaKit
articles.text:
AI is giving early-stage founders more room to experiment before raising significant amounts of capital, and this is changing how entrepreneurs think about when to raise and where that money gets deployed.
“What has become possible with a small team of really good people is phenomenal.”
George Babu, Aire Labs
George Babu is taking a more deliberate fundraising approach to his latest venture, Toronto-based Aire Labs. In 2007, he joined David Stein and Daniel Debow to co-found Toronto-based performance management company Rypple, which was acquired by Salesforce in 2011. He later co-founded San Francisco and Toronto based robotics firm Kindred Systems before it was acquired by the Ocado Group in 2020.
When he built Kindred, the company raised substantial capital early, which Babu said created room for mistakes. With Aire Labs, he is focused on keeping the company lean while it experiments.
“You can take very little capital, have a lot of control, and do a lot of experiments until you feel confident, and then you take a lot of capital,” Babu said on a recent episode of The Gradient Ascent Podcast.
The episode, hosted by CIBC Innovation Banking Executive Managing Director Paul McKinlay and CIBC Capital Markets Managing Director Daniel Lee, featured Babu and Gideon Hayden, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Leaders Fund.
The conversation explored a changing funding calculus for tech companies as AI raises investor expectations, expands what small teams can accomplish, and shifts where startups allocate their spending.
Capital follows conviction
At project development platform Aire Labs, AI has already helped Babu’s team run more experiments without having to add headcount. The company has accumulated hundreds of transcripts from customer discovery calls that can be searched and analyzed when the team is considering building a new feature. AI tools also allow Aire Labs to customize and test messaging for particular customers and market segments, without the need for a 40-person team.
“What has become possible with a small team of really good people is phenomenal,” Babu said. “I can run way more experiments on much less capital, until I find that thing that then can be venture-fuelled. And you can keep doing that again and again and again, and ultimately that’s how you build an enduring company. You just keep making these bets.”
Babu pointed to Shopify’s early development as an example, noting the company did not take much capital in its early days because the market didn’t have conviction that another e-commerce company was needed at the time.
“They were very lean,” Babu said of Shopify. “They had to build their culture, build their processes, find where the real product-market fit was, and then they could raise a ton of money and go and just dominate the market.”
Staying lean early has become particularly important as expectations for venture-backed startups have skyrocketed. Babu noted that the bar for Seed and Series A startups is considerably higher compared to a few years ago, and raising a larger round creates an expectation that the money will be put to work quickly.
“If you’re going to take a lot of money, you better go fast and very far,” Babu added. “I don’t think it changes that you still need a lot of capital to build an enduring company.”
What a round buys
None of this means that AI has made building a successful company cheap, according to Hayden. “We have not seen the cost of building come down at all. If anything, it’s gone up,” he said.
His firm, which invests primarily at the seed and Series A stages across enterprise software, cybersecurity, and AI-native infrastructure, has seen a change in the composition of startup spending. He explained that many R&D-heavy teams plan to add employees at a slower pace because existing engineers can do more in less time with the help of AI tools. He has seen budgets increasingly account for both engineers and the token or compute spending required to equip those employees.
“What these tools effectively allow you to do is buy time,” Hayden said, noting that AI can give a company the capacity of many engineers working simultaneously, which compresses the time it takes to pursue an opportunity.
McKinlay noted that product development is only one part of a company’s cost base, and that reaching and retaining customers remains the most expensive part of company building. Babu estimated that a company may end up spending 30 percent of the budget on R&D and 70 percent on go-to-market, sales, and marketing, which makes the application of AI in the latter functions of the business particularly important to him.
AI also introduces a new variable into startup spending: model costs can be difficult to predict. “Part of enterprise buying enterprise software as a subscription is [that] you have some predictability to what that line item is,” McKinlay said. “AI can throw a wrench in that to some extent.”
While he expects the cost of AI tools to get cheaper in time, Babu has already seen Aire Labs’ bills rise enough in the short term to accelerate plans for multi-model workflows. His company has made its own architecture model-agnostic, which allows it to switch between providers if prices change.
“Right now, everyone’s exploring and no one minds the bills, but once you operationalize something, you don’t want to pay that bill,” Babu said. “The vendors that optimize [for model costs] from the beginning are going to be in a better position than those that don’t.”
At the seed and Series A stages, Leaders Fund places relatively little emphasis on a company’s margin profile, though the firm does need to believe the business can eventually produce sustainable unit economics.
The more immediate concern is whether the company is creating products customers find sufficiently valuable. Hayden expects this test to become more important as the enthusiasm around AI adoption matures. He sees many businesses currently buying AI products because of pressure to demonstrate that they have an AI strategy. Hayden expects that buying frenzy to eventually subside.
“There’s going to be this rationalization period that will come,” Hayden said, “when companies are going to say, ‘OK, this is cool, but is this actually delivering value?’”
Building the capital flywheel
The changing economics of company building also raises questions about whether Canadian founders can access the early capital required to fuel the experimentation stage. Research from Leaders Fund found that from 2015 to 2020, roughly 75 percent of Canadian-founded startups were started in Canada. But in 2024, nearly half of Canadian founders who had raised over $1 million were based in the United States.
Hayden, who presented his firm’s research in the House of Commons last year, has argued that Canada could encourage more early-stage investment through measures such as a long-term capital gains exemption and an angel investor tax credit. The latter, he said, would be particularly useful for companies raising their first angel round, often one of the more challenging milestones for young startups.
McKinlay said successful startup outcomes create a “flywheel effect,” as founders who build wealth in the sector reinvest it in former colleagues and new ventures.
“That’s one of the things you see in the Valley that is so powerful,” McKinlay added. “To enable that here further would be amazing.”
Creating that cycle also requires financing beyond the first cheque. As startups move from experimentation toward larger rounds and global expansion, their capital needs to evolve alongside them. CIBC Innovation Banking has spent more than 25 years providing financial advice, growth capital, and debt financing to tech companies and investors across Canada, the US, and Europe.
“Silicon Valley is a gravitational force. We’re not going to replicate that,” Hayden said. “But I think if we can create an environment for entrepreneurs that convinces more of them to build here, I think that’s healthy.”
Watch the full episode of The Gradient Ascent Podcast : The Future of Canadian Startups: AI, Capital, and Brain Drain here.
PRESENTED BY
CIBC supports entrepreneurs and investors as they finance growth, scale globally, and build companies for increasingly competitive markets. Learn more.

articles.title: Jensen Huang talks about AI and climate change like a supervillain
articles.text:
As Jensen Huang puts it, AI can help fight climate change — but only if it inflicts “an enormous amount of pain and suffering” first.
Jensen Huang talks about AI and climate change like a supervillain
With AI, he says, ‘in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first.‘
The Nvidia CEO discussed the future of energy and AI’s impact on our planet in the latest episode of The Ezra Klein Show. But his comments boil down to the same accelerationist spin we’ve seen from a variety of tech leaders as well as President Donald Trump. They promise that AI will be such a gift to humanity that it’s worth the damage caused by data centers currently running on dirty energy.
Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring
Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring in the interview. He’s right that there will be pain. People are already suffering from fires and floods exacerbated by climate change. People are already dying earlier because of air pollution from fossil fuels. But Huang, with a net worth of around $192.6 billion, will not pay the price of the pollution his company creates through energy-hungry chip factories and data centers.
Huang tells Klein, after complaining that the US hasn’t built out enough fossil fuel plants, that:
It’s kind of like, in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first — that’s the nature of surgery. They’ve got to cut you open to save you. They’ve got to inflict an enormous amount of pain and suffering on you so that they can save you. And so I think AI’s kind of like that.
That’s the bit that gives Thanos energy. Resources are too limited and so after disappearing half of humanity, the Marvel supervillain believes, things will be much rosier. (“I will shred this universe down to its last atom, and then create a new one, teeming with life that knows not what it has lost but only what it has been given,” he tells the Avengers.)
Huang goes on to say:
Over the next several years we have to unfortunately use fossil fuels, because we just don’t have enough sustainable energy to make a difference. And then after that, hopefully, we can transition to that.
For context, nearly every country on Earth agreed to limit climate change when they adopted the Paris agreement in 2015. The accord sets a goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 and reaching net zero around 2050. That can only happen with swift transition to carbon-free energy like renewables and nuclear. Here’s just a short list of terrible things getting worse when we stall that progress to pursue advances in AI:
- Earth is expected to lose 99 percent of its coral reefs. Those reefs support coastal economies, and also serve as a buffer protecting communities from tropical storms, flooding, and coastal erosion.
- One in 10 people around the world, 770 million people, already face “acute risk” from sea level rise.
- Since 2001, peak daily wildfire growth rates have more than doubled in the western US. Wildfires are faster, more frequent, and more intense.
These effects are showing up in Huang’s backyard, even if he’s insulated from them. He mentions in the interview that he doesn’t know what his own address is. However, he reportedly bought a $7.5 million home on Maui in 2004 — before wildfires devastated the island in 2023. That year, an Nvidia spokesperson confirmed with The Verge that the Huangs “have owned the same home in Maui for many years.”
Huang’s property reportedly escaped damage, and the Nvidia spokesperson told me that the Huangs “donated significantly to local relief efforts.” But despite the philanthropy from tech billionaires with residences on Maui, the inferno also inflamed tensions over luxury properties’ hold on Maui’s water supply.
“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community,” Maui County Councilmember Keani Rawlins-Fernandez told me at the time. “It underscores the stark disparity between Indigenous people who want to mālama ‘āina, care for our land, and those who see Hawaii as a vacation destination.”
“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community.”
While greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels makes wildfires more dangerous by exacerbating hot, dry conditions, climate change isn’t entirely to blame for the flames that razed much of Lahaina on Maui. I reported at the time that previous generations of wealthy land grabbers primed the islands to burn. The US annexed the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1898, egged on by American plantation owners who wanted to evade import taxes. They cleared native vegetation for their businesses, allowing invasive grasses to take hold and make the landscape much more flammable than it used to be.
So when I hear Huang make the case now that there will need to be sacrifices in the name of AI progress, it reminds me that we’ve seen this playbook before. An industry that wants to grow at any cost. And nearby communities and their descendants are just supposed to live with the aftermath.
Huang mentions growing community opposition to data centers in the interview with Klein, and scolds other companies for not spreading the good news with residents about how efficient data centers purportedly are before they start construction. “If they don’t want data centers to be built in their town or whatever it is, then so be it. But if you’re going to build in their town, be sure to go there and let them know what’s coming,” he says.
“I am inevitable,” Thanos notoriously said — and apparently, so are AI data centers.
Even so, data centers don’t actually have to be as polluting as they are turning out to be.
In the interview, Huang also (unfairly) attributes record renewable energy purchases to AI. He blames climate action for stalling the construction of energy infrastructure, presumably for fossil fuels.
I think we just have to acknowledge that we got ourselves really gummed up in climate change and sustainable energy, and as a result, we just didn’t plan enough energy production.
Then he proclaims that AI is “the best opportunity we have” to “turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable.” He sees AI accelerating demand for clean energy in the long term. But AI already needs a lot of energy now, and fossil fuels are what we’ve got.
“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable.”
But renewables were already the fastest-growing sources of new electricity generation before the recent generative AI boom. It’s generally cheaper to generate power from a wind or solar farm than a new gas or coal plant. But Trump, who lined his campaign coffers with money from the fossil fuel industry, is incentivizing the development of gas and coal plants to power data centers.
And now, data centers are in turn spurring the development of far more fossil fuel infrastructure. Air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028, according to a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology.
Nevertheless, “A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, a senior director of the Environmental Protection Network, a group made up of EPA alumni, said in a recent press briefing on the growing health risks posed by data centers.
It also depends on the attitudes of industry leaders like Huang. If other people’s pain and suffering is the price you’re willing to pay for so-called progress, that says less about what’s possible and more about your own personal priorities.

articles.title: Autonomy Levels For Design Agents: L1 To L5 Explained
articles.text:
Determining what a system can decide, the scope it owns, how work is validated, when it asks for help, and who remains accountable for fallback and final signoff.
Agentic AI plays an important role in chip and system design, but not every “agentic” capability has the same degree of autonomy. In practice, autonomy is not binary. It is a progression from AI that optimizes bounded engineering tasks to systems that understand natural language, reason through design problems, and orchestrate multi-step workflows, each representing a different degree of autonomy.
That difference matters. When design teams compare autonomy, the useful question is not simply whether a system is “agentic.” It is what the system can decide, what scope it owns, how its work is validated, when it asks for help, and who remains accountable for fallback and final signoff.
This blog explains the practical progression from L1 through L5 and why a level label alone tells you very little unless it is tied to engineering scope, decision rights, validation depth, and human responsibility.
As designs grow larger, more heterogeneous, and harder to verify, engineering teams face a familiar challenge: the amount of work keeps expanding faster than the available time. More engineers and more scripts can help, but they do not fully solve the problem when design exploration, verification closure, implementation convergence, and signoff all require faster iteration across increasingly connected workflows.
This is where Cadence agentic AI strategy comes in. Cadence describes its agentic AI approach as super agents that orchestrate and implement complex, multi-step workflows while remaining grounded in Cadence’s AI-optimized, physics-based design and verification tools. That positioning is important because EDA autonomy is only useful when decisions can be checked against trusted computational models, design rules, electrical models, and engineering best practices.
The levels below are therefore not a race from “manual” to “fully automatic.” They are a way to compare how things change as AI takes on more responsibility: the scope of work, the degree of decision ownership, the validation loop, and the point at which the engineer must intervene.
Cadence Agentic AI transforms chip and system design with design agents. This changes the engineer’s role from manual task execution to outcome-driven oversight, increasing productivity and accelerating the delivery of higher-quality designs. In leading-edge deployments, autonomous workflows have reduced development cycles from weeks to days. The Cadence framework defines five increasing levels of autonomy.
These levels distinguish different types of capability, but they should not be treated as mutually exclusive product categories. A more autonomous workflow can incorporate Optimization AI, conversational capabilities, complex reasoning, and specialized agents from the levels beneath it.
Nor do higher levels make the earlier ones obsolete; higher-level agentic workflows depend on strong underlying agents, engineering engines, and optimization technologies. A workflow built from inadequate individual capabilities will not produce an adequate overall result.
At L1, AI improves a bounded engineering task without owning the broader workflow. The system can explore alternatives, learn from results, and optimize parameters to meet an objective defined by the engineer.
The differentiator is scope. AI may run extensive experiments in the background, but the engineer still owns the design intent, constraints, success criteria, and tradeoffs. Cadence Cerebrus AI Studio is a relevant example of AI-driven optimization for SoC implementation, using agentic AI workflows, advanced analytics, and optimization techniques to accelerate design closure and improve productivity.
If Level 1 is about computational heavy lifting, Level 2 is about reducing the communication barrier between human intent and machine syntax. Natural language becomes a practical interface to engineering tools and knowledge, enabling engineers to ask questions, request help, generate or debug code, and navigate tool capabilities in a conversational way. At L2, AI owns the interaction layer, not the full engineering objective; a fluent interface can make a tool easier to use without giving it independent authority over a design task.
L3 crosses an important threshold: the AI is no longer only optimizing parameters or translating natural language. It can reason through a bounded engineering problem, generate a proposed result, check that result through engineering tools or evaluators, and iterate based on feedback.
The differentiator is the reasoning-and-validation loop. A general-purpose model may produce plausible output, but EDA reasoning becomes useful when it is connected to linters checking, formal engines, simulation tools, APIs, or other evaluators that can test a result and provide feedback for the next iteration.
Here, mental models act as structured knowledge representations that capture design intent, hierarchy, relationships, specifications, and historical context. At this level, that context helps agents reason about a bounded task with more discipline than a prompt-only interaction could. The engineer still defines the problem, reviews consequential conclusions, and can redirect or reject the result. L3 gives the AI more responsibility for reasoning, but not unrestricted ownership of the design objective.
At L4, autonomy expands from a bounded reasoning task to a connected engineering workflow. Specialized agents coordinate planning, execution, validation, optimization, and iteration across multiple steps.
The differentiator is orchestration. Cadence AI Super Agents coordinate specialized agents across domains and tools. Cadence describes ChipStack, ViraStack, InnoStack, and AuraStack as applying agentic AI across front-end design and verification, analog design, digital implementation and signoff, PCB, and advanced packaging workflows. The engineer defines the goal, constraints, and acceptance criteria, while the system coordinates the path forward. What makes L4 different from L3 is not simply “more AI.” It is the coordination of multiple skills, tools, and agents toward a broader engineering outcome.
As the scope expands, governance becomes more important because one agent’s output may affect later steps in the flow. Shared design context, tool-based validation, monitoring, and exception handling help keep orchestration anchored in engineering reality.
L5 represents autonomous execution within a defined engineering scope. Cadence ChipStack AI Super Agent operates at Level 5 autonomy for complex chip design and verification workflows, while engineers can inspect, guide, and collaborate as needed.
The differentiator is dynamic execution. Rather than relying only on step-by-step prompts, the system evaluates intermediate results, determines next actions, and iterates toward closure across tasks such as specification understanding, RTL generation, verification planning, formal analysis, simulation, debug, and design convergence. Cadence has also described RTL validation workflows using Xcelium Logic Simulation and Jasper Formal Verification to accelerate validation.
This should not be read as AI replacing engineers across the entire chip-to-system lifecycle. The autonomy is bounded by workflow scope, trusted engines, validation, governance, and human oversight. Engineers remain responsible for critical decisions and final signoff.
The difference between L4 and L5 is not whether agents are present. Both levels can involve multiple agents, tool calls, reasoning, and validation.
At L4, the most important capability is orchestration: specialized agents coordinate work across a broader flow, but the workflow remains strongly shaped by the objectives, constraints, and checkpoints that engineers define.
At L5, more responsibility shifts to the system for determining the next action based on intermediate results. Autonomy is therefore deeper, but it is still not unlimited. A system may be highly autonomous in RTL validation or front-end design and verification without being autonomous across every design, system, or signoff decision.
That is why a level alone tells you almost nothing. It must be paired with the workflow boundary, the design domain, the validation mechanism, the fallback behavior, and the human decision points.
When evaluating an autonomy claim, design teams should ask:
As autonomy increases, human expertise moves to a different layer of the flow. The engineer’s role shifts from directing individual tool actions toward setting intent, supervising outcomes, managing exceptions, and approving consequential decisions. The location of human involvement changes. Accountability does not.
Fallback ownership is therefore part of the taxonomy. Engineering organizations need to understand what happens when an output fails validation, a constraint cannot be met, or the system encounters an exception. An autonomy level is credible only when the fallback path is explicit.
Autonomy in EDA should not be evaluated solely by the level label. The practical value of the L1-to-L5 taxonomy is that it gives design teams a neutral way to compare capabilities without assuming that every “agentic” system provides the same independence, engineering coverage, or governance. The best question is not “What level is it?” but “What can it decide, what can it execute, how is it validated, and where does the engineer remain accountable?”
Achieving higher autonomy requires more than adding a large language model to an EDA interface. A practical design-agent architecture typically needs several interconnected layers.
First is context: agents need access to design intent, specifications, constraints, hierarchy, tool outputs, historical experiments, and the design’s current state. In Cadence’s five levels, shared mental models help convert specifications, design sources, and historical context into a structured knowledge base that downstream agents can use.
Second is reasoning: the system must determine what action is appropriate given that context. In EDA, that reasoning must be domain-grounded because chip design decisions depend on design hierarchy, constraints, verification state, physical behavior, and tool-specific semantics.
Third is tool execution: agents need controlled access to synthesis, simulation, verification, implementation, analysis, and other engineering tools. Cadence AI Super Agents are grounded in trusted EDA engines, AI-optimized, physics-based design and verification tools.
Fourth is feedback: key actions must produce observable or measurable results—such as logs, violations, coverage signals, simulation outcomes, PPA metrics, or verification status—that can inform the next decision. Finally, orchestration coordinates specialized agents, tracks workflow state, and supports governed execution, enabling teams to monitor progress, intervene when needed, and keep autonomous activity within defined engineering boundaries.
This is why domain-specific agentic AI matters in EDA. Generic language models can produce plausible artifacts, but reliable chip design requires structured design context, tool-specific semantics, verification feedback, and trusted computational engines.

articles.title: Gemini 3.8 : Google dévoile une IA texte‑vers‑voix plus naturelle que jamais
articles.text:
Avec Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS et sa version Flash-Lite, Google fait passer sa synthèse vocale de 30 à plus de 2 000 voix, dans plus de 100 langues. Les développeurs peuvent diriger chaque réplique d’un script en langage naturel. En revanche, Google a exclu l’Europe de sa nouvelle fonction de réplication vocale.
Jusqu’ici, les développeurs de l’API Gemini disposaient de 30 voix prédéfinies pour faire parler leurs applications. Une semaine après le lancement de Gemini 3.8 Live, Google leur propose deux nouveaux modèles de synthèse vocale et, avec eux, plus de 2 000 voix prêtes à l’emploi, jusqu’aux variantes régionales du français québécois.
Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS est conçu pour la direction artistique et la création de personnages. Google destine sa version Flash-Lite aux usages en gros volume à moindre coût, du doublage aux agents vocaux. Par rapport à Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, l’entreprise annonce de nets progrès sur les contenus longs et les dialogues à deux voix. Les deux modèles sont accessibles dans l'API Gemini et dans Google AI Studio.
Des voix dirigées réplique par réplique
Dans un script, le développeur peut préciser en langage naturel le ton ou le rythme attendus pour chaque réplique. Il a également la possibilité d’insérer des balises de sons non verbaux, <laughs> pour un rire ou <sigh> pour un soupir, ainsi que des interjections d’écoute active du type « mhm ». Google gère nativement les scènes à deux interlocuteurs, avec des tours de parole enchaînés au sein d’une seule génération audio. Sur les formats longs, la voix d’un personnage est conservée pendant des heures d’enregistrement continu, avec un timbre stable et une dérive minimale du locuteur, d’après l'’entreprise.
Avec un échantillon audio de 30 secondes, un utilisateur peut aussi reproduire une voix existante. Avant toute création, Google exige que le propriétaire de cette voix donne oralement son accord dans un enregistrement, puis vérifie que ce locuteur correspond bien à celui de l’échantillon.
- Multimodalité texte, voix et fichiers
- Intégration poussée aux services Google
- Applications Web, mobile et bureau
- Réponses toujours à vérifier
- Quotas variables selon le forfait
Le groupe intègre en outre à chaque fichier généré un filigrane SynthID imperceptible à l’oreille, pour faciliter la détection des contenus synthétiques, et des certificats de provenance C2PA. Prochainement, les utilisateurs pourront remixer une voix et en modifier le timbre, la hauteur, le débit ou l’accent par une simple consigne écrite, du type « ajoute un léger accent du sud des États-Unis ».
Côté grand public, Google a intégré Flash TTS à Gemini Notebook, où les utilisateurs peuvent transformer leurs documents en résumés audio. Flash-Lite TTS est de son côté arrivé dans Google Vids, l’outil de création vidéo de Google Workspace. Les entreprises devront patienter jusqu’à l’arrivée des deux modèles dans l’API Gemini Enterprise.
Gemini 3.8 en tête d’un classement de Hume AI
Comme on vous le disait précédemment, Google avait recruté Alan Cowen, patron de Hume AI, et sept de ses ingénieurs grâce à un accord de licence. Cette start-up américaine est spécialisée dans l’IA émotionnelle et dans la reproduction du timbre et de l’intonation des voix. Elle a poursuivi ses activités après le départ de son dirigeant. Alan Cowen cosigne aujourd’hui l’annonce de Gemini 3.8 TTS en tant que directeur de recherche scientifique chez Google. Or les principaux scores mis en avant par Google sont ceux du Voice Design benchmark de Hume AI.
Dans ce classement, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS est premier au général avec un score de 71,4, et premier sur la modélisation des accents avec 60,8. Sur l’indice de qualité globale de la start-up, les deux modèles de Google sont aux deux premières places. Dans le classement Voice Arena, Google est aussi en tête pour six langues, dont le japonais et l’hindi. Le français est absent de cette liste.
La réplication vocale est indisponible dans l’Espace économique européen, au Royaume-Uni, en Suisse et en Inde, et dans deux États américains, l’Illinois et le Texas. Ces deux États sont dotés de lois spécifiques sur les données biométriques. Pour la France, Google est resté… Muet.

articles.title: Après l'annonce des AirPods 5 par Apple, Cdiscount déstocke les AirPods 4 avec ANC
articles.text:
Apple a présenté ses AirPods 5 le 9 septembre 2026, pendant la keynote d’Apple Park. Cette nouvelle génération améliore la réduction active du bruit (ANC) et la propose dès le modèle d’entrée de gamme, vendu 149 €. Avec les AirPods 4, il fallait choisir la version vendue 199 € pour en profiter.
Cette version est aujourd’hui en promotion. Cdiscount propose les AirPods 4 avec réduction active du bruit à 124 € au lieu de 199 €, une fois le code promo 15DES129 appliqué dans le panier. Cela représente 75 € d’économie sur le prix de lancement.
C’est quoi, les AirPods 4 avec réduction de bruit active ?
Les AirPods 4 conservent le format ouvert caractéristique de la gamme, sans embouts en silicone, mais Apple a retravaillé leur conception pour améliorer leur maintien. Les écouteurs adoptent notamment un contour affiné et une tige plus courte, tandis que les commandes s’effectuent en appuyant sur la tige. Chaque écouteur pèse 4,3 grammes, assez peu pour les oublier pendant une longue écoute.
Les AirPods 4 avec ANC embarquent la puce H2, qui gère la réduction de bruit, le mode Transparence pour entendre ce qui vous entoure et l’Audio adaptatif, qui ajuste le tout selon l’environnement. La Détection des conversations baisse également le volume lorsque vous prenez la parole. On retrouve aussi l’audio spatial personnalisé, l’isolement de la voix pour les appels et les interactions avec Siri.
Depuis le déploiement d’iOS 27, ils profitent aussi d’un égaliseur personnalisable, une première pour les AirPods : vous pouvez enfin régler les graves, les médiums et les aigus à votre goût. Il faut simplement que les écouteurs soient eux aussi à jour. Ils proposent également la traduction en direct, pour écouter dans vos écouteurs la traduction des propos de votre interlocuteur, à condition de les utiliser avec un iPhone compatible avec Apple Intelligence, sur lequel cette fonction est activée.
Côté autonomie, Apple annonce jusqu’à 5 heures d’écoute sans réduction de bruit, contre 4 heures lorsqu’elle est activée. Avec les recharges du boîtier, comptez respectivement jusqu’à 30 et 20 heures.
À ce prix, les AirPods 4 sont-ils une bonne affaire ?
Les AirPods 5 intègrent désormais la réduction de bruit sur les deux versions, à 149 et 169 €. Ce n’était pas le cas des AirPods 4 : il fallait choisir la version la plus chère pour en profiter. Ici vous avez le meilleur modèle de la génération. Sur le papier, les nouveaux AirPods 5 font certes mieux. Ces derniers promettent surtout une meilleure réduction de bruit : selon Apple, ils filtrent jusqu’à 50 % de bruit extérieur en plus que les AirPods 4. Ils résistent aussi mieux à l’eau, avec une certification IP57 contre IP54 auparavant.
Avec leur boîtier, les AirPods 4 offrent déjà jusqu’à 20 heures d’écoute avec la réduction de bruit, autant que les AirPods 5 à 149 €. Le modèle à 169 € gagne une heure par charge, mais seulement deux heures au total. Un progrès qui ne justifiera pas forcément d’y mettre 45 € de plus pour tout le monde.

articles.title: Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 : comment Qualcomm prépare nos futurs écouteurs à voir et comprendre leur environnement
articles.text:
Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 : comment Qualcomm prépare nos futurs écouteurs à voir et comprendre leur environnement
Qualcomm muscle sérieusement sa plateforme audio avec le Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2. Plus compacte, moins énergivore et jusqu’à deux fois plus puissante en IA, cette puce ouvre la voie à des écouteurs plus intelligents, capables à terme de comprendre leur environnement.
Avec le Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2, Qualcomm veut faire franchir un nouveau cap aux écouteurs et casques sans-fil. Présentée comme la nouvelle génération de sa plateforme audio, cette puce ne se contente pas d’améliorer le traitement du signal sonore. Elle mise aussi sur davantage de puissance pour l’intelligence artificielle, une meilleure efficacité énergétique et l’arrivée de nouvelles fonctions logicielles.
Le principal changement concerne les capacités d’IA embarquées. Qualcomm annonce jusqu’à deux fois plus de puissance de calcul dédiée à l’IA que sur la génération précédente, tout en réduisant la consommation d’énergie de 40 %. La puce est également jusqu’à 30 % plus compacte. Cette combinaison pourrait permettre aux fabricants d’augmenter l’autonomie, d’intégrer davantage de composants ou de libérer de la place pour de nouveaux usages sans augmenter la taille des écouteurs.
Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 : l'IA au cœur du traitement local et visuel
Le Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 associe traitement audio et unité de calcul dédiée à l’IA. Les écouteurs pourront ainsi exécuter plusieurs tâches simultanément : suppression du bruit, détection et suivi de données liées au bien-être, traitement de la voix ou interaction avec un assistant IA. Une partie de ces traitements pourra être réalisée localement, sans dépendre systématiquement du smartphone.
Qualcomm introduit aussi une connectivité wifi 6E à faible consommation, permettant aux appareils compatibles de communiquer directement avec les services cloud. Cette architecture pourrait notamment réduire les délais lors des échanges avec un assistant IA et rendre possibles des fonctions comme la traduction ou la transcription en temps réel, avec moins de dépendance vis-à-vis du smartphone.
Cette puissance supplémentaire ouvre aussi la voie à une évolution plus ambitieuse. À l’image de ce que prépare Apple pour ses prochains AirPods Pro, les futurs écouteurs pourraient devenir des interfaces capables de comprendre leur environnement.
Qualcomm prévoit ainsi la prise en charge de produits audio équipés de caméras. Ces dernières pourraient fournir à l’IA des informations visuelles sur ce qui entoure l’utilisateur afin de permettre des interactions contextuelles ou d’établir des résumés des temps forts de la journée. L’enjeu n’est donc plus seulement de faire fournir une réponse vocale à l’utilisateur, mais de permettre à l’appareil de comprendre ce qu’il voit.
Une réduction du bruit annoncée comme deux fois plus efficace
Qualcomm annonce également une réduction active du bruit jusqu’à deux fois plus performante. Le traitement devrait mieux s’adapter aux changements de position des écouteurs, aux mouvements de l’utilisateur et aux variations de l’environnement sonore, avec une attention particulière portée aux bruits graves et aux situations dynamiques.
La plateforme conserve par ailleurs les fonctions audio haut de gamme de l’écosystème Snapdragon Sound, avec notamment le son sans perte (lossless), la faible latence et la technologie XPAN, qui entend améliorer la portée et la stabilité de la connexion grâce au wifi. La prise en charge du Bluetooth 7.0 fait aussi partie des évolutions annoncées.
Les premiers produits équipés du Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 seront développés notamment par Bose, HP et Cleer, mais il ne serait pas étonnant de le voir s'intégrer aux appareils de Sennheiser, Bowers & Wilkins, etc., qui utilisent déjà les puces Qualcomm. Il ne faut toutefois pas s’attendre à voir des produits équipés dans les prochains mois. Les fabricants doivent encore finaliser leurs modèles, effectuer les phases de développement et de validation, puis préparer leur commercialisation.
Leur arrivée permettra surtout de vérifier jusqu’où les constructeurs exploiteront cette nouvelle plateforme, car au-delà des gains d’autonomie, d’ANC et de qualité sonore, Qualcomm cherche à transformer les écouteurs en véritables plateformes informatiques capables de faire tourner de l’IA et, à terme, de comprendre leur environnement.

articles.title: Meta dégaine 2 nouvelles lunettes connectées Ray-Ban, dont une version sans caméra
articles.text:
Meta continue d’étoffer son catalogue de lunettes connectées. Face au succès de ses précédents modèles, le géant de Menlo Park a dégainé une nouvelle génération de lunettes intelligentes, les Ray-Ban Gen 3 et les Meta Ray-Ban Audio. La firme a décliné ses lunettes sous plusieurs formes, avec pour objectif de proposer « une paire de lunettes pour chaque personnalité ». Plus de 100 modèles différents, réparties entre Ray-Ban, Oakley et Meta Glasses, devraient arriver sur le marché d’ici la fin de l’année.
A lire aussi : On a essayé les Meta VR Glasses, le Vision Pro moins cher et plus léger, en avant-première
Une édition uniquement audio
La première nouveauté est Ray-Ban Meta Audio, la toute première paire de lunettes 100% audio de la marque, sans caméra. Dépourvue d’appareil photo, elle bat un record de légèreté pour Meta. L’offre permet de viser les utilisateurs qui veulent une alternative aux écouteurs Bluetooth et veulent pouvoir converser avec Meta AI sans les questions de vie privée liées à une caméra intégrée. L’audio est « la fonctionnalité la plus populaire des lunettes Meta depuis leurs débuts
 », nous explique Meta.
Côté endurance, la paire offre jusqu’à 12 heures d’autonomie. Les lunettes seront disponibles en précommande dans les styles Burbank et Clubmaster à partir du 23 septembre 2026 au prix de 349 euros. Elles seront sur le marché dès le 13 octobre 2026.
On a pu prendre en main les lunettes à l’issue de la conférence. Dès le premier contact, on a été frappé par la légèreté de la paire. Elle ne pèse que 43 grammes. Les lunettes sont aussi légères et discrètes qu’une paire de lunettes classiques. Impossible de déterminer que vous portez des lunettes Bluetooth, même à une petite distance. Si vous voulez une alternative aux écouteurs, à porter toute la journée au boulot et dans vos activités quotidiennes, c’est peut-être une bonne option, surtout si vous devez porter des lunettes pour votre vue.
A lire aussi : Les lunettes connectées d’Apple veulent éviter le piège des Ray-Ban Meta
Une troisième génération de Ray-Ban
La deuxième annonce de Meta concerne les Ray-Ban Meta de troisième génération, la gamme phare avec caméra et IA embarquée. La génération gagne en finesse, atteint jusqu’à 9 heures d’autonomie (une heure de plus que la Gen2) et intègre un bouton d’action personnalisable pour accéder plus rapidement à Meta AI, ou à une autre fonctionnalité. Le porteur peut choisir lui-même ce que déclenche ce bouton, situé sur la branche droite de la monture. On trouve un bouton analogue sur les lunettes Oakley Meta, dont les fameuses Vanguard, que nous avons testées.
Du reste, la nouvelle génération n’offre rien de particulier en plus par rapport à la seconde mouture. Au moment de la prise en main, on s’est néanmoins rendu compte que l’accessoire était sensiblement plus léger et plus confortable que la Gen 2, auquel nous sommes habitués. Meta nous explique d’ailleurs avoir mis au point de nouvelles charnières ergonomiques et de nouveaux embouts ajustables afin de s’adapter à davantage de morphologies de visage.
Deux nouveaux styles, Aviator et Zena, achèvent la collection, avec une édition limitée Aviator en beige laiteux et verres marron. Cette génération sera disponible dès le 23 septembre 2026 au prix de 449 euros. Du côté des Meta Glasses, lancée il y a quelques semaines sans Ray-Ban, l’entreprise ajoute également deux nouveaux styles, Meta Capri et Meta Nova, disponibles eux aussi à partir du 23 septembre 2026.
Côté logiciel, l’entreprise annonce les « photos dynamiques ». Concrètement, lorsqu’on prend une photo, les lunettes capturent en réalité plusieurs images en une fraction de seconde autour de l’instant où le déclencheur est actionné, puis l’intelligence artificielle de Meta analyse ces prises et sélectionne automatiquement celle qu’elle juge la meilleure. Vous pouvez aussi choisir vous même la photo qui vous plaît le plus. Citons aussi l’arrivée sur toute la gamme d’un mode paysage, et de la capture audio en Dolby Atmos, une première pour ce type de produit.
L’épineuse question de la vie privée
Meta n’a pas hésité à évoquer l’éléphant dans la pièce, à savoir l’épineuse question de la vie privée. De nombreuses personnes se sont en effet servies de l’accessoire pour filmer des individus, surtout des femmes, à leur insu, notamment dans l’espace public.
Comme nous l’a expliqué Meta, une foule de choses ont été mises en place pour éviter ces utilisations abusives des lunettes. Le groupe rappelle avoir intégré une lumière LED, qui s’active quand l’utilisateur filme ou prend une photo. Si cette lumière est masquée, ou trafiquée par l’utilisateur, l’appareil photo ne fonctionnera pas. L’appareil photo va également se désactiver si la LED est couverte pendant l’enregistrement.
« Ce que nous avons observé, c’est que les utilisateurs trouvent des moyens créatifs de contourner ces limites. Nous avons donc mis en place plusieurs mesures ces derniers mois et ces dernières semaines, et je pense que nous avons fait de réels progrès pour comprendre ces comportements, les anticiper et y répondre rapidement », nous relate Meta.
Par ailleurs, Meta se dit conscient que les usagers avec de mauvaises intentions vont continuer de chercher des moyens de contourner les restrictions. C’est pourquoi l’entreprise s’est engagée à prendre des « mesures agressives » à mesure que des abus seront enregistrés. C’est aussi, et surtout, pourquoi Meta décidé de commercialiser des lunettes sans appareil photo.

articles.title: 5 GHz im Smartphone: Qualcomms neuer Chip schafft PC-Leistung
articles.text:
5 GHz im Smartphone: Qualcomms neuer Chip schafft, was bisher nur PCs konnten
Android-Handys könnten bald schneller werden: Der Chipspezialist Qualcomm hat zwei neue High-End-Chips für Smartphones vorgestellt: Den Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 und die stärkere Variante Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Der Gen 6 löst den bisherigen Gen-5-Prozessor ab und ist laut Qualcomm der erste Smartphone-Chip, der 5 GHz Taktrate erreicht – zumindest mit seinen beiden Prime-Kernen. Solche Werte kannte man früher nur von PCs.
Was der Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 drauf hat
Neben den beiden Prime-Kernen stecken sechs Performance-Kerne in der Oryon-CPU des Elite Gen 6, die bis zu 4 GHz schaffen. Gegenüber dem Vorjahreschip verspricht Qualcomm zehn Prozent mehr Rechenleistung oder 37 Prozent höhere Energieeffizienz bei gleicher Leistung. Die Adreno-Grafikeinheit soll um 35 Prozent zulegen. Möglich macht das vor allem ein neues Fertigungsverfahren. Qualcomm spricht grob von 2 Nanometern. Vermutlich wechselt das Unternehmen vom N3P-Prozess auf N2P beim Produzenten TSMC aus Taiwan.
Zu Verbesserungen an den CPU-Kernen selbst sagt Qualcomm bislang nichts. Der Grund dürfte schlicht sein, dass es abseits des höheren Takts kaum welche gibt. Der Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 schafft bis zu 4,6 GHz, der Nachfolger liegt knapp neun Prozent darüber. Den restlichen Prozentpunkt dürften übliche Feinarbeiten an der Sprungvorhersage bringen. Dabei rät der Prozessor vorab, welche Befehle er als Nächstes abarbeiten muss.
Allerdings hat Qualcomm die wichtige KI-Hardware des Chips überarbeitet. Ein neuer „Element Accelerator“ soll den Hexagon-NPU stärker machen – jene Einheit, die KI-Berechnungen übernimmt. Der Sensing Hub, der im Hintergrund sparsam Sensordaten auswertet und etwa Sprachbefehle erkennt, bekommt zwei eigene KI-Einheiten. Dazu kommen zwei Bildsignalprozessoren (ISP), mit denen sich zwei Kameras ansteuern lassen, um durchgehend Daten aufzunehmen.
Die Extreme-Variante setzt bei der Grafik an
Der Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 bringt alle Eigenschaften des Schwesterchips mit, dazu einige Extras. Die CPU-Kerne sollen durch ein optimiertes Package etwas mehr leisten – denkbar ist eine verbesserte Signalführung auf dem Träger. Wie groß der Unterschied ausfällt, beziffert Qualcomm nicht.
Deutlich aufgewertet hat das Unternehmen die Adreno-GPU. Der Grafikchip bekommt drei Matrix-Cores, die auf KI-Berechnungen ausgelegt sind. Damit erhöht sie in Spielen die Auflösung und erzeugt zusätzliche Zwischenbilder. Qualcomm nennt das „Neural Fusion“ und zieht damit mit ARM gleich: Dessen Mali-GPU G2-Ultra NX bietet dieselben Funktionen.
Die ersten Geräte mit den neuen Chips stehen kurz bevor. In den vergangenen Jahren kamen sie meist von chinesischen Marken wie Honor und Xiaomi. Xiaomi zeigt das 18 Pro und das 18 Pro Max noch in dieser Woche für den chinesischen Markt, später sollen die Modelle auch global erscheinen. Auch Motorola ist früh dran und kündigt mit dem Signature 27 ein erstes Smartphone mit dem Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 an.

articles.title: Cómo traducir mensajes de WhatsApp al instante con el ícono flotante de Google Translate
articles.text:
Google Translate tiene una función que permite traducir mensajes de WhatsApp sin salir de la conversación ni cambiar de aplicación. Se trata de la herramienta “Tocar para Traducir”, que despliega una burbuja flotante en pantalla con la traducción de cualquier texto copiado.
La opción está disponible sobre todo en Android, ya que iOS restringe las superposiciones flotantes sobre otras aplicaciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Para aprovechar esta función solo se necesita tener instalada y actualizada la aplicación Google Translate desde Google Play Store. A partir de ahí, el proceso se divide en la activación del permiso correspondiente y el uso posterior dentro del chat.
Cómo activar el ícono flotante en Google Translate
El primer paso consiste en habilitar el permiso que permite que la aplicación se superponga sobre otras apps, incluida WhatsApp. Para lograrlo, hay que abrir el Traductor de Google y tocar la foto de perfil o el menú de la cuenta, ubicado en la esquina superior derecha de la pantalla.
Desde ahí se ingresa a Ajustes (o Configuración) y se selecciona la opción Tocar para Traducir. Dentro de ese menú se debe activar el interruptor de Usar Tocar para Traducir.
PUBLICIDAD
En algunas versiones de Android aparece además la opción Mostrar icono flotante, que conviene activar de forma independiente si el sistema la presenta por separado. Cuando el teléfono solicite el permiso para “Mostrar sobre otras aplicaciones”, es necesario aceptarlo, ya que sin esa autorización la burbuja no podrá aparecer en pantalla.
Pasos para traducir mensajes recibidos en WhatsApp
Una vez configurado el permiso, la traducción de mensajes dentro de WhatsApp se realiza de forma directa. Hay que abrir la aplicación e ingresar al chat donde se encuentra el mensaje que se quiere traducir.
Luego se mantiene presionado el mensaje recibido y se selecciona la opción Copiar. En ese momento aparece de manera automática la burbuja flotante de Google Translate sobre la pantalla.
PUBLICIDAD
Al tocar ese ícono flotante se despliega una ventana rápida con la traducción del mensaje al instante, sin necesidad de abrir la aplicación de Google Translate ni de salir de la conversación de WhatsApp.
Traducción del texto antes de enviarlo con Gboard
La función también permite invertir el proceso: traducir lo que el usuario está por escribir antes de enviarlo. Esta opción depende de que el teclado utilizado sea Gboard, el teclado de Google disponible para dispositivos Android.
En ese caso, en la barra de herramientas ubicada sobre las teclas aparece el ícono del Traductor. Al tocarlo, el usuario puede escribir su respuesta en su propio idioma y el sistema la traduce de forma automática dentro del campo de texto, antes de que el mensaje sea enviado por WhatsApp.
PUBLICIDAD
Traducción de voz en tiempo real: cómo funciona Gemini 3.5 Live Translate de Google
Google confirmó el funcionamiento de Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, su sistema de traducción de voz en tiempo real, dentro de la aplicación Google Translate para Android e iOS. La herramienta opera en más de 70 idiomas, entre ellos el español, según informó la compañía en un comunicado oficial.
El anuncio precisó que la función no quedó limitada a Google Translate: también se incorporó a Google Meet y quedó disponible para desarrolladores externos que quieran integrarla en sus propias aplicaciones.
El modelo identifica de manera automática el idioma que habla cada persona en la conversación y produce una traducción hablada casi de forma inmediata. El usuario no necesita realizar ninguna configuración previa para que el sistema empiece a funcionar.
PUBLICIDAD
De acuerdo con Google, la voz generada por la traducción respeta la entonación, el ritmo y el tono originales de quien habla, un aspecto que la compañía destacó como diferencial frente a versiones anteriores de la herramienta.
Ese punto marca, precisamente, la principal diferencia con los sistemas previos de traducción por voz: mientras esas versiones aguardaban a que el interlocutor completara una frase entera antes de traducirla, Gemini 3.5 Live Translate genera el audio de manera continua, sin pausas forzadas en la conversación.
La compañía sostuvo que el resultado se ubica apenas unos segundos detrás del habla original, lo que permite mantener un intercambio más fluido entre personas que hablan idiomas distintos.
