articles.title: ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Review A New AMD EPYC 8005 Sorano Motherboard
articles.text:
A couple of months back AMD launched their EPYC 8005 “Sorano” lineup of processors, which brought AMD’s Zen 5 architecture to its mid-tier SP6 platform. With up to 84 CPU cores and 96 lanes of PCIe Gen5, Sorano is a balanced EPYC offering with all of the Zen 5 architecture’s features, just in a smaller serving. And as a replacement for AMD’s earlier EPYC 8004 “Siena” processors, Sorano is especially remarkable, as it replaces the former’s Zen 4c cores with full-fat Zen 5 cores, allowing Sorano to hit far greater performance levels.
While Sorano is fully backward compatible with existing SP6 motherboards after a BIOS update, a few board manufacturers have opted to launch new boards specifically to align with the newer SP6 EPYC processor, and ASRock Rack is among them. For Sorano, the company has released the plainly named SORANOD8-2L2T, a basic server and workstation motherboard that brings all of Sorano’s key features to bear.
| ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Key Specs |  | 
| Processor Family | AMD EPYC 8004/8005 | 
| Socket | SP6 | 
| Memory | 8x DDR5 RDIMM Slots (2DPC*) Max Speed: DDR5-5200 | 
| PCIe Slots | 4x PCIe x16 (Gen5 x16 Electrical) 1x PCIe x8 (Gen5 x8 Electrical) | 
| Storage | 2x M.2 22110/2280 (Gen5 x4) 2x MCIO x8 (Gen5 x8/SATA 6Gbps x8) | 
| Ethernet | 2x 10GbE (Intel X710-AT2) 2x 1GbE (Intel I210) | 
| Rear USB | 2x 5Gbps USB-A | 
| Front USB | 2x 5Gbps USB-A | 
| Video | VGA (DB15) | 
| BMC | ASPEED AST2600 | 
| Form Factor | “ATX-like” (12-inch x 10-inch) | 
The SORANOD8-2L2T is essentially an upgraded version of ASRock Rack’s earlier SIENAD8-2L2T, with a slightly larger board and minor I/O changes. In addition to exposing all of Sorano’s I/O for server use, the other notable aspect of the SORANOD8-2L2T is its networking capabilities. The “2L2T” in the name refers to the two pairs of network adapters built into the motherboard. It includes a pair of 10GbE adapters and a pair of 1GbE adapters, giving the motherboard strong network capabilities out of the box. As a result, the SORANOD8-2L2T is a simple yet highly flexible motherboard for server or workstation deployments.
ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Hardware Overview
ASRock Rack has a well-earned reputation for simple and rock-solid server motherboard designs, and the SORANOD8-2L2T lives up to that pedigree. Other than networking controllers, there is very little extra hardware on the motherboard. This is a board designed to run a CPU, run it well, and expose all of that I/O so that the server builder can do with it as they please.
In terms of size, the SORANOD8-2L2T is what ASRock Rack classifies as an “ATX-like” motherboard. With dimensions of 12-inches x 10-inches, the board is ever so slightly too wide to meet the ATX specification. Few cases should have an issue with this, especially as the even larger EEB form factor is routinely used in this space. But it is notable since it can present an issue in cases that accept a regulation ATX motherboard – and no larger.
As always with server boards, a good chunk of the SORANOD8-2L2T’s space is dominated by the CPU socket and RDIMM slots. While the SP6 socket is smaller than the mighty SP5 (with over 1000 fewer pins), it is by no means a small socket. And 8 RDIMM slots take up a good amount of space on their own.
Those 8 RDIMM slots are designed to be eye-catching, and for a good reason: SP6 is natively a 6-channel platform. So we would usually expect to see either 6 or 12 RDIMM slots on a motherboard, for 1DPC or 2DPC operation respectively. But for all of their SP6 motherboards, ASRock Rack has taken things in an interesting direction by installing 8 RDIMM slots, effectively making this a 2DPC-ish motherboard.
The RDIMM slot coloring, in turn, is meant to signify which channel each slot belongs to. The blue slots are all the first RDIMMs for their respective channels, and are the slots that should be filled first. Meanwhile the black RDIMM slots are the second RDIMM slots on two of SP6’s six channels, and as such need to be the last slots filled. Two-tone DIMM slots are nothing new, of course, but ASRock Rack’s unusual organization means that there will never be any doubt about which color is for the first RDIMM versus the second RDIMM.
As for the purpose behind 8 slots, it is meant to balance the memory capacity of the board versus how much size the RDIMM slots take up. A traditional 7 PCIe slot layout does not afford enough space for 12 DIMMs, but it does for 8. And thus this is the direction ASRock has gone, squeezing in an extra two RDIMM slots in order to increase the amount of memory the board can address to 2TB.
The trade-off, however, is that this means the SORANOD8-2L2T is meant to function like a 2DPC motherboard through and through, and that means taking the memory frequency penalty. While a 1DPC board can clock as high as DDR5-6400, the SORANOD8-2L2T tops out at DDR5-5200 in exchange for its extra memory capacity.
Memory matters aside, looking around the CPU socket and DIMM slots we find the usual collection of chokes and MOSFETs that make up the board’s VRM system. The MOSFETs are under some very basic heatsinks here. As SP6 chips top out at 225 Watts (and presumably no one is going to be throwing liquid nitrogen at them), the power delivery system does not need to be too exotic. By the same token, however, server boards are designed around significant airflow, so the heatsinks do not need to be massive to be fit for purpose.
Speaking of power, we find a trio of ATX12V connectors spread out over the board, and these are where the SORANOD8-2L2T draws its power from. Curiously, ASRock Rack has built two of them as vertical connectors, and a third as a right-angled connector. All three are necessary for the board’s operation, so they are functionally equivalent. Presumably, the right-angled connector is meant to better fit server vendors’ needs, though we have seen plenty of server boards without such an angled connector.
Being that this is a server board first and foremost, ASRock Rack also eschews a full 24-pin ATX connector. In its place is a simple 4-pin micro-fit connector that only provides signaling.
Since you do not get a standard ATX power header, you plug the 24-pin ATX power supply connector into the included adapter, and into the 4-pin connector on the motherboard. We tend to prefer full-size ATX connectors to this solution on larger boards, though in the case of the SORANOD8-2L2T, the edges of the board are already pretty packed.
Moving on, let us talk about I/O and storage expansion, as the SORANOD8-2L2T provides a lot of it.
First and foremost, ASRock Rack has equipped the board with 5 PCIe slots. Four of these are full PCIe Gen5 x16 slots, while the final is an open-ended PCIe Gen5 x8 slot. This accounts for 72 of SP6’s 96 PCI Gen5 slots right here, and provides a great deal of flexibility with PCIe expansion cards. All of the x16 slots are double-spaced, though using the x8 slot will cut into the space for the top slot.
The top slot is a particularly special slot here since, alongside PCIe (and CXL) connectivity, it can also be switched over to providing 16 SATA 6Gbs connections. This does require a special riser card – ASRock Rack recommends their own 1U2G-RB1U2SL-G4 – but in effect it allows switching the PCIe lanes over to SATA connections.
For more fixed storage needs, the SORANOD8-2L2T also provides for a pair of M.2 Gen5 x4 slots. Both of these slots are designed to accept either M.2 22110 or M.2 2280 SSDs, with movable standoffs used to adjust the slot.
As is usually the case for ASRock Rack motherboards, the company also provides for a pair of thumbscrews to secure the SSD slots. We cannot say enough nice things about how much we appreciate thumbscrews here.
For the final set of storage options, towards the top corner of the motherboard, ASRock Rack has placed a pair of MCIO x8 connectors. These connectors normally carry 8 lanes of PCIe Gen5 each (accounting for the final 16 lanes provided by the CPU), which in turn is normally split up among two EDSFF SSDs each. However, in a feature that is new to the SORANOD8-2L2T and sets it apart from its Siena predecessor, these MCIO slots can also be configured to carry SATA signaling instead. This converts each MCIO connector into an eight-port SATA 6Gbps host, allowing for up to (another) 16 SATA drives, ideal for high-density storage servers.
As for external I/O, the SORANOD8-2L2T goes heavy on Ethernet ports, and light on everything else.
On the rear I/O panel for the motherboard, we find no less than 5 different RJ45 ports. These cover a pair of 10GbE ports, a pair of 1GbE ports, and finally an IPMI management port.
Farthest to the left is the IPMI management port, which is attached to the ASPEED AST2600 BMC. The AST2600 continues to this day to be the most prevalent BMC we see in boards that cross our labs.
To the right of that, the stacked RJ45 ports are 1Gb Ethernet ports. These are hanging off of a pair of Intel I210 Ethernet controllers.
Meanwhile, farther to the right and spread out over two rows are the 10GbE ports. These are powered by an Intel X710-AT2 controller, which provides for full 10Gbps bandwidth in each port along with the ability to negotiate to 5Gbps, 2.5Gbps, 1Gbps, and lower speeds.
All of the network controllers, along with the BMC, are located under a heat sink at the edge of the board, behind the PCIe slots. None of these components is particularly hot, but the 10GbE controller in particular is just hot enough to require some extra cooling, which the low-profile heatsink supplies.
Finally, farthest to the right is an old-school DB15 VGA port, which is part of the BMC and provides video output from the management controller. Given that the SORANOD8-2L2T is a brand-new motherboard, it is a bit odd to see a VGA port in 2026, but even with the AST2600 supporting DisplayPort for digital displays, VGA still sees significant use in data centers.
For all of those Ethernet jacks, what you will not find on the SORANOD8-2L2T is much in the way of USB ports. The rear of the motherboard has only two USB ports, both 5Gbps USB-A ports.
For the front panel connector, there is a single 20-pin USB connector to provide another pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports.
For a server installation, this is fine, as it is rare for more than a couple of USB ports to ever be in use. It also means that although ASRock Rack pitches the SORANOD8-2L2T as both a server and a workstation motherboard, you would look to fill more USB connectivity via PCIe for the workstation role. This is very clearly a server motherboard first and foremost.
The number of fan headers further drives this point home. Towards the front edge of the motherboard, there are six 6-pin fan headers, with the 6-pin variant being something of an ASRock Rack specialty.
Next, let us get to the block diagram.

articles.title: Astrana Health Data Breach Impacts Private, Confidential Information
articles.text:
Astrana Health says private and confidential information was stolen from its servers after employees were targeted in a social engineering attack.
Astrana Health is a California-based physician-centric healthcare management company that provides back-office services, including claims and billing.
The incident involved the company’s subsidiary Astrana Health Management, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Hackers used social engineering to access the company’s servers, impersonating Astrana Health personnel and spoofing its main phone number to contact employees.
After detecting the attack, the company engaged a third-party cybersecurity firm, notified the relevant authorities and its partners, and launched an investigation.
In response to the intrusion, Astrana Health rotated credentials, restricted remote access tools, rebuilt certain systems from clean backups, and improved its monitoring, logging, and detection.
The investigation has determined that the threat actors have accessed and exfiltrated certain private and confidential information from the company’s servers, Astrana Health told the SEC.
“The company continues to assess whether, and to what extent, patient, employee, credentialed provider, confidential business and financial information, intellectual property, or other information may have been accessed, acquired, or exfiltrated and continues to evaluate the potential impact of the unauthorized activity,” it said.
According to Astrana Health, the incident is material due to the “potential confidential and sensitive nature of the data that is involved”, but it is not expected to impact its financial condition and operations.
The company did not name the threat actor behind the attack, and SecurityWeek has not seen any known ransomware or extortion group claiming responsibility for the incident.

articles.title: The real lesson of Uber’s departure from Nigeria
articles.text:
On September 2, Uber shut down its Nigerian business after 12 years and left the same day. No notice to drivers, no goodbye to riders. It was the fourth African market Uber left in under a year.
The easy way to read this is as a market-share story: Uber’s gone, so Bolt and inDrive split the spoils of a market worth around $450 million with more than 200,000 drivers. That read isn’t wrong. It’s just shallow.
Uber didn’t lose Nigeria because its app was worse than anyone else’s. It lost because the math stopped working, and no app feature fixes math.
Look at the number underneath the whole business. Petrol now sells for between ₦1,100 and ₦1,400 a litre. For a driver working full days in Lagos traffic, fuel isn’t a line item. It’s most of the business. When the single biggest cost climbs past what a rider will pay for a trip, the platform either covers the gap or watches cars go off the road.
Semafor reported this month that in Nigeria, Uber was paying its drivers more than it charged passengers. You can carry that for a while, but not for twelve years. So Uber left.
Here is the part I think the industry is missing. The app was never the hard part.
Matching a rider to a driver is close to a solved problem. What is genuinely hard, and genuinely defensible, is everything underneath the app: knowing who the driver actually is, keeping fraud out, moving money reliably, and understanding a driver’s economics well enough to keep them on the road. That layer, not the interface, is where platforms now live or die. And in Nigeria, more of it is being built by local companies.
I should be upfront: my company is one of them, so weigh what follows accordingly. inDrive verifies its Nigerian drivers through Zeeh. When a driver signs up to earn on one of the world’s largest ride-hailing platforms, active in 48 countries with more than 400 million downloads, the check that clears them runs on infrastructure built in Lagos, not imported. I don’t say that to advertise. I say it because it points to something bigger than my company.
For years, the story of African tech was one of foreign platforms arriving with foreign infrastructure, while local markets adapted to them. That is quietly reversing. The identity rails, the open banking connections, and the credit and payment systems that these global platforms depend on to operate here are increasingly built in Africa, because the people who understand a Nigerian driver’s documents, bank accounts, and cash flow are Nigerian. Infrastructure built for this market, by people from it, simply works better here than infrastructure ported in from elsewhere.
Uber’s exit makes this visible. When a giant leaves, everyone asks who takes the riders. The better question is who owns the layer that the riders and drivers actually run on, because that layer doesn’t leave. It compounds.
The next chapter is already forming around driver economics. If fuel is what broke the model, the fix is cheaper fuel, which, in Nigeria, means a shift to compressed natural gas. CNG runs 40 to 60 per cent cheaper per kilometre than petrol, and a conversion pays for itself inside a few months of driving. But almost none of these drivers have a formal credit file a bank will lend against, so the bottleneck isn’t the gas. It’s the financing, and the underwriting behind it. That, again, is an infrastructure problem, not an app problem. Whoever solves it will do so on rails that verify a driver, read their actual earnings, and safely move money to them. Those rails are being built here, now.
This is the part that should interest anyone thinking about Africa’s digital future. The value in the platform economy is migrating from the app you see to the infrastructure you don’t. If that infrastructure is built and owned locally, the value stays local, and so does the resilience. When a foreign platform exits a market that runs on its own rails, that market barely flinches. A market that rents everything from abroad feels it immediately.
Uber leaving Nigeria isn’t the end of the story. It’s a marker in a longer one about who builds the layer beneath the apps and who retains the value when the apps come and go. On the evidence, that layer is increasingly ours to build.
David Adeleke is the co-founder & CEO of Zeeh Africa, an AI-powered open banking and fintech infrastructure platform. He is driving financial inclusion and secure KYC/KYB data verification across Africa, earning recognition as a 2025 AfricaTech Awards winner at the Viva Technology conference in Paris, France.

articles.title: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
articles.text:
Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
A breakthrough nanolaser could let future computer chips communicate with light, potentially doubling down on speed while cutting energy use in half.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- Scientists have created an ultra-small nanolaser that could eventually allow microchips to transmit information with light instead of electricity, potentially making computers faster while cutting energy use roughly in half. Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.
- Share:
The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.
In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.
"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.
Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.
Using Light Inside Computer Chips
Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.
Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.
Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.
The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.
Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers
The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.
At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.
When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.
The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.
Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use
The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.
Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.
In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.
Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

articles.title: Pangram, una herramienta casi infalible para detectar textos y novelas creadas por IA
articles.text: Un ejemplar del libro "C'etait ca ou mourir", novela del escritor Thelyson Orélien, en una librería en Paris. El libro C’était ça ou mourir ha recibido el premio de novela Fnac, el Medusa y algún otro, lleva más de 35.000 ejemplares vendidos y está entre los candidatos a los grandes galardones del otoño literario. Desde este miércoles, el libro tiene otro mérito: es el primer gran escándalo francés de literatura presuntamente hecha con inteligencia artificial (IA). Su autor, el canadiense de origen haitiano Thélyson Orélien, lo niega. Dice que acabó el primer borrador en 2019 (ChatGPT salió a finales de 2022) y que su tradición literaria “haitiana y caribeña” puede haber causado confusión porque “las imágenes, las repeticiones y el ritmo transmiten una palabra viva”, ha explicado en medios franceses. Su editorial, Grasset, de momento le apoya . La denuncia contra Orélien surgió de una cuenta anónima en X. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: SpaceX lança Starship em missão inédita – assista ao vivo com o Olhar Digital
articles.text:
Com a missão de colocar pela primeira vez o maior foguete do mundo em órbita, a SpaceX deve realizar o 14º voo de teste do Starship na próxima segunda-feira (28), representando um avanço histórico no audacioso projeto. E você pode assistir tudo em tempo real com o Olhar Digital!
Diferentemente dos testes anteriores, que realizaram trajetórias suborbitais, este voo ampliará o tempo de operação da nave no espaço para testar a resistência do veículo em órbita.
A janela de lançamento de 75 minutos abre às 9h15 (pelo horário de Brasília). Isso significa que a decolagem só pode acontecer até 10h30. Como a Terra não para de girar, o lugar exato onde o foguete precisa entrar no espaço muda de posição com o tempo. Se atrasar além da janela prevista, ele erraria esse caminho. Se der qualquer falha técnica ou se o tempo fechar dentro desse período determinado, a missão é cancelada.
Para não perder nenhum detalhe desse momento histórico para a exploração espacial, acompanhe a transmissão ao vivo no YouTube e nas redes sociais do Olhar Digital, a partir das 8h30, com apresentação de Bruno Capozzi, editor-executivo do site, e do astrônomo Marcelo Zurita.
A espaçonave transportará 26 novos satélites da rede de internet Starlink projetados para aumentar a capacidade da frota. Após a implantação no espaço, os equipamentos abrirão seus painéis solares para navegar de forma autônoma até a altitude correta de operação.
Três desses satélites levarão câmeras especiais apontadas para o escudo de proteção térmica da nave. A empresa pretende registrar imagens detalhadas do desgaste do material durante o voo, além de reutilizar pela primeira vez peças térmicas que já voaram em missões anteriores.
Starship vai orbitar a Terra seis vezes em 10 horas
O foguete é dividido em dois estágios. O inferior, chamado de propulsor Super Heavy, recebeu melhorias nos motores para evitar falhas que ocorreram no teste anterior. O objetivo é garantir um retorno controlado e um pouso seguro no oceano.
Após lançar a nave principal ao espaço, o propulsor iniciará sua manobra de volta e deverá cair no Golfo do México cerca de sete minutos depois da decolagem. Desta vez, a estrutura não passará pela tentativa de captura na torre terrestre, pousando diretamente na água.
Já o estágio superior Starship, que dá nome a todo o complexo veicular, permanecerá quase 10 horas no espaço, completando cerca de seis voltas ao redor da Terra a 275 km de altitude. De acordo com um comunicado pré-voo da SpaceX, o teste ajudará a desenvolver tecnologias para que o veículo seja totalmente reutilizável no futuro.
Ao final do trajeto orbital, a nave acionará um de seus seis motores Raptor para sair de órbita e iniciar o mergulho na atmosfera. A missão será concluída com uma descida controlada e um pouso no Oceano Pacífico, a oeste do Chile.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: Ando wants to take on Slack with a team messaging app that lets humans and agents work together | TechCrunch
articles.text:
When Sara Du was helping companies build MCP servers in 2025, people kept asking her how they could use AI agents from within Slack itself. But there were a bunch of technical hurdles in the way: moving messages back and forth and getting agents the right context, all without burning through token budgets.
Upon digging into the problem, Du realized that there was a deeper issue that stemmed from how communication platforms were designed. “The deeper I went, the more I felt Slack and Teams were built for a world that was starting to pass us by,” Du told TechCrunch. “Agents were treated as apps you install even as they were becoming participants in the team.”
The solution, Du thought, could be a system that eliminates “meat proxies,” as Du calls the phenomenon of people having to relay AI agents’ work to their teams. “The human effectively becomes the messenger between the agent and the rest of the company,” she said.
An ideal system would instead let agents “participate in the shared conversations where work already gets coordinated,” Du said. “They should be able to understand why a decision was made, ask a colleague a question, build on another agent’s work, and bring in a human when judgment is needed.”
Her startup, Ando, on Thursday came out of stealth with an app that sets out to do exactly that: It’s a team messaging platform designed for both human and AI workers.
Ando bills itself as a full replacement for Slack or any other messaging platform that companies using AI agents might want for internal communication. The app gives agents their own identities and inboxes and lets them partake in conversations as naturally as people can.
The app has channels, DMs, group conversations, and even live calls that can be transcribed and viewed by an agent, Du said. Agents can browse channels, pick which ones to join, and can even join conversations without being tagged. If a company’s agent thinks a human worker needs to be notified of something, it can message them on its own rather than waiting for approvals.
To continue building the app, Ando on Thursday said it has raised $20 million in pre-seed and seed funding from investors including Accel, Index Ventures, and Emergence.
Du’s idea isn’t a new one. Most of the major players in the workplace collaboration space have already built in support for AI agents — Slack, for instance, has turned its native bot into an AI agent, and Microsoft has gone to great lengths to integrate Copilot into Teams in ways that connect to the rest of its Office 365 suite.
But there is still a market for apps to challenge the incumbents given how quickly AI is invading workplaces. Just a few months ago, Twitter and Block co-founder Jack Dorsey announced Buzz, which brings together people and AI agents into one messaging app, though it’s more targeted at developers.
Du also feels there’s still enough of an advantage in building an AI-agent-native team messaging platform as legacy incumbents try to figure out how to pivot their existing software.
Regardless, she seems to understand that Ando has an uphill battle ahead of it, and said that things were slow in the beginning. “A lot of people we showed it to early on were understandably unimpressed. It was, in many respects, just a jankier messaging platform. People would get stuck on that before they even got to what was different about the agents,” she explained.
But she said her team knew they were onto something when more and more customers started using Ando for longer periods. With Ando, she started to see that agents could do more than people expect: An agent could notice two conversations being held in different channels about the same problem, and without being asked to, could bring everyone together in a group chat, explain the context, and even suggest a decision.
“That was really delightful for me,” she said, “I felt agents could better manage people than humans can because they can process a lot more messages than a human can in a shorter span of time.”
She said Ando is currently working with customers in software, real estate, and finance across 15 countries, though many of the teams it serves right now are small. The fresh capital will be used to hire more people and burn through more tokens, she said.
“I think agents will let very small teams operate at a scale that previously required hundreds of people,” she said. “They can take on more of the execution, research, and coordination work, while humans spend more of their time on judgment, strategy, and deciding what should happen next.”

articles.title: Meta is going to let you build games with AI right on your phone
articles.text:
Meta has a new plan to get people to make games for its Horizon social platform. The company today announced two new development tools that will let you create games with AI prompts: Horizon Create, a mobile app, and Horizon Studio, a browser app that offers more granular controls. The apps will be available in early access, and interested users can sign up for a waitlist.
Meta is going to let you build games with AI right on your phone
The next push for Meta’s Horizon platform involves AI-generated video games.
Horizon has struggled as a platform, but Meta has a plan to give these new Horizon games significantly more reach: It’s going to let published games made with Horizon Create and Horizon Studio get recommended on Facebook and Instagram, where they also will be playable.
“Someone scrolling through Instagram can tap a clip of your game and be in a multiplayer session within seconds, without needing to download an app or being redirected,” Meta says. “Your game lives natively in the feeds where people already discover content and connect with friends.” Games that are “engaging, stable, culturally relevant, and keep players coming back” will get more reach, according to the company.
The company’s announcement comes as Roblox, a similar platform to Horizon that is vastly more popular, is also making a significant push into AI-powered development, including a feature in its mobile app that similarly allows users to generate games with a prompt.
Meta’s news about Horizon, which launched as a VR app, follows a recent pivot to primarily focus on mobile. With Meta stuffing AI into basically everything it can, it’s perhaps no surprise that AI is becoming a big part of Horizon as well.
Giving people the tools to quickly make those could give people more options for things to play. I’m pretty skeptical that a bunch of AI-generated games will be as engaging as a handcrafted experience, but the games made in Create and Studio sound as if they’ll at least have the elements of video games (unlike Google’s Project Genie, which can create brief but empty AI-generated interactive experiences). “Both enable creators to turn any idea into a complete 2D or 3D mobile game, complete with progression systems, balanced difficulty, art direction, multiplayer, and more, then refine every element to their standards,” Meta says in a blog post.
Meta also likely has a very long way to go to reach the scale of Roblox, which has 123 million daily active users. Horizon, by contrast, hasn’t ever really taken off; The Verge reported in early 2022 that it hit 300,000 monthly users.

articles.title: When chat is the wrong UI
articles.text:
Burke Holland
Technologist, author, speaker, and creator. Working at GitHub where I focus on AI-powered development.
What is a developer to do when they need something more tangible than a chat box? Enter canvases.
We’re 176 years into this AI experiment.
Wait…it’s only been three years?
Are you sure?
Sometimes I remember things that happened last year, but it feels like it was so long ago. Did that really happen to me, or was it something that happened to my dad and he just told me about it when I was a kid?
Anyway… we’re three years into this AI experiment and the primary interaction surface we have with LLMs is still chat. I’m pretty sure it was @pmarca who first argued for a textarea component in the HTML spec. And I’m pretty sure of that fact because I asked AI about it. In a textarea.
But I would like to propose to you that perhaps, just maybe, chat is the wrong UI. Well, at least most of the time.
The Academic Steven Pinker said it this way…
It’s kind of a shame that the first large-scale implementation of AI was kind of a gimmick—a first-person chatbot. But there is tremendous promise for AI if it is task oriented.
Steven Pinker, academic
And if an academic says it and then I write it down as a quote in a blog post, then you know it’s true.
Chat is the primary way of working with AI because it was the first thing that people clicked with. And chat works really well as a universal solution simply because we don’t know what people are going to try to do with AI.
But as the user you know what you’re going to do with it, and at that point chat is often the wrong UI.
What you need, dear reader, is some sort of customizable UI that you can manifest out of thin air to work with the AI (or fight with—you do you) in the way that works for what you are trying to do in the moment.
There are lots of ways to pull this off, but in the GitHub Copilot app, this is called a canvas.
A canvas is a little full-stack application that runs inside of the GitHub Copilot app with no browser chrome. The agent can communicate with the server part of that app and the server can communicate back. So what you end up with is a surface that can do anything a normal computer program can do, plus can communicate bi-directionally with the GitHub Copilot agent.
That sounds very hand-wavy and I did use the word bi-directional which sounds like it’s straight off of a PowerPoint, so let’s look at this concept in practice and see if we can solve actual problems with the mighty canvas.
We’ll start with a simple example: using a canvas to create a Connect 4 game where you can play with the agent inside of the GitHub Copilot app.
Watch me absolutely DESTROY GPT-5.6 Sol on high reasoning…
OK. But I definitely did beat GPT-5.6 Luna with no reasoning so…LISTEN…CONNECT 4 IS A HARD GAME!!
Building a canvas is as simple as asking for it…
Create a new canvas that uses the Connect 4 game to demonstrate the ability for the user to interact with the canvas for the canvas to talk to the agent and for the agent to control the canvas
The GitHub Copilot app knows what a canvas is, so we don’t need to explain ourselves any more than that.
Now because these canvases are actually full stack apps and not just web pages, they can call third-party APIs, yes, but they can also execute code locally on your machine.
For example, here is a UI for Winget that can browse for packages on the registry, as well as manage my local packages, including installing and uninstalling.
There’s no AI here, but that’s the point.
When chat is the primary interface, it encourages you to use the agent to do everything. This is often just a pure waste of tokens. It’s almost always better to have the agent build a tool where all future interactions are free vs treating the agent itself as the tool. Stop asking GPT-5.6 Sol Max to “stage and commit”. (I know you do that. Because I’ve done it. Don’t token shame me, I have a fragile ego.)
Another great example would be instead of using the chat to ask the agent to do things with your SQLite database, how about you throw up a canvas and, you know, do it yourself.
I mean, you can even have intellisense here. Why not? Its 2026, and AI is a magical box that just does whatever you want.
Isn’t that pleasant?
It’s nice to write a little SQL every now and again. I said every now and again. Relax.
Or why write your Jekyll blog posts in plain Markdown when you can literally bring Windows Live Writer back from the dead.
Ok, these are all fun and mildly useful examples, but the value of custom UI gets a lot more clear when you use it to automate your development workflows.
I’m not going to tell you how to live your life, but my process for working with agents looks more or less like this…
It’s pretty simple, but each one of these steps requires me to be at the keyboard to interact, view prototypes, guide and move between steps.
But here’s the thing. I don’t actually need to be around for most of this process. The agent is capable of researching and generating prototypes and then letting me know when it’s ready for a review. The goal with agents is always to take yourself out of the loop as much as you can. That’s difficult though, because it’s not clear how to do that when all you have is a chat box.
Here’s a full example of how you can use a canvas to automate your own workflow, removing yourself from the loop as much or as little as you like.
I’m not saying you should copy this workflow or that this is the perfect example of how to work with agents. I mean, it might be. It probably is. Let’s ask AI…
OMG.
In all seriousness, I do think being boxed in by the chat UI may be working against us all right now. This is making it hard to figure out how to solve actual problems, because it’s not at all obvious what to do when your only method of interaction is a textarea.
Give canvases a try today. Some things like the SQLite canvas you can one shot. The workflow one took the better part of a day to get the design and automation right.
But I think you’ll find that you can go much further with AI when you think…wait for it…outside the chat box.

articles.title: 3D Chips Push EDA Into New Territory
articles.text:
As AI chips move to stacked, chiplet-based architectures, EDA vendors are reworking mature tools for cross-domain analysis, faster exploration, and agentic AI assistance.
Key Takeaways:
As demand for AI power and performance grows, chip designs increasingly involve 3D stacking, chiplets, and heterogeneous integration within a single package.
In a virtuous cycle, EDA tool vendors are leveraging advanced chips to simulate multi-physics challenges in a single tool instead of running individual solvers. Agentic AI is adding another layer of analysis to enable faster design exploration and automate various tasks. However, a few speed bumps remain due to the rapid progression of chip technology.
One challenge is that HPC/AI chip design must be considered across compute, memory, interconnect, power, and thermal constraints. “Today, nearly every AI accelerator has a process threshold where the hardest problems no longer live inside the chip. They live at the system boundaries,” said Artour Levin, vice president of AI silicon engineering at Microsoft.[1] “A standalone chip is not very beneficial for AI because very few things can be run on a single chip. You really need to look at the system level, and if you look at the history of EDA tools when they started, 30 or 40 years ago, it’s natural that EDA tools were designed to design chips, not a system.”
The chip-to-system threshold is where customers are facing challenges. “The design toolchain grew up around clean abstraction boundaries — cell, block, chip — with physics handled as episodic, domain-by-domain validation at the end,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO and co-founder of Vinci. “That operating model worked when the hardest problems stayed inside those boundaries. It breaks when heat, stress, and electrical behavior move across the entire physical stack, because the physics insight arrives after the decisions that needed it have already been made. Hardware teams don’t need physics after the design is done changing. They need physics while the design is still moving.”
That requires new approaches, not a faster version of the old workflow. “It’s deterministic, solver-accurate physics that’s continuously available across chip, package, board, and system — treating physics as infrastructure rather than a late-stage checkpoint,” said Kabaria. “In hardware, plausible isn’t enough. Outputs have to be measurable, deterministic, and accurate enough to support real design decisions, which is why solver-grounded results and run-to-run reproducibility matter as much as speed.”
The central question is whether to augment existing EDA tools that have been fine-tuned and proven over many years, or create new tools because AI/HPC chip designs are so different from the monolithic chips of days gone by.
“There are decades of embedded knowledge for good reason, and a lot of long-held beliefs that work in single isolation, but maybe not when you go cross-domain,” said Henry Sheng, executive director of R&D at Synopsys.[2] “This has to be reflected within the tooling itself. How do you manage not to try to boil the ocean? If you try to reinvent everything, you won’t do it. You have to reinvent how you put things together to maintain coherency, so you don’t have different data representations and terminologies for the same thing across domains. Then, how do you bring all that into a cohesive tool?”
Heterogeneity puts more pressure on floor-planning challenges, in particular. “It becomes much harder, and that’s one of the conversations that people are having,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “Can we do the floor planning upfront? Can we make sure we all agree that this is the budget that you get for loss here, and this is the budget I get for signal path, and this is the way we are going to supply power to this complex 3D environment? That conversation starts happening up front, and it leaves very little room for negotiation later.” And while the big money says to use 3D design for AI chips, it can be applicable anywhere, Kamdar added.
Maybe in the future, 3D and heterogeneous design will be out of the box, but that’s not the reality now. “Because the manufacturing and packaging technology is evolving fast, there’s still different solutions out there,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer at Arteris. “You can do it this way. You can do it that way. It’s not yet one size fits all. Because of that, people want some differentiation. But is the technology 80% there? Is it 90% there, where anybody who actually wants to do it can do it? Yeah, I think so.”
Specific customer challenges
Customers designing 3D-ICs and multi-die assemblies for AI/HPC chips are using existing EDA tools, but they want improvements in some areas.
One challenge is interoperability across established vendors and startups. “If you want to put out compelling products in the industry, EDA tools should be very interoperable,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D for advanced packaging technology and manufacturing at Intel. [3]. “I happened to look at a design last week. Just by experience, I said, ‘I don’t see enough density in some of these layers. Copper density is critical for warpage.’ I was very concerned that this might be a technical glitch. I reached out to my mechanical analysis person. I said, ‘Here you go. I think it is one of the other industry formats, but it doesn’t matter. We need to let the design team know that they might have to co-optimize the design, so they don’t get into issues later.’ It took 10 days for the analysis and a response. People looked at the design. They saw it wasn’t complete. It didn’t have some properties. Maybe it wasn’t completely routed. Then I pulled in a design engineer. They finished up with AI. They wrote some scripts, routed it, but then the extraction didn’t happen in a very prominent industry analysis capability. What I got was three pictures. One is yellow. One is red, and who knows what the other color is. And if I am a customer, as a design person, I look at it and don’t know what I need to do to the design. It makes no sense. Then I’ve got to bring 10 PhDs in a room [to fix it].”
Fig. 1: Intel’s Immaneni details the impact of complexity in AI chips. Source: Intel/DAC
Interoperable tools make it easier for customers to bring findings together. “Each of the customers should be able to pick and choose the best in class from each vendor, whether it’s mechanical analysis, design enabling, connectivity checkers, whatever it is. And all these EDA tools should agree to a CAD-neutral format, so the extractions don’t become this complex,” Immaneni noted.
For now, HPC customers are doing the best they can. “We have been living in pain for probably the last five or six years,” said AJ Tufano, distinguished engineer at Broadcom.[2] “We’re getting by, we’re surviving, we’re producing chips, but we can do a lot better.”
In the custom accelerator space, every six months — and in some cases every three months — fundamental architectural changes are happening. “The challenge that we’re faced with is how to match the pace of software, and how to do that while complexity keeps increasing. 3.5D is a large part of that,” Tufano observed.
Fig. 2: Challenges in 3D-IC and heterogeneous design. Source: Broadcom/DAC
There are wins with the challenges. “I will pause and give kudos to the folks creating these tools because it does really impress me that for the scale of the design we have, we can get this thing to run in its entirety at the level of detail that is needed,” said Tufano. “That’s phenomenal. If I look at the number of orders of [magnitude] at any given point in time to do one chip, it’s like a brownout of the lab. The compute resource there is pretty stagnant, so we’re left with a dichotomy of early analysis flows to catch gross issues, which are important, then full-blown IR signoff, which happens much too late. There’s a gap of issues that could potentially be solved in between.”
Others point to similar challenges. [3] “We are surviving right now,” said Venu Sanaka, senior director of engineering at Qualcomm. “The thermal and IR analysis are much more advanced than the other stages of analysis in terms of the multi-physics. The challenges right now are more on the exploration front. Exploration is pretty manual. I can venture out to say, where do you put the bump locations and TSVs (through-silicon vias) and thermal? Those trade-offs aren’t fast enough for our analysis in a normal design cycle. Say it’s one year or so. For this kind of partitioning analysis, we need to start much earlier, maybe three to six months. For that, you don’t have designs ready to run through all the detailed analysis, so you need an early trade-off mechanism.”
Die-to-die PPA optimizations are also tricky. “We wanted to move one block from one die to the other die in a different technology,” said Sanaka. “The power and placement implications of that are all manual right now. We don’t have any quick way of analyzing it, so we floorplan it in 2D, then we put it together and analyze it.”
Multi-chip compounds the challenge. “When I say one chip, I mean when you put in the physical index directory it is related to one chip,” said Sanaka. “Now you have multiple chips trying to come together with different technologies. The data management aspect itself is a little more challenging, and we have a lot of partners within our teams that we need to exchange data with. How do you exchange that data? These are all in the recent stages.”
Fig. 3: EDA tool solutions needed by companies designing AI chips. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The opportunity to improve tools is large, even if there are pain points right now. “It’s clear that there’s sub-optimality,” Sheng observed. “These chips are phenomenally successful, so it’s okay for now. To fully appreciate the transformation, we’re going from fully manual to automation. We’re going from many single-domain problems to cross-domain problems. In many cases, manual design is experience-driven.”
EDA tools have undoubtedly made incremental improvements, noted Sheng. “But transformational readiness goes through everything.”
Agentic AI as an additional layer on existing tools
EDA vendors have two paths to meet HPC customers’ needs  — augment existing tools or start over. Agentic AI is making both paths possible.
“Three or four years ago, when we saw the technology starting to take off, we had this discussion,” said Vinay Patwardhan, product management group director at Cadence. [3] “When we went to customers, one piece of feedback we received was, ‘We have a hundred 2D designers. We don’t have any 3D designers, so whatever you build, make sure those hundred people can adapt your existing technology.”
Another problem concerned taping out the chip. “We say, ‘It’s a new technology. We just wrote it.’ And the customer would respond, ‘Can you build on something that is trusted so we don’t have to go through this palm tree validation loop again?’ So we made a conscious decision to say that we have our industry-standard tools. The foundries are qualified with extensive certification flows,” Patwardhan explained. “It makes sense to build on that, make it three-dimension aware, use some optimizations to do full 3D or stacking, then see how the industry is moving. When an inflection point comes, we either redevelop the whole flow, or we use some of the new techniques. That’s where we are now with the agentic flow that has come to the top. The exploration capabilities are tremendously improved, and will be tremendously improved because there are a lot of variables.”
Fig. 4: Synopsys’ Sheng and Cadence’s Patwardhan debate the readiness of EDA tools for 3D design at the Design Automation Conference. Source: Semiconductor Engineering [3]
Others agree that agents offer the extra layer needed. “AI is increasingly being used to explore configurations and identify optimal tradeoffs much faster than traditional flows, accelerating design-space exploration, especially for 2.5D and 3D-ICs, where complexity grows significantly,” noted Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing, at Arteris. “But AI-generated design decisions must be explainable, traceable, and validated against deterministic EDA engines and established verification methodologies before signoff.”
The latest tools already help with some of the upfront floor-planning analysis for 3D-ICs, and the agentic layer with natural language prompts can be turned on or off to save token use.
“At a very abstract level, we can look at boxes in different colors and with a few clicks, you can change the materials or properties,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You can choose to have a very deep via layer, and you can see what the impact would be on your electrical performance. Or you can have a very thin via layer. It’s a choice of, ‘What if?’ This is not a deep optimization problem. This is an architectural problem. The architecture of these designs has some boundary conditions. You can’t just shoot for the moon. Largely, it’s the materials that people are operating in. The size constraint is fixed. The depth constraint, the number of layers you can have, is fixed. For the chiplet die itself, you have a good understanding of whether you are going to do this in 2nm or stay with 6nm, but you may have a little bit of room to negotiate that.”
Electrical performance can already be analyzed in the 3D tool, and IR drop, power integrity, thermal, and other multiphysics will be added soon. “At the floor planning level, not only do you get to see electrical performance, but if you change the package material, what happens to signal performance? What happens to power? What happens to thermal? All of that at a floor-planning level should be available to the architect,” Kamdar noted.
Post-training, continuous learning in agentic AI also offers promise for EDA tools to evolve to the needed complexity.
To enable agentic autonomous research, engineers set up research targets and create a benchmark suite. “You kind of cut your agents loose and say, ‘Here’s what I want you to get better at,’” said Jeff Dyck, vice president of R&D at Siemens EDA. [4] “That’s working extremely well for building better tools. It’s in the self-learning theme, and agents are extremely good at this. Then you say, ‘You guys have to build your own models that are better for this.’ Auto fine-tuning, auto distillation, and the like are strong opportunities in that auto-learning space.”
Agentic AI as the foundation for startup solutions
Many startups aim to disrupt traditional EDA tools with a unique selling proposition that leverages AI and/or agents.
“The platform we built is completely scalable for anything — die level, 3D-IC level, and advanced packaging level,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “You can leverage our workflow to solve any kind of problem from chip to system to analog. Then you have to tune the workflow, to make it more advanced, so that your time to results and your cost continue improving, meaning that you can do your advanced packaging in one day instead of taking months. That requires more tuning.”
Fine-tuning of the agentic platform requires strong collaboration with customers. “To achieve this, the customer needs to understand their ontology, their know-how, the way that they are doing certain things,” said Rahim. “The second thing is you need to have both design expertise and domain expertise. Based on that, you can then build some advanced intelligence to tackle those problems. Tuning is building that advanced intelligence, and that advanced intelligence is a brain. You’re actually tuning a brain. We’re not talking about the LLM. We’re talking about a brain sitting in the workflow that is collecting a lot of data, the ontology, and the intelligence of our R&D to solve the customer’s problem and create an algorithm, but that algorithm is much more complex than the traditional algorithm that is capable of taking all this data and working with the LLMs to get to the outcome that you need. That’s what we call the tuning.”
Startup Architect Labs puts proprietary, specialized agents into an end-to-end, full-stack co-design system. “We’re elevating you from an RTL engineer to a human architect,” said Dan Ganousis, head of sales at Architect Labs. “We read the spec and ask, ‘What are you trying to build?’ They say, ‘We’re using a UCIe interface.’ We can go get that. ‘We’re using an Arm core.’ We can go get that and put it in such that the engineer is not writing Verilog to design. He’s writing at the spec level, the architectural level, of what we are trying to accomplish, and then our system takes that, sits on top of all the existing flow, and feeds logic synthesis. We have formal methods that we have customized in our system, so we’re formally verifying as we’re building.”
Another company developed a two-way AI virtual platform, from spec to RTL and from RTL to spec, to enable hardware/software co-design. “With our technology, you give it a spec or model and instead of generating RTL directly, it generates a high-level model, which runs 30´ faster,” said Badru Agarwala, CEO of Rise. “It’s loosely timed. It’s not RTL. Then, using our high-level synthesis tools, you can lower it to RTL. On the other hand, we have other technology that goes from RTL to spec. There, it is the opposite problem. Designers can start verification immediately because these models are timing-dependent. They have all the information, and one advantage of high-level models is that you can explore. If you want to change the memory bandwidth, or you want to change the performance, throughput, timing, 7nm, remove the functionality, all the benefits are available once you have the high-level models to do that.”
Meanwhile, a South Korean startup focuses on a no-code, diagram-first approach to solve power and clock problems in early-stage RTL design. “We make the DFT logic at the RTL design level, so we can shift left the DFT design to the very early stage,” said Jihwan Lee, strategy planning team leader at ITDA. “Our tool is based on a graphical user interface (GUI), so an engineer can just drag and drop the components in our tool and get all the outputs for the synthesis — RTL code and some SDC and UPF for the plug and power synthesis, and DFT tool input file.”
Other companies offer multi-physics simulation tools at extremely high speeds. “There is a crisis in the industry, in my opinion, and the only solution is extremely deep innovation that will give you very high accuracy, but much, much faster,” said Yehea Ismail, co-founder of Suitera, who declined to explain how the high speeds were achieved except that it took seven years.
The shift toward physics-based, AI-enabled tools has proof in the numbers. “A 200-case design sweep that used to take about 16 hours on a legacy thermal workflow now runs in roughly an hour, with setup in under a minute,” said Vinci’s Kabari. “The more telling number, though, is what happens after that. The physics analysis scales near-linearly for runtime inference beyond 10 billion degrees of freedom, because a real system isn’t one component.”
Conclusion
Ultimately, the success of 3D-ICs will depend not only on packaging and process breakthroughs, but also on EDA tools that can keep pace with rapidly changing design requirements. AI tools, machine learning, and agentic systems have value, and there is shared agreement that deterministic physics cannot be left out of the probabilistic AI equation.
From a commercial standpoint, the chip industry consists of EDA, design, and manufacturing. “The technical problem is that these three are still heavily interacting, and so we can see a lot of collaboration,” said Sheng. “If you want to do incremental change [in EDA tools for 3D/HI], each one of these can march forward on its own, but only for a certain amount of time. If you really want non-incremental change, then this has to be done in concert across the three systems. In other words, EDA alone does not optimize what design you can formulate. It’s not that you don’t know what you want. It’s really, can you codify the design and make it programmatic with what you want, and define your boundary conditions in a more disciplined way?”
For now, the physics are not changing. “Light is light, masks are masks,” said Arteris’ Siwinski. “Until we figure out some other way — maybe at some point in the future, there will be some other materials that allow us to make bigger wafers — chiplets are given, 3D packaging is a given, and everything is going to go vertical. Everything needs to be chiplet first, multi-die first, physically-aware first, including package considerations.”
3D is an exciting space. “The fun thing is going to be, will logic dies go the way that memory dies are going?’ Siwinski observed. “Are we really going to start doing 3D logic cubes and rethinking about how packaging is to evolve for that, much more than what’s happening on the memory side? We’ll see.”
— Brendan Heffernan contributed to this report.

articles.text:
What happens when the app you started in high school goes viral?
For Zach Yadegari, the answer was more than 15 million downloads, $30 million in annual revenue, and an acquisition by MyFitnessPal — all before his 20th birthday. Yadegari was just 17 when he co-founded Cal AI, the AI-powered nutrition app that lets users track what they eat by snapping a photo.
But those numbers leave out the part most founders would like to know: How did Cal AI get that kind of viral attention in the first place? And once millions of people showed up, how did the company make the most of that momentum?
At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Yadegari will take the Builders Stage for the fireside chat “How to Create Viral Growth and Capitalize On It.” He’ll get into Cal AI’s rapid growth, the product pressure that came with it, and the challenge of turning breakout attention into durable retention and long-term company building.
Trying to break through in a crowded market? Save up to $200 when you secure your pass by September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT and hear what Yadegari learned building a breakout consumer app. Got a colleague who’d like to join? Get a second pass for 50% off.
How did Cal AI turn viral growth into a $30 million business?
Cal AI is built around a simple proposition: Snap a photo of a meal, and the app uses image recognition and the phone’s depth sensor to calculate calories, protein, carbs, and fat.
Zach Yadegari was still a high school senior when he co-founded Cal AI, but it wasn’t his first experience attracting a large online audience. At 16, he sold Totally Science, a gaming platform he founded that drew more than 5 million users during the COVID-19 pandemic, for six figures.
Cal AI moved even faster. In less than two years, it had more than 15 million downloads and was generating more than $30 million in annual revenue. MyFitnessPal took notice, acquiring the company in a deal that closed in December 2025. The deal kept Cal AI as a stand-alone app, retained its seven-person team, and left Yadegari at the helm.

articles.title: Questionnaire sur l'Australie, site gouvernemental infiltré, mail générique : ce que l'on sait de la nouvelle dérive agentique d'OpenAI
articles.text:
C’est un incident qui date de juin dernier, mais qui vient seulement d’être officialisé.
Le Premier ministre australien Anthony Albanese a révélé le 23 septembre 2026 qu’un agent d’OpenAI avait « infiltré un site web du gouvernement australien » alors qu’il cherchait des statistiques médicales. Le portail concerné héberge des données liées à Medicare, le régime national d’assurance maladie du pays.
OpenAI, de son côté, reconnaît les faits et assure que ses modèles ont agi sans que l’entreprise l’ait voulu.
Des fichiers publics et non publics consultés
Selon la version d’OpenAI, tout est parti d’une évaluation interne. Les modèles de l’entreprise devaient répondre à des questions portant sur l’Australie et ont cherché des réponses et des statistiques sur plusieurs sites et services du gouvernement australien. « Nos modèles ont alors entrepris des actions que nous n’avions pas prévues », explique un porte-parole de l’entreprise au média britannique The Register.
Pour répondre aux interrogations qui lui étaient soumises, l’agent est parti dénicher un accès non autorisé au portail de statistiques de Medicare. D’après Anthony Albanese, des fichiers publics et des fichiers non publics ont été consultés.
Le Premier ministre précise toutefois que ce portail contient des informations « non sensibles », comme des données de dépenses. OpenAI indique pour sa part que l’agent a eu accès à des statistiques de santé agrégées et à des noms de fichiers internes.
Une adresse mail générique pour prévenir Canberra
À ce stade, le gouvernement australien estime qu’aucun autre de ses systèmes n’a été compromis et qu’aucune donnée personnelle n’a été consultée. Deux gouvernements d’États ont toutefois été prévenus que leurs sites avaient aussi été visés, celui d’une agence de lutte contre la criminalité et celui d’un département de la santé.
De son côté, OpenAI dit avoir découvert l’incident en passant en revue les comportements « désalignés » de ses agents et n’a informé Canberra que le 10 septembre. Un délai que l’entreprise justifie par le temps nécessaire pour vérifier les faits mais que le Premier ministre Albanese juge « beaucoup trop long ».
Autre point de colère, la manière dont l’incident a été communiqué. OpenAI se serait en effet contentée d’écrire à l’adresse générique de signalement de l’agence concernée, publicdisclosures@, plutôt qu’à des responsables gouvernementaux.
Présent comme Sam Altman aux réunions des Nations unies, Anthony Albanese dit s’être entretenu avec le patron d’OpenAI pour lui faire part de « l’extrême inquiétude » de l’Australie.

articles.title: On a essayé les Meta VR Glasses, le Vision Pro moins cher et plus léger, en avant-première
articles.text:
Dans la foulée de la présentation des Ray-Ban Gen 3, le groupe a aussi, et surtout, levé le voile sur les Meta VR Glasses, une alternative de taille au Vision Pro d’Apple. Conviés par Meta, nous avons eu l’occasion de tester, pendant quelques heures, les lunettes connectées en avant-première, lors d’un événement organisé à Londres.
A lire aussi : Lunettes Ray-Ban Meta désactivées à distance – l’entreprise part à la chasse aux modèles trafiqués
Meta VR Glasses, les lunettes qui font mal au Vision Pro
Présentées comme une rupture par rapport aux casques Quest de la marque, les VR Glasses sont des lunettes de réalité mixte, qui combinent réalité augmentée et réalité virtuelle. Le focus est néanmoins mis sur les usages qui dépendent de la réalité virtuelle. Meta parle d’ailleurs d’une « nouvelle ère pour la réalité virtuelle ».
Divulguées en petit comité avant d’être dévoilées par Mark Zuckerberg lors de la Meta Connect, les Meta VR Glasses se présentent comme une alternative plus abordable, et prometteuse, au Vision Pro d’Apple. Comme le souligne Meta, les VR Glasses ont une « forme innovante proche de véritables lunettes », et s’éloignent du casque de réalité virtuelle. On n’y trouve d’ailleurs pas de sangles destinées au porteur. Exit l’engin volumineux qui provoque des regards en coin, place à de véritables lunettes.
En miroir du Vision Pro, l’appareil de Meta délègue batterie et puissance de calcul à un boîtier séparé relié par un câble optique. Cette approche permet de réduire considérablement le poids de l’engin, et ça se sent. Lors de nos tests, les lunettes nous ont semblé très légères, et très agréables à porter. On s’imagine facilement passer des heures avec les lunettes vissées sur le nez, sans faire souffrir nos cervicales. C’est évidemment à confirmer lors d’un test plus poussé.
Meta précise que les performances sont assurées par une puce Snapdragon Reality Elite de Qualcomm. Le géant californien promet « trois heures d’autonomie en lecture multimédia haute résolution », compensée par un système de recharge rapide 45W. En clair, c’est suffisant pour regarder un film d’une seule traite.
À lire aussi : Les Meta Ray-Ban Display débarquent en France – on a pu les prendre en main en avant-première
Une salle de cinéma et une console de jeu
Meta précise par ailleurs que toutes les applications taillées pour ses casques Quest sont compatibles avec les VR Glasses. Nous avons pu participer à une démonstration complète des possibilités offertes par les lunettes, et on a été bluffés par l’expérience immersive mis au point par le groupe. Nous avons notamment pu tester plusieurs des applications Quest, comme Disney+.
Meta cherche à séduire les cinéphiles avec un écran de haut vol. L’appareil embarque en effet un écran 5K micro-OLED avec une définition de 37 pixels par degré, contre 25 pour le Quest 3. C’est premier « casque » certifié IMAX Enhanced. Il permet de regarder des films au format 1,43:1, comme voulu par les cinéastes. La définition atteint 37 pixels par degré, un niveau de précision qui rend notamment le texte particulièrement net et facile à lire, détaille Meta. Le tout est complété par la certification Dolby Vision, et par le son Dolby Atmos intégré directement dans la monture.
On a notamment regardé une scène d’Avengers : Infinity War, dont l’environnement s’est étiré tout autour de nous grâce à la fonction VR Enhanced Cinema. Les lunettes nous ont en effet plongés au cœur d’un environnement virtuel inspiré des décors du film Marvel. Cette fonctionnalité, réservée à une poignée de films, selon Meta, offre une expérience immersive plutôt réussie. Mais, une fois la bonne surprise passée, on se voit mal s’attarder sur le décor virtuel en regardant un film complet. L’option tient plus du gadget que de la « killer feature ».
Les lunettes sont aussi taillées pour le jeu vidéo. Toute la bibliothèque Quest sera d’ailleurs disponible dès le premier jour, complétée par 75 jeux pensés pour une utilisation sans manette. Les manettes Quest sont néanmoins compatibles avec les lunettes. Le service Xbox Cloud Gaming sera également disponible. Il permettra de diffuser des centaines de jeux, si vous avez une manette Bluetooth compatible.
Un bureau géant
Meta présente aussi l’appareil comme un poste de travail nomade, avec un immense affichage multiécrans. Les lunettes permettent en effet de créer un environnement à plusieurs moniteurs dans un café, un avion ou n’importe quel espace réduit, sans se balader avec le moindre accessoire supplémentaire. L’expérience bureautique était particulièrement convaincante, d’autant qu’on continue à percevoir tout ce qui nous entoure. Dans les faits, c’est simplement comme si trois écrans géants apparaissaient devant vos yeux. Meta explique qu’il est possible de connecter sans fil ou via USB-C un Mac ou un PC Windows.
Par ailleurs, les VR Glasses n’isolent pas le porteur dans un environnement fermé. Les « côtés ouverts et la caméra de vision augmentée permettent de rester conscient de son environnement », explique Meta. Grâce aux caméras intégrées, vous pouvez en effet voir ce qu’il se passe autour de vous. C’est pourquoi on peut parler de réalité augmentée. Le rendu de l’environnement est plutôt réussi. On aperçoit clairement ses propres mains et les personnes qui se trouvent à proximité. L’image est simplement un peu floue, selon notre propre expérience.
Meta révèle aussi avoir mis au point une technologie similaire à celle de Persona d’Apple. Les lunettes vont en effet générer une représentation numérique et photoréaliste de l’utilisateur pour les appels vidéo. Cette technologie d’hologramme sera notamment utilisée pour les appels WhatsApp ou sur Zoom.
Naviguer avec les yeux, il faut s’y habituer
La navigation se fait par le regard et de simples gestes des doigts, complétés par les commandes vocales de Meta AI. En clair, il suffit de regarder une icône, une application ou une touche quelconque pour la sélectionner. Ensuite, un petit geste de la main permet de valider la sélection, ou de revenir en arrière. Bardées de capteurs, les lunettes sont capables de détecter tout ce que font vos mains, et ce, même si vous les glissez derrière vous. C’est assez déstabilisant au début, mais on se fait assez rapidement à cette nouvelle façon de naviguer dans l’interface. En quelques minutes, on a pris l’habitude de fixer une icône du regard avant de la sélectionner avec les doigts. C’est presque magique.
Lors de la démonstration, l’écran avait tendance à se décentrer régulièrement. Un employé Meta devait impérativement intervenir pour remettre l’écran dans mon champ de vision. C’est un problème qu’on a déjà rencontré avec plusieurs autres lunettes pour la réalité virtuelle. Gageons que ce phénomène soit corrigé en amont de la sortie.
Durant les expérimentations, le câble s’est plusieurs fois mis dans notre chemin, surtout lorsque nous testions des jeux vidéo en réalité virtuelle. C’est inévitable, mais c’est clairement le principal point faible de la proposition. Les lunettes peuvent se distinguer par leur légèreté, elles restent enchaînées à un boîtier. La technologie actuelle ne permet pas encore de faire entrer tous les composants dans un accessoire qui ne soit pas excessivement volumineux. En dépit de ce boîtier, les VR Glasses nous ont particulièrement convaincus. Au terme de la démonstration, on a eu l’impression d’avoir testé une version affinée du Vision Pro d’Apple.
Un prix alléchant
Les lunettes se distinguent de leur rival ultime par leur prix. Meta annonce un prix de départ de 1 299 dollars, contre plus de 3 500 dollars pour le casque Apple. Malheureusement, il faudra faire preuve de patience pour pouvoir mettre la main sur les VR Glasses. Les lunettes pour la réalité virtuelle n’arriveront sur le marché qu’au cours du printemps 2027. Meta n’a pas précisé dans quels pays les lunettes seront commercialisées.

articles.title: US Court Sentences Armenian Man to Prison for Ryuk Ransomware Attacks
articles.text:
Karen Vardanyan, a 35-year-old Armenian national, has been sentenced to prison by a US court for his role in Ryuk ransomware attacks, the Justice Department announced this week.
Vardanyan was charged by a grand jury in the United States in February 2024 with conspiracy, fraud, and extortion in connection with computers.
He was arrested in Ukraine in April 2025 and extradited to the United States in June 2025. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy and computer fraud in July 2026.
Vardanyan has now been sentenced to 24 months in federal prison, followed by 3 years of supervised release.
Under federal law, time spent in pretrial detention is credited toward the prison term. Vardanyan has been in custody since his extradition, so he has already served a substantial portion of the 24-month sentence.
According to authorities, the Armenian man was involved in Ryuk ransomware attacks between March 2019 and June 2020.
Based on the DOJ’s description, Vardanyan was likely a ransomware affiliate or initial access provider rather than part of the team that developed the malware and operated the infrastructure supporting Ryuk attacks.
He extorted more than $1 million from several victims via ransomware attacks, and he has now been ordered to pay more than $1.2 million in restitution to victims.
Several individuals involved in ransomware operations have been sentenced to prison this year. Most recently, a Ukrainian Conti ransomware developer received a 4-year prison sentence in the United States, and a Ukrainian accused of creating the Lockergoga, MegaCortex, and Nefilim ransomware families has been sentenced to 13 years in prison by a Swiss court.
Related: Two Scattered Spider Hackers Sentenced to Jail in UK
Related: Snowflake Hacker Pleads Guilty in US Court
Related: Ukrainian Man Pleads Guilty in US to Conti Ransomware Charges

articles.title: Linux arrive enfin sur les ordinateurs portables équipés de puces Snapdragon X
articles.text:
Linux arrive enfin sur les ordinateurs portables équipés de puces Snapdragon X
Absent des ordinateurs portables équipés de puces Qualcomm, Linux prépare son arrivée officielle. Entre annonces de distributions et matériels déjà disponibles, l'écosystème ARM s’élargit pour offrir toujours plus de souplesse aux utilisateurs.
Les ordinateurs portables ont entamé une diversification vers l'architecture ARM, emmenée par les puces Snapdragon X de Qualcomm depuis bientôt trois ans. Si ces processeurs apportent des gains en matière d'efficacité énergétique du fait de leur conception initiale, ils souffraient jusqu'ici d'un manque d'intégration logicielle. En dehors des usages habituels, les ordinateurs équipés de ces SoC laissaient de côté une partie des utilisateurs avancés et amateurs d’OS libres en raison de l'absence de prise en charge des distributions Linux. Lors de son Snapdragon Summit annuel, Qualcomm a présenté une feuille de route destinée à combler cette lacune.
Snapdragon X et X2 : un calendrier de déploiement Linux étalé jusqu'en 2027
Malgré la présence ancienne de Qualcomm dans le secteur mobile avec Android, dont les fondations reposent sur des bases Linux, les premiers ordinateurs sous Snapdragon X n'offraient pas de compatibilité directe avec les distributions traditionnelles. Cette situation doit évoluer progressivement au cours des prochains mois.
Le calendrier annoncé débutera avec la distribution Debian, dont la prise en charge est prévue d'ici la fin de l'année. La démarche se poursuivra avec Ubuntu, qui sera proposé sur la seconde génération de processeurs, les Snapdragon X2, au début de l'année 2027. Les fabricants préparent leurs gammes autour de ces échéances, à l'image d'Asus qui prévoit de proposer Ubuntu sur ses machines équipées de Snapdragon X2 avant le milieu de l'année 2027.
Googlebook et Android 17 : un accès à Linux dès le 5 octobre sur Snapdragon X
Si les utilisateurs de distributions classiques doivent attendre ces déploiements échelonnés, un autre accès à l'environnement Linux s'apprête à débarquer le 5 octobre.
Ces ordinateurs fonctionnent sous une version adaptée d'Android 17. Le système d'exploitation s'appuyant sur Linux, ces machines donnent un accès direct au terminal. De quoi exploiter les capacités de cet environnement sans attendre l'adaptation de systèmes tiers, bien que la formule diffère d'une distribution de bureau standard.
HP Googlebook 14c
Distributions Linux : une nouvelle jeunesse pour les PC Snapdragon X modestes
Cette ouverture progressive à Linux apporte une diversité intéressante sur le marché des systèmes d'exploitation. Les développeurs disposeront de choix plus larges pour leurs ordinateurs portables, avec des environnements mieux adaptés à leurs besoins de programmation sur architecture ARM.
Pour le grand public, cette évolution logicielle pourrait redonner du souffle à certaines machines. C'est notamment le cas des ordinateurs portables équipés de la puce Snapdragon X (X1-26-100). Cette dernière est souvent intégrée dans de petites configurations techniques, associant 8 Go de mémoire vive et 256 Go de stockage sous Windows 11. Le système d'exploitation se montre bien trop gourmand en ressources pour ce genre de configuration. L'installation future d'une distribution Linux, par nature moins exigeante, favoriserait une exploitation plus efficace du matériel de ces ordinateurs accessibles.
